“Faced with this new challenge … our position is very clear. Live-action dramas are the mainstay of high-quality production and should be strongly supported,” said Wang, who heads the department overseeing online audiovisual content.
item.content:encoded:
China’s broadcasting regulator has called for greater support for live-action dramas as the government seeks to steer the booming microdrama industry towards higher-quality production and tighter rights safeguards amid the rapid rise of AI.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has created innovation and production possibilities for microdramas, while also posing challenges over content quality and rights protection, according to Wang Xiaoliang from the National Radio and Television Administration.

“Faced with this new challenge … our position is very clear. Live-action dramas are the mainstay of high-quality production and should be strongly supported,” said Wang, who heads the department overseeing online audiovisual content.

AI has rapidly expanded the scale and efficiency of microdrama production in China while intensifying concerns over copyright and the mounting pressure on human creators.

Wang’s remarks, made at a press conference on September 17, follow a proliferation of formulaic and derivative content as producers race to churn out more dramas in pursuit of hits and profits.

The scale of the shift is striking. Around 430,000 microdramas were released in China in the first eight months of 2026 – as much as 13 times the figure for the whole of last year – with AI dramas accounting for more than 90 per cent of new releases, Wang said.

According to Wang, the regulator will step up its initiative to promote and distribute high-quality microdramas, guiding platforms to create dedicated sections for live-action dramas while providing financial support so that quality productions can find audiences and generate returns.

Microdramas or duanju, meaning short or mini dramas, have exploded in popularity in China in recent years.

Built for mobile screens and short attention spans, the fast-paced, scripted and often melodramatic shows are divided into dozens of episodes, usually in a vertical format, with each lasting just a few minutes.

AI is moving beyond a supporting tool and into almost every stage of production – from story adaptation and scriptwriting to character and scene generation, and onwards to post-production – upending an industry that supports more than 2 million jobs nationwide.

The change has spawned a new format known as AI microdramas – AI-generated animation and live action-style dramas featuring lifelike digital characters that reduce the need for conventional filming.

Companies can now churn out AI-generated content at a pace that was previously impossible, lowering production costs and technical barriers while allowing producers to test more titles in the hope of finding hits.

Johnny Chan, a senior lecturer in information systems at the University of Auckland in New Zealand, said microdrama platforms created a self-reinforcing cycle: the more you watch, the better the algorithm learns what keeps you hooked.

Creators keep refining the cliffhangers and paywalls that work, while the platforms invest more money to make the experience even stickier, he wrote in a paper published in August by the journal Systems Research and Behavioural Science.

Chan wrote that while people would usually get bored eventually by the formula, the ability of AI to rapidly generate endless fresh stories and variations meant the natural “boredom brake” might never fully kick in, causing viewers to keep scrolling for longer.

According to data from the China Netcasting Services Association, more than 275,000 AI microdramas were released online in the first half of 2026, an average of about 1,500 each day.

The explosion in numbers has created a broader regulatory challenge for Chinese authorities: how to encourage this form of cultural production while preventing speed, scale and platform-driven consumption from coming at the expense of quality, originality and rights.

The expanded use of the technology has given rise to various types of regulatory abuse, including content plagiarism and repackaging, as well as AI face-swapping and voice cloning, along with copyright infringement involving online literature.

Many high-profile actors and the general public alike have accused AI microdrama producers of using their likenesses without consent.

The speed at which AI is reshaping the industry has also exposed a growing gap between production capacity and the quality and originality of what gets made.

In the first half of 2026, only 0.48 per cent of new AI microdramas released on the social media platform Douyin surpassed 100 million views, according to industry data provider DataEye.

Lydia Chen, a 30-year-old AI microdrama writer and director producing live action-style dramas for overseas audiences, said the industry’s rush for hits had made copying almost routine.

Platforms and production companies often copied each other’s hits and were used to taking dramas that had already gone viral in China, tweaking the plot and transplanting the story to a foreign setting, she said.

For example, a Chinese tale of a ba zong – internet slang for a bossy president or a powerful, domineering businessman – and a female lead from the countryside can be repackaged as a New York billionaire falling for a woman from rural America.

“You can see the productions becoming increasingly like internet products,” said Chen, who worries that as real-world filming declines, the craft itself will stagnate while AI models will have fewer new examples of real filmmaking to learn from.

“If everyone keeps copying past hits, where will the new ideas of the future come from?”

Chen also noted that some storylines adapted for overseas audiences reproduced traditional and conservative Chinese cultural attitudes towards gender, relationships and family – as they catered to the tastes of the mass-market microdrama audience.

She pointed to the plotline of a “bossy president” falling for a rural woman whose virginity is portrayed as part of her appeal, along with plots idealising women as stay-at-home mothers with multiple children.

“Sometimes I wonder whether this is really the kind of culture we should be exporting,” she said. “To me, some of these ideas feel quite outdated.”

Beijing has responded to the challenges by tightening oversight of both the content and the systems through which it reaches audiences.

The National Radio and Television Administration launched a two-month campaign in June targeting “harmful, lowbrow and pirated” microdrama content.

The campaign focused on material harmful to children as well as sexually suggestive scenes, wealth-flaunting, “distorted” views on marriage and relationships, along with superstitions, violent revenge, sensationalist titles and copyright violations.

Everyone was working themselves to the limit just to … make money.

Shiliu, microdrama director

Wang told the press conference that since the beginning of the year, regulators had removed 68,000 microdramas that violated the rules and guided platforms to punish more than 1,200 accounts.

More than 90 per cent of the problematic content involved AI dramas, he said.

The government has also introduced rules specifically addressing the use of AI in production.

The microdrama development and management measures, which took effect on September 1, require clear labelling for every episode of AI-generated microdramas, along with “respect for original works, copyright protection, fair competition and more orderly industry development”.

Platforms must also regularly review and assess their recommendation algorithms, models and data, give priority to high-quality microdramas and prohibit suggestions that are designed to encourage user indulgence or excessive consumption.

The pressure is also being felt by people working inside the industry, with microdrama actors facing a harsh reality.

Since the beginning of the year, many have said they are struggling to find roles, with some actors taking on part-time work as AI-generated dramas increasingly replace live-action productions.

For those still working in AI microdrama production, greater efficiency has not necessarily meant an easier workload.

Shiliu, a 28-year-old AI microdrama director who joined the industry 2 ½ years ago, said his team was expected to complete five dramas a month, each running for 50 to 70 episodes.

As the team shrank, he found himself taking on multiple roles and working 14 to 16 hours a day, said Shiliu, who asked not to be identified by his real name.

“Because AI is so convenient, bosses only focus on efficiency,” he added. “Everyone was working themselves to the limit just to [fulfil demand] and make money.” The workload eventually took its toll, prompting him to quit the industry.

The state-run Economic Daily urged the industry last month to move away from scale-driven growth in favour of higher quality, more original and professionally produced content.

Familiar formulas were being repeatedly recycled while a flood of lookalike content competed for limited attention, the paper said in an article published on August 13.

“Promotion and computing costs rise, leaving producers caught in a cycle of producing more without earning more,” it noted. “Audiences’ willingness to pay is further eroded while the industry’s reputation is bound to suffer.”

DataEye estimates that the overseas market for Chinese microdramas will exceed US$6 billion in 2026, with AI-generated animated and live-action style dramas accounting for more than US$4 billion.

The netcasting services association said that China’s AI microdrama industry was reaching a turning point, shifting from rapid, loosely regulated expansion towards more disciplined and quality-driven growth.

In Chen’s view, as AI lowers the technical barriers to content creation and more people without a professional background are able to turn their ideas into original works, individually created non-formulaic projects will have a better chance of standing out.

“We must strike a balance between encouraging innovation and upholding safeguards,” Wang said.

“Ultimately, AI is a tool, while people remain the creators. The faster AI dramas develop, the more important it is to ensure content quality.”

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s Forest City wants a rebirth. Scams, crime stand in the way
item.description:
Behind the unmarked door of a shoplot along a quiet commercial stretch of Forest City in Malaysia’s Johor state, four customers sat tapping away, playing slot-style games on tablets.

A stern-looking man stood guard at the entrance, his eyes darting around.

The customers could place bets starting from around 20 ringgit (US$4.89). Instead of handing over cash, they paid for gambling credits using Malaysia’s Touch ’n Go e-wallet. They were then issued tablets from behind the counter with pre-installed slot games.
item.content:encoded:
Behind the unmarked door of a shoplot along a quiet commercial stretch of Forest City in Malaysia’s Johor state, four customers sat tapping away, playing slot-style games on tablets.

A stern-looking man stood guard at the entrance, his eyes darting around.

The customers could place bets starting from around 20 ringgit (US$4.89). Instead of handing over cash, they paid for gambling credits using Malaysia’s Touch ’n Go e-wallet. They were then issued tablets from behind the counter with pre-installed slot games.

“Most of our customers are foreigners. Many play for hours and usually top up their credits a few times,” said the woman manning the counter. Many of them are workers living in Forest City, she said.

The apparent gambling operation observed on a recent visit is among several questionable or controversial activities that have emerged at the sprawling development as it tries to leave its “ghost town” reputation behind.

A US$100 billion megaproject on the southwestern edge of Peninsular Malaysia, Forest City comprises high-rise flats, landed homes and villas interspersed with commercial shop lots.

In July, Johor police arrested 335 people in raids on alleged online scam operations there.

The police seized computers and mobile phones and said the syndicates were involved in schemes including fraudulent cryptocurrency investments and romance scams targeting victims overseas.

That same month, the authorities ordered Network School, a community catering to technology entrepreneurs and digital nomads, to cease operations after finding breaches of licensing conditions and the approved use of its premises.

Residents, property owners and experts said the episodes are a fresh setback for Forest City as it tries to rehabilitate its image and attract investment.

The development has been trying to reinvent itself as an investment destination, anchored by its status as a special financial zone (SFZ).

The SFZ is expected to surpass its 2 billion ringgit investment target this year after attracting more than 250 inquiries from prospective investors including financial institutions, family offices and business services firms.

Criminologist P Sundramoorthy said the scam operations and episodes like Network School have “reputational consequences” for the development.

“It can affect property values, business confidence, tourism, investment decisions and the willingness of people to live and work there,” added Sundramoorthy, who is with Universiti Sains Malaysia.

For some residents, the recent police raids have raised concerns about crime.

Muhammad Aidi Rashid, who rents a two-bedroom flat at Ataraxia Park on the southwestern part of the development, installed closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras outside his door and additional locks after hearing of alleged scam operations in neighbouring blocks.

“I worry for the safety of my wife because she is alone at home when I’m at work,” said Aidi, 33, a technician at nearby Tanjung Pelepas port.

Property agent Aqil Amran, who manages Forest City flats through local firm Ceiloz Realty, said his company has encountered suspected scam operations involving tenants even after the police crackdown.

In one case, a flat owner became suspicious after a tenant’s electricity bill exceeded 1,000 ringgit a month.

“When we went down to the unit to do checks, we saw many tech devices for [alleged] scam activity and we terminated the rental contract and chased the tenant out,” Aqil said, adding that the case was referred to the police.

Sundramoorthy said Forest City’s sizeable number of vacant residential and commercial properties could make it vulnerable to such operations. Based on figures provided by Country Garden in 2023, 9,000 people were living in the development across 28,000 residential units.

“It can provide opportunities for illicit operators to rent premises without immediately attracting attention,” Sundramoorthy said.

Forest City’s location about 10km (6 miles) from the Tuas Second Link and proximity to Singapore could also be attractive to transnational criminal networks, he added, given that the city state is a global air hub.

The July raids underscored the cross-border nature of such operations: police said 332 of the 335 people arrested were foreigners, most of them Chinese nationals, and their targets included people beyond Malaysia’s borders.

Not all of Forest City’s recent controversies have involved alleged criminal activity.

Network School was closed over licensing and premises-use breaches, but Johor-based property consultant Samuel Tan said the episode nevertheless “dealt a blow to Forest City’s public image”.

“In the short term, [both Network School and the scam raids] have naturally heightened buyer and tenant circumspection,” said Tan, CEO of Olive Tree Property Consultants.

“Retail investors and prospective occupiers are understandably cautious, leading to a temporary chilling effect on casual inquiries and rental momentum.”

Before the controversies, Forest City was already seeing weakening prices and thin transaction volumes.

According to property transaction service Datanah, Forest City’s median transaction price between June 2025 and June 2026 was 547 ringgit per sq ft, down 12 per cent from the preceding 12 months.

It recorded only 13 sales between June 2025 and June 2026 in a development with at least 28,000 residential units.

Its latest recorded transaction was on June 18, before the scam raids and Network School saga.

However, experts cautioned that transaction data can lag and there is not enough evidence to attribute the subsequent absence of recorded sales to the controversies.

Forest City’s property market has already struggled for years.

According to Tan, its residential and commercial properties have historically traded at a discount to the wider Johor Bahru market. A three-bedroom Forest City flat is currently valued at around 550,000 ringgit, compared with upwards of 1 million ringgit in Johor Bahru, according to Aqil.

“Because much of its organic residential demand was already subdued, the reputational hit has manifested more as headline noise than a catastrophic collapse in core asset values,” Tan said.

But expectations had been growing that the SFZ and wider Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) could improve Forest City’s fortunes this year, he added.

The development remains firmly a buyer’s market. “On sales especially, demand has been low because there are many owners looking to sell, but there are not many buyers,” Aqil said.

Commercial property owners are feeling another consequence of the recent controversies: greater scrutiny.

Singaporean Justin Ong, 59, who owns a Forest City shoplot for investment, said the management and local authorities have been asking businesses for permits, documentation and proper tenancy agreements following the Network School episode.

Ong is currently renting his shoplot out to a food stall operator on an informal basis and now needs to draw up legal paperwork for submission.

“It makes things cumbersome and businesses will be more wary [of moving operations to Forest City],” he said. “It also adds a layer of administrative work that was previously not required.”

Tan, however, said tighter checks could ultimately benefit Forest City.

“Legitimate financial institutions, family offices and corporate tenants require a well-regulated, clean jurisdiction,” he said.

“Enforcing strict permit protocols signals to the market that the authorities are serious about governance.”

CNA has asked master developer Country Garden about Forest City’s current occupancy rate and whether it has seen recent changes in residential or commercial demand.

CNA has also asked Country Garden and the Johor police about measures to detect and deter illegal activity, and the latter for statistics on crimes reported in Forest City.

Despite the recent bad press, some property owners remain optimistic.

Singaporean investor Tan Kin Lian, who owns two Forest City flats, said the recent episodes have had little impact on residents’ everyday lives.

“Even if these [operations] occupy some of the residential units, they don’t bother the other residents. Now that they are gone, I think life will continue as before,” he said.

He acknowledged that his Forest City properties have declined in value over the years, but believes their relatively low prices and the opportunities created by the SFZ and the JS-SEZ leave room for growth.

“The prices of property in Forest City as compared to that in Singapore are roughly eight times [less], so for Singaporeans, if you’re keen on purchasing a second home and don’t want to pay too much money … it’s an inexpensive option,” he said.

Country Garden has publicly backed the police crackdown and called for a permanent police presence in Forest City.

Munira Mustaffa, executive director of security consultancy Chasseur Group, said this could deter crime but would not address the underlying conditions that allow illicit operations to take root.

Residential areas in Forest City can be accessed by registered owners and tenants using access cards and there are security guards at every entrance. However, Munira noted that this protocol has not been sufficient in deterring scam operations.

The authorities and developers should also improve control of its access and surveillance, engage the community and find legitimate uses for vacant spaces, Munira said.

Sundramoorthy suggested a broader framework involving the police, immigration and customs authorities, the local council and Forest City’s management.

Property owners and agents could also flag warning signs such as unusually high electricity consumption, frequent short-term occupancy or excessive numbers of occupants, he said.

Amid the negative publicity, there have been some promising signs.

Besides the hundreds of investor inquiries about the SFZ through the Invest Malaysia Facilitation Centre Johor, Malaysian entrepreneur Jeff Yew in August reportedly proposed reviving the former Network School site as a technology campus with a “Malaysia first” approach.

“These are indeed substantive reasons for cautious optimism,” Tan said.

Shedding the “ghost town” label will ultimately require legitimate businesses, jobs and people willing to live and work in Forest City for the long term, he added.

For residents such as Aidi, a sense of security is the starting point.

“Hopefully if people feel safe, the right businesses will open and the community will be more vibrant,” he said.

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] China warns Japan over WWII history as business delegation visits Beijing
item.description:
China’s top diplomat Wang Yi and Vice-Premier He Lifeng met Japan’s former foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya in Beijing, marking the highest-ranking Chinese official reception for a Japanese visit in nearly a year.

Analysts, however, cautioned that the high-level reception should not be seen as an opening to a diplomatic thaw. Instead, they viewed the encounter as a calculated exercise by Beijing in selective engagement.

Iwaya arrived in the Chinese capital on Sunday at the head of a 50-member delegation of corporate executives, in a trip aimed at restoring stability to bilateral ties amid heightened friction.
item.content:encoded:
China’s top diplomat Wang Yi and Vice-Premier He Lifeng met Japan’s former foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya in Beijing, marking the highest-ranking Chinese official reception for a Japanese visit in nearly a year.

Analysts, however, cautioned that the high-level reception should not be seen as an opening to a diplomatic thaw. Instead, they viewed the encounter as a calculated exercise by Beijing in selective engagement.

Iwaya arrived in the Chinese capital on Sunday at the head of a 50-member delegation of corporate executives, in a trip aimed at restoring stability to bilateral ties amid heightened friction.

Meeting Iwaya on Monday, Wang warned that bilateral relations were facing a “severe situation” and had “yet to be normalised” ahead of next year’s 55th anniversary of diplomatic ties, according to a read-out from the Chinese foreign ministry.

“A country that challenges its post-war ‘peace constitution’ or attempts to rewrite the history of wartime aggression … cannot face the world, let alone open up a future,” Wang cautioned.

Wang also urged Tokyo to “correct the erroneous words and deeds” of its leadership regarding Taiwan as soon as possible.

Japan must learn from historical lessons on the 80th anniversary of the Tokyo Trials, established by the Allies to try Japanese war criminals after World War II, he added.

Wang is a member of the ruling Communist Party’s elite 24-man Politburo and director of the Central Foreign Affairs Commission office. Iwaya previously travelled to Beijing in December 2024, during his tenure as foreign minister in Shigeru Ishiba’s government.

On Tuesday, Iwaya also met Vice-Premier He at the Great Hall of the People, according to Kyodo News.

The Japanese mission’s arrival in Beijing closely followed last week’s summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump in Washington, where the two leaders hailed the two countries’ wartime alliance against Japan during World War II.

Tokyo has been watching the signs of a stabilising momentum between Beijing and Washington with unease, prompting a 20-minute telephone call on Saturday between Trump and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

Iwaya’s visit, as head of the Japan Association for the Promotion of International Trade, is part of an effort to help break a prolonged bilateral stalemate ignited by Takaichi’s remarks last year about Taiwan.

In November, Takaichi told the Japanese parliament that a Taiwan contingency could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” that could permit Japan to respond as part of collective self-defence.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

The political fallout from Takaichi’s remarks brought official ministerial exchanges between Beijing and Tokyo to an abrupt halt.

On Tuesday, the Chinese foreign ministry issued a scathing rebuke, accusing Tokyo of “abandoning” bilateral diplomatic agreements.

Asked about the “grave difficulties” in relations as the two sides mark 54 years of diplomatic engagement, ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said that Takaichi’s Taiwan remarks “openly challenge China’s national sovereignty and renege on both the original spirit of normalising diplomatic ties and Japan’s political commitments to China”.

Formal channels blocked

The depth of the chill was on display in July when Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi reported a brief interaction with Wang on the sidelines of Asean-related meetings in Manila. Beijing swiftly issued an outright denial, insisting no such contact took place.

With formal channels blocked, Japanese commercial and parliamentary groups have stepped in to keep communications open.

Xu Weijun, an associate research professor at the Institute of Public Policy at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou, said Wang’s reception reflected an upgrade in diplomatic protocol, and that Beijing was beginning to selectively raise its level of engagement with Japan.

China was drawing deliberate distinctions between the Takaichi administration’s security posture and the pragmatic interests of companies, friendship organisations, and moderate factions within the ruling party, he added.

“For Beijing, the primary function of this meeting is not a thaw, but an occasion to reiterate Beijing’s conditions for normalising China-Japan relations.”

Toru Horiuchi, a China-Japan relations expert at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, echoed this view, saying that Iwaya’s visit was a good opportunity for Wang to “reiterate the demand” that Takaichi retract her remarks on Taiwan “if she is serious about promoting better relations”.

The ongoing trade association mission, originally scheduled for June, was delayed following the death of its long-time president, former foreign minister Yohei Kono, who met Chinese Premier Li Qiang in Beijing during a similar trade delegation last year.

During Monday’s talks, Iwaya acknowledged that current ties were “worrying”. He pledged that the association would honour Kono’s legacy and work to steer relations back to the principles of the four foundational China-Japan political documents.

Zhang Yun, a professor of international relations at Nanjing University, said Wang’s remarks reflected a hope that Iwaya could carry forward Kono’s legacy, continue contributing to China-Japan ties, and encourage other friendly Japanese figures and groups to contribute to the advancement of bilateral ties.

He added that Japan’s current strategy – maintaining cordiality with the US while lacking communication with China – risked leaving it diplomatically compromised.

“Out of fear of being bypassed, Takaichi rushes to meet the US beforehand to talk up the China threat, and afterwards hopes to be better informed about what was discussed. This model is unsustainable.”

Rather than worrying about being bypassed, it would be better for Tokyo to contemplate how to actually improve relations with Beijing, Zhang said.

The Wang-Iwaya meeting builds on a succession of Japanese business and legislative delegations to Beijing.

Chinese foreign vice-minister Hua Chunying received an interim four-member mission of the Japanese trade association June, while Lu Kang, a deputy director of the ruling party’s international department, met a bipartisan group of young Japanese parliamentarians in late August.

In mid-September, another delegation of young lawmakers from the Japan-China Friendship Parliamentarians’ Union was received by assistant foreign minister Liu Bin.

Meanwhile, with Takaichi showing no signs of retracting her remarks, Horiuchi expressed doubts that the encounter would pave the way for a bilateral leaders’ meeting at the Apec summit in Shenzhen in November.

“Such a meeting without Japanese concession would be politically risky for Xi,” he observed.

In a recent nationwide survey by Japanese media outlet Asahi Shimbun, 57 per cent of respondents were of the view that Takaichi should make efforts to improve ties with China.

Among supporters of Takaichi’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party, 58 per cent said an improved relationship with China was necessary.

item.title: [SCMP] JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon on how growth can untangle US-China strife, thorny global issues
item.description:
Jamie Dimon’s recent whirlwind visit to Hong Kong followed a similar script: a schedule packed with meetings involving the entrepreneurs and business leaders connecting China with global markets.

But it was his increasingly visible stance on global issues that appeared to extend his career beyond market strategy and financial industry leadership as CEO of JPMorgan Chase.

His preoccupation with economic growth and world affairs drew particular attention in Hong Kong last week, shortly before boarding a private plane and jetting back to Washington for a state dinner at the White House to welcome President Xi Jinping.
item.content:encoded:
Jamie Dimon’s recent whirlwind visit to Hong Kong followed a similar script: a schedule packed with meetings involving the entrepreneurs and business leaders connecting China with global markets.

But it was his increasingly visible stance on global issues that appeared to extend his career beyond market strategy and financial industry leadership as CEO of JPMorgan Chase.

His preoccupation with economic growth and world affairs drew particular attention in Hong Kong last week, shortly before boarding a private plane and jetting back to Washington for a state dinner at the White House to welcome President Xi Jinping.

“My biggest concern is geopolitics – world peace,” Dimon, the longest-serving CEO of a major Wall Street bank, told the South China Morning Post on Wednesday.

His emphasis on global economic growth also echoed US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s views and the decades-old philosophy of China’s leaders, including Xi, that “development is of overriding importance”, laying the groundwork for China-US trade talks that were recently held at the bank’s New York headquarters.

Markets: prepared, not scared

Global markets have endured repeated panics this year, driven by surging oil prices, rising US Treasury yields, the Federal Reserve’s interest rate increase to fight inflation, and soaring debt – factors that have fuelled concerns about another major financial crisis.

The world economy and global markets are also grappling with geopolitical conflicts – including the Ukraine war that began in February 2022 and the US-Israeli war on Iran that just crossed the seven-month mark – as well as persistent trade tensions between China and the United States, and increasingly louder warnings about artificial intelligence.

You always need to be prepared. Because if you look at economic history, the market isn’t always right

Jamie Dimon, JPMorgan Chase

Dimon, whose signature financial strategy – a combination of low debt-to-equity ratios, high liquidity and large cash reserves known as the “fortress balance sheet” – often resurfaces in times of crisis, expressed concerns about “sticky inflation” in the US that has persistently hovered above 2 per cent for more than five years.

“If you are in business, you should be thinking about whether you can handle higher rates, higher credit spreads,” Dimon said, speaking from the JPMorgan office in Central district, the bustling financial centre of Hong Kong. “Just as a normal course, how do you manage risk?

“You always need to be prepared. Because if you look at economic history, the market isn’t always right.”

However, Dimon noted that current conditions were “different” from the 2008 crisis, driven by excessive speculation on financial instruments backed by mortgage loans. Banks, the backbone of the financial system, are currently not overleveraged and have much more liquidity, while American corporations and consumers are not overleveraged either, he observed.

“The highest debt is sovereign debt. So, governments need to be financially responsible. And hopefully, they will be before a crisis forces the issue.”

Government data shows that US sovereign debt has doubled in a decade, topping US$40 trillion last month. The cost of capital is jumping as oil, grain and other shocks resonate, with the yield on benchmark 10-year Treasury bills at 5.234 per cent as of Monday afternoon, the highest in over 20 years.

Although Dimon maintains that the US remains a permanent investment destination, and that its economy is still “hugely powerful”, talk of diversification and de-dollarisation has accelerated. This is accompanied by Beijing’s growing efforts to lure international investors and push for global use of the yuan.

Many central banks and institutional investors also altered their strategies since March, reducing US bill holdings, purchasing gold, and diversifying away from the US dollar. Even Japan, an American ally, trimmed a total of US$135.4 billion in US Treasuries from March to July – a 10.9 per cent drop.

While acknowledging that stock prices were quite high and credit spreads were quite low, Dimon said people should never be surprised about market fluctuations.

“The markets aren’t always right,” he said. “Things are very good today, and there’s reason for some happiness.”

China-US: growth is the antidote

In the days preceding Dimon’s Hong Kong visit, JPMorgan Chase’s New York headquarters hosted a round of trade talks between Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US negotiators, including Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

Underpinning these discussions was Dimon’s notion of government-business collaboration and a shared focus on growth, which he mentioned repeatedly in his interview, considering them vital to tackling many global problems.

“Secretary Bessent mentioned the other day – which is dead right – growth is the best antidote,” Dimon said. “So, countries should be thinking about what policies will maximise growth.

“You see a lot of politicians always speaking about raising taxes or cuts. Before you do that, why don’t we all fix the things that are inhibiting growth? Growth is good for all the citizens, not just good for business. When you have growth, you have more employment, more wages.”

Such thoughts are strikingly similar to Beijing’s stance, which views economic growth as the foundation for well-being, social stability and debt resolution.

“My view is: engagement is the best thing – at multiple levels and consistently,” Dimon said of bilateral relations, highlighting the importance of high-level meetings. “I’m glad that they are meeting and engaging. I think it’s important to hear each other out.”

The latest talks yielded some results – Beijing and Washington agreed to extend a nearly year-long trade truce for two more months, until January 10. And for the first time, the two sides discussed AI, according to their official statements.

Ahead of Thursday’s state dinner, in their speeches to officials and top American business executives – including Dimon – presidents Xi and Trump praised past friendships and downplayed current rivalries.

While competition persists over AI, biotech and many other sectors, Dimon identified potential areas for cooperation between the two superpowers, such as working towards world peace, nuclear non-proliferation and counterterrorism.

“We should keep reminding ourselves that China wants to lift up its people, America wants to lift up its people,” he noted.

On AI: roll up your sleeves

Despite market debate over the rapid deployment of AI, Dimon argued that the progression of the technology would move from machine learning to large language models and then, eventually, artificial general intelligence – thinking that matches or surpasses human cognitive ability.

Dimon said the technology would transform lives and industries. “AI is real. We’ve been doing it for 13 years,” he said, citing its customer-oriented use to prevent fraud and to facilitate marketing, prospecting, design and call centres.

“It’ll save lives, prevent car accidents and develop drugs and composite materials. If you have kids, they may live to 100. We may not have some of the diseases we were all afflicted with. So, yeah, you should applaud that.”

As any technology carries potential downsides, he called for broad government actions to redeploy or retrain workers, but remained broadly positive on the technology’s future gains.

“I think AI’s productivity benefits are still some way down the road. We don’t yet know exactly when they’ll be fully realised, but I believe it will be a huge plus.”

It does create real vulnerabilities and drives the need for increased spending on cyber protection, Dimon said, mentioning possible threats through open-source code and internet access.

“Again, my attitude is: roll up your sleeves, get to work,” he said. “It’s not like we’re ignoring it.

“It may cause some disruption. But I don’t spend much time debating it. My job is to do a better job for my customers. We use computers, we use technology, and we’ll use AI the same way. The north star is serving customers better. AI is just another tool to help us do that.”

If you make it ideological – Democrats against Republicans – and make moral statements about what works, then you lose sight of the facts

Jamie Dimon, JPMorgan Chase

The next chapter

After spending more than two decades at the helm of one of the world’s most valuable banks, Dimon still maintains a sharp sense of global market risks and business deals. Increasingly, however, the 70-year-old multibillionaire has set his sights beyond bank profits and personal wealth towards some of the “big issues” facing the world.

“You know, the war in Ukraine is terrible, and it’s causing a lot of issues in Europe now,” he said. “And it’s getting worse. Obviously, that affects oil and grain prices. And now you have the war in the Middle East – Iran – and that’s also affecting oil.”

He is also keen on advising younger generations to develop critical-thinking skills and a strong work ethic.

“You can’t have critical thinking without deep curiosity and an open mind and asking yourself, ‘Does this really work that way?’” he said, adding: “And learn, learn, learn, learn, learn.”

When asked about any personal goals he may have, Dimon, who is already a business icon respected across Wall Street and Washington, started laughing. “It’s getting a little late for me to have personal-development goals,” he quipped, before quickly adding: “I want to be smarter and better and help people, and help lift up the world.”

At a JPMorgan town hall meeting immediately before the interview, the CEO touched on global chaos. Later, with the SCMP, he expressed pride in the “vibrant, healthy, innovative” US economy while also flagging some of his home country’s shortcomings.

“In America, there are things we have done really badly,” Dimon said. “And whether it’s Democrat or Republican policies, we’ve done a bad job for inner cities; our schools aren’t graduating enough kids. The only way you fix that is to acknowledge it, and then you can attack it.

“But, if you make it ideological – Democrats against Republicans – and make moral statements about what works, then you lose sight of the facts. Sometimes our policies don’t work, and we have to be willing to say they don’t work.”

Regarding questions about how he would help change the situation, Dimon shied away from personal pursuits, focusing instead on his company’s strategy.

“I tell people that at JPMorgan, we hope we help cities, states, schools, hospitals, companies, governments,” he said. “We bank all the development banks, we bank the United States government.

“And that’s what we’re there for.”

item.title: [SCMP] China-US dialogue will ease concerns, but competition will remain, Paul Chan says
item.description:
Competition between China and the US will persist, but increased dialogue between the two economic superpowers will provide greater global certainty and ease geopolitical concerns, with Hong Kong positioned to play a unique role, the city’s financial secretary has told the South China Morning Post.

In a wide-ranging interview, Paul Chan Mo-po said more communication and dialogue between the two nations would be “good for everyone”, as Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart, Donald Trump, wrapped up a historic summit in Washington last Friday, local time.

Chan also shed light on his expectations for the coming Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting, which takes place in Hong Kong on October 20 and 21, and will bring together hundreds of global leaders in the city. He anticipated that visiting political leaders would see Hong Kong and its vibrancy with their own eyes.
item.content:encoded:
Competition between China and the US will persist, but increased dialogue between the two economic superpowers will provide greater global certainty and ease geopolitical concerns, with Hong Kong positioned to play a unique role, the city’s financial secretary has told the South China Morning Post.

In a wide-ranging interview, Paul Chan Mo-po said more communication and dialogue between the two nations would be “good for everyone”, as Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart, Donald Trump, wrapped up a historic summit in Washington last Friday, local time.

Chan also shed light on his expectations for the coming Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting, which takes place in Hong Kong on October 20 and 21, and will bring together hundreds of global leaders in the city. He anticipated that visiting political leaders would see Hong Kong and its vibrancy with their own eyes.

The event will take place ahead of this year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, which will be held in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19.

Chan said Beijing supported Hong Kong’s hosting of the finance ministers’ meeting, as the central government wanted to elevate the city’s profile as a global financial centre.

With the current Hong Kong administration having less than a year before the new term, Chan was also asked about his future plans.

He said that officials had worked hard under the “capable leadership” of the chief executive.

“At the moment, we are concentrating our energy and efforts on pushing forward the various policy agendas and initiatives. So this will remain our priority focus,” he said.

Chan also touched on the three-day China-US summit last week, which saw tensions ease and a trade truce extended by two months until January.

“We do believe more communication and dialogue are good for everyone,” he said.

“And this is important, not just for the two countries or Hong Kong but for the global community, providing more certainty and removing some of the geopolitical concerns.”

But Chan anticipated China-US competition would persist in areas such as financial services, adding that Hong Kong would strengthen its status as an international financial centre to further attract foreign capital and connect mainland China to the rest of the world.

“So for us, under the ‘one country, two systems’ arrangement, we play the unique role of connecting the mainland with the rest of the world,” he said.

Despite geopolitical tensions, Chan said Hong Kong had become a destination for investors to park their money over the past two years.

Net inflows into Hong Kong-domiciled funds stood at HK$118 billion (US$15 billion) in the first five months of 2026 following a 118 per cent year-on-year surge to HK$357 billion in 2025.

Total assets under management also grew by 20 per cent to HK$42.2 trillion in 2025 from a year earlier, with most coming from outside the mainland and Hong Kong.

“Capital investors really vote for Hong Kong with their feet,” Chan said.

He said China-US relations were bound to have “ups and downs,” and Hong Kong’s top priority was to ensure financial stability while taking advantage of development opportunities.

At the core of Hong Kong’s financial development was the city’s stock market, which had recorded robust trading volumes and a larger number of new listings in recent years, Chan said.

The stock market is also set to benefit from a series of measures floated in the policy address and the city’s first five-year plan, which were both released earlier this month.

Proceeds raised in initial public offerings (IPOs) in the first eight months of 2026 were 153 per cent higher than in the same period last year, at HK$342.4 billion.

The eight-month total has already surpassed last year’s IPO proceeds of HK$286.9 billion. The 2025 figure already represented growth of 226 per cent year on year.

“So all these indicate that we remain focused on doing the right thing, enhancing our competitiveness, improving our listing regime, for example, expanding the possibility of attracting additional liquidity. Then, quality companies will come,” Chan said.

“We are taking this window to further build, further strengthen our equities market. But at the same time, develop FIC [fixed income and currencies], develop commodities, trading and gold. This takes time, but we move on; we’ll invest in it.”

Chan also highlighted plans to expand the global use of the yuan.

While Hong Kong currently served as “a firewall” for the wider nation’s financial security, the city also planned to drum up yuan product offerings to raise liquidity and act as a testing bed for yuan products, the finance chief said.

Hong Kong has the world’s biggest pool of yuan outside the mainland, sitting at about 1.1 trillion yuan (US$163 billion).

“Our idea is that if we want to gather more liquidity, gather more investors coming to our market, then we need to enrich the product offering. We need to build the necessary infrastructure. We also need to provide the liquidity that is needed,” Chan said.

He added that several central banks were planning to increase their yuan holdings in an effort to pursue diversification, which would generate more investment opportunities.

Asked whether the push risked diminishing the role of the Hong Kong dollar – which is pegged to the US dollar – amid so-called de-dollarisation, Chan said “no”, and remained adamant that the linked exchange rate system, which debuted in 1983, had worked well and was an anchor for the city’s currency regime.

“This is very core to us in terms of strength,” he said. “We have no intention at all to change this. This is very fundamental.”

As the city is fast-tracking its push into gold trading and storage and a commodity ecosystem, Chan said the government planned to launch a “gold connect scheme” to facilitate more cross-border trade.

Hong Kong and the mainland already operate various connect schemes that grant global financial institutions access to mainland stock and bond markets through the city.

“The competition is keen,” Chan said, referring to competition between gold markets in Hong Kong, London and Singapore.

“But our advantage is the strong hinterland. China is a major user of gold. The Shanghai gold exchange is very keen and has a strong market, but it needs to have an international connection. Hong Kong can play the role.”

item.title: [SCMP] How Hong Kong’s old businesses are adapting to new times
item.description:
In the second of a two-part series on Hong Kong’s economic transformation, Ambrose Li and Wynna Wong profile three established enterprises that have rejuvenated their brands and reinvented their businesses. Read part one here.

Late into the night, Hong Kong football fans in their twenties, thirties and forties sat in Lin Heung Lau restaurant on Wellington Street watching World Cup matches over dim sum rather than pints at a sports bar.

The historic restaurant, traditionally associated with elderly morning-tea regulars, extended its operating hours during the World Cup in the summer, drawing on the expertise of chairman Rocky Wong Hei-yan, a nightlife industry veteran behind once-bustling Lan Kwai Fong venues such as Club No 9, Club Beijing and Magnum.
item.content:encoded:
In the second of a two-part series on Hong Kong’s economic transformation, Ambrose Li and Wynna Wong profile three established enterprises that have rejuvenated their brands and reinvented their businesses. Read part one here.

Late into the night, Hong Kong football fans in their twenties, thirties and forties sat in Lin Heung Lau restaurant on Wellington Street watching World Cup matches over dim sum rather than pints at a sports bar.

The historic restaurant, traditionally associated with elderly morning-tea regulars, extended its operating hours during the World Cup in the summer, drawing on the expertise of chairman Rocky Wong Hei-yan, a nightlife industry veteran behind once-bustling Lan Kwai Fong venues such as Club No 9, Club Beijing and Magnum.

“On that occasion, we were not calculating money only,” he said. “We were looking at brand-building and opening another channel through which we could find customers.”

The century-old Lin Heung Lau brand has been rejuvenated with new marketing and business strategies since 2024, when its management was revamped amid a decline in the tradition of people going out for dim sum.

The restaurant has hosted a series of “dim sum raves”, taking social media by storm with its tea-infused cocktails and electronic music paired with steaming towers of pork buns and shrimp dumplings.

Lin Heung Lau’s football and rave nights illustrate one solution to a question confronting established Hong Kong businesses: how can they follow changing customer habits and find new sources of revenue without discarding the identity that made them valuable?

Interviews with family-business scholars and companies ranging from a traditional dried-seafood retailer to a long-established transport operator suggest that transformation does not follow a single formula.

It can involve creating new experiences, rebuilding unglamorous back-end systems, adopting artificial intelligence (AI) or allowing a younger generation to experiment.

Winnie Peng Qian, director of the Roger King Centre for Asian Family Business and Family Office at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, cautioned against assuming that every established company needed to pursue rapid or radical innovation.

“People always think you need to innovate, need to react fast,” she said.

“But you see a lot of century-old family businesses in Japan. They’re very small, fewer than 10 people, just a store doing the same thing.”

Such companies could instead innovate gradually, she said, while adapting their traditions to remain relevant to the environment they faced.

Nightlife meets yum cha

Wong saw an opportunity in Lin Heung Lau when it closed during the Covid-19 pandemic, believing its brand had untapped potential despite the difficult environment facing Hong Kong’s catering industry.

Wong, the restaurant’s chairman and primary investor, was granted the perpetual right to use the Lin Heung Lau brand in Hong Kong rather than ownership of the underlying intellectual property.

He had known the restaurant for more than 25 years, having regularly visited for morning tea after finishing work at his clubs.

“I was very familiar with the brand and knew its strengths and weaknesses,” he said.

“It was not simply a matter of me taking over and benefiting from a powerful brand. It had already closed. I was setting out with it again and that was a major challenge.”

Despite the obvious differences between running nightclubs and operating a traditional Chinese dim sum restaurant frequented in the morning, Wong said both businesses ultimately depended on the same thing: management.

“If you manage people properly and they naturally follow the organisation’s instructions, you can succeed in even selling salted crispy peanuts,” he said.

“But if management is poor and everything becomes too personalised, it will destroy the entire management system.”

Since taking over the operation, Wong has sought to preserve Lin Heung Lau’s traditional yum cha atmosphere and handmade dim sum while reaching beyond the predominantly elderly clientele historically associated with such restaurants.

“We are not taking a single direction and targeting only the silver-haired market,” he said.

“We are adding new elements to attract different customers – middle-aged people, young people and even children.”

Wong did not provide figures for the investment, sales or footfall generated by the football screenings but said they were profitable and attracted a largely younger crowd.

He argued that their greater value was promotional, estimating that the equivalent publicity would have cost millions of dollars to reproduce through conventional advertising.

Lin Heung Lau had opened or substantially redeveloped five outlets in just over two years, Wong said.

Its latest restaurant occupies about 13,000 sq ft at the airport, while other locations include Mong Kok and Tsim Sha Tsui.

About 95 per cent of the menu is shared among its restaurants, but each has distinctive dishes or design features.

Wong said operators could no longer simply open their doors and assume customers would arrive.

“You have to catch the trend,” he said. “A business has to change. If it does not change, customers will not come.”

More affordable ready-to-eat abalone

At On Kee Dry Seafood, founded in the 1930s, transformation has been less visible to customers but no less extensive.

The family business has made traditionally expensive dried gourmet seafood such as abalone more affordable by creating mouth-sized snacks that proved popular with younger shoppers at the city’s signature food fair.

As preparing and cooking items like abalone, sea cucumber and duck’s feet can take a couple of days, the group has diversified into ready-to-eat offerings such as frozen and pre-cooked seafood, as well as ready-to-consume soups and desserts.

“Our ready-to-eat products have proved to be very popular because they cater to the busy lives of Hongkongers who have a preference for convenience,” said Henry Poon, 27, the fourth generation of the family business.

“About two years ago, we developed an individually wrapped abalone snack that could be consumed right away, designed for when people are feeling peckish.”

The company was still relying heavily on handwritten notes and fax machines as recently as five years ago.

Its six retail stores also handled about 1,000 online orders a day, forcing employees to pack e-commerce purchases on crowded shop floors while serving customers.

“After all, we are a very traditional company,” Poon said.

“Even five years ago, we weren’t a particularly digital company, relying heavily on handwritten notes and using fax.”

Over the past two years, Poon has led a digital transformation, describing it as a “timely catch-up” with the market amid the growing popularity of e-commerce.

An enterprise resource planning system consolidates orders placed through On Kee’s website and third-party platforms, streamlining stocking, packing and delivery.

The company can process about 1,800 online orders a day, an 80 per cent increase from before.

On Kee also introduced a point-of-sale system capable of handling more complex promotions, such as a 10 per cent discount on a second item and 20 per cent off a third.

AI has reduced the time needed to calculate how much stock should be taken to exhibitions – important events for the business – from several days to minutes.

“We’d typically look at the trend from the past three to four times we took part, as well as our previous orders,” Poon said.

“The press of a button generates you a very good forecast table.”

The transition remains unfinished. Poon estimated that it could take another three to four years for all the new systems to operate smoothly.

‘Standing still means falling behind’

At Kwoon Chung Bus Holdings, one of Hong Kong’s largest franchised and non-franchised bus operators, the changes in its business and strategies have been sweeping.

Founded in 1948 as a car-cleaning service by the late entrepreneur Wong Kwoon-chung, the firm, which earned 82 per cent more year on year in net profit in 2025-26, at HK$268.4 million, is aiming high – literally.

It made a breakthrough in the 1990s, taking over bus operations on Lantau Island and coach companies that catered to hotel and tour group operators.

A landmark change took place in 2023, when third-generation family members Timothy and James Wong pushed through a new venture, KC Smart Mobility, by investing in electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft (eVTOL), alongside autonomous vehicles, drones and ride-hailing services.

In August, the company worked with mainland Chinese autonomous aerial vehicle manufacturer EHang and tech hub Cyberport to bring an eVTOL to Hong Kong, culminating in the city’s first successful demonstration flight of an unmanned heavy-duty aircraft.

“These are medium- to long-term investments that will not be profitable soon,” said Newton Ng, business development director of KC Smart Mobility.

“Standing still means falling behind. If we remain the same as we are today, there will not be expansion.”

The company plans to buy 30 eVTOLs from EHang for more than HK$70 million, although the aircraft remain at the testing stage. Charging can take more than an hour for a flight lasting about 20 minutes, while Hong Kong does not yet have regulations for commercial operations.

Ng said acting early could help the company capture market share.

“If government policies are also directed towards newer modes of transport, the earlier we act, the sooner we can possibly capture a larger market share,” he added.

Kwoon Chung has already encountered changing customer behaviour in its traditional passenger-transport operation.

Its existing limousine customers previously had to telephone the company to reserve vehicles, but increasingly wanted to arrange their journeys online.

The operator responded by partnering with ride-hailing company Uber to launch Uber Elite, a premium service combining Kwoon Chung’s vehicles, full-time chauffeurs and local operating experience with the US-based firm’s widely used booking platform and customer reach.

The service, Uber’s first of its kind outside the United States, offers pre-booked rides in Mercedes-Benz vehicles for groups of up to six passengers, targeting C-suite executives and business travellers.

Customers can book between two hours and 90 days in advance. Ng said demand during the first month was strong enough that the company could not always accommodate requests made at shorter notice.

“It’s a changing consumption pattern,” he said. “If we do not develop a model that caters to the trend, some customers will of course drift away over time.

“We’ll have to follow the habits of the younger generation and have a presence where they book their commutes.”

Space for the next generation

Kwoon Chung’s decision to place its experimental businesses in a subsidiary headed by third-generation members reflects one way family companies can pursue transformation without immediately disrupting their core operations.

Jeremy Cheng Chi-yeung, an adjunct associate professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s business school, said such companies could initially be slower to adopt the latest trends but often committed substantial resources once they decided to proceed.

One model, he said, was to allow the rising generation to establish a smaller agile unit, the kind created by Kwoon Chung.

“The rising generation will build their own team, a small unit, which is meant to be agile, and they can lead faster changes,” Cheng said.

“Once they are successful with that particular experiment, they tend to cross-fertilise that in different units in the business itself.”

Victoria Wang, a professor at the same institution, said slower adoption did not necessarily mean a family business lacked the ability to survive.

“They change slowly to go faster,” she said. “Tradition is legacy, purpose and identity. They very much want to make sure their identity continues.”

Transformation, however, does not always require radical innovation.

“If a tradition remains relevant, it is valuable,” Peng of Hong Kong University of Science and Technology said. “But if the family is static, very traditional and refuses to change, of course it cannot survive in the long term.”

For Lin Heung Lau, this has meant continuing to serve handmade dim sum while challenging assumptions about who should eat it and when.

At On Kee, the dried seafood remains, but the handwritten orders and fax machines are disappearing.

For Kwoon Chung, the coaches continue operating while the next generation explores modes of transport extending from smartphones to the skies.

Peng said the family businesses that endured tended to share two deeper characteristics – a long-term outlook and a sense of responsibility towards society.

Their experience of surviving economic and political upheavals helped them look beyond immediate difficulties, while a broader purpose gave future generations a reason to continue beyond preserving their own wealth.

“Sometimes you need to stick to who you are and your family values,” Peng said. “The first thing that stands out is a long-term perspective. The other is altruism. You need to care about society.”

item.title: [SCMP] How Hong Kong firms are future-proofing business in challenging times
item.description:
Hong Kong’s economic transformation is at a critical juncture, and the private sector must adapt along with it, as Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has noted. In the first of a two-part series, Ambrose Li and Wynna Wong examine the forces driving change among established enterprises.

Before visiting a vendor in mainland China’s Jiangsu province, a salesman from Hong Kong bottling giant Swire Coca-Cola can now use a mobile phone to see which drinks customers in the neighbourhood are most likely to buy.

The recommendations, generated by artificial intelligence (AI) and based on factors such as the area’s consumer profiles, turn information held across the firm’s operations into what Swire Coca-Cola calls “suggested orders”.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong’s economic transformation is at a critical juncture, and the private sector must adapt along with it, as Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has noted. In the first of a two-part series, Ambrose Li and Wynna Wong examine the forces driving change among established enterprises.

Before visiting a vendor in mainland China’s Jiangsu province, a salesman from Hong Kong bottling giant Swire Coca-Cola can now use a mobile phone to see which drinks customers in the neighbourhood are most likely to buy.

The recommendations, generated by artificial intelligence (AI) and based on factors such as the area’s consumer profiles, turn information held across the firm’s operations into what Swire Coca-Cola calls “suggested orders”.

Swire Coca-Cola’s mainland plants are also using AI-powered robots that can make decisions and adapt to changing operating conditions as they pick and sort heavy, shrink-wrapped loads of drinks from pallets at high speed – a breakthrough in the labour-intensive industry.

These were some of the cutting-edge technologies Swire Coca-Cola had piloted on the mainland to transform its business, while looking to scale them to other provinces and even to Southeast Asia through and in Hong Kong, chief executive Karen So told the South China Morning Post.

“Due to our geographic coverage, we’re exposed to many geopolitical risk factors which we have to manage,” So said, adding that one of the most obvious recent impacts had been rising raw material costs, including those of aluminium and sugar.

“We have to stay very vigilant. Overall, we’ve had to make sure our brand and operations stay relevant in the past few decades to mitigate our external risks,” she said.

The company, which started business in 1965, is now the fifth-largest Coca-Cola bottling partner in the world.

As Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan sets out the blueprint for the city’s economic upgrade, businesses like Swire Coca-Cola are working to future-proof themselves against geopolitical headwinds and compete in an increasingly challenging environment.

City leader John Lee Ka-chiu last week urged Hongkongers and businesses to adopt a long-term vision, saying enterprises had to stay competitive even as the government rolled out measures to cultivate new growth drivers for the city.

“While the government works hard, business operators need to think of ways themselves because, after all, this is a highly competitive society,” he said.

An uneven economic recovery

Hong Kong’s economy has powered ahead in recent months, with merchandise exports hitting record highs on the back of overseas demand for AI-related products.

The government has consequently upgraded its 2026 full-year economic forecast to 3.5 per cent to 4.5 per cent, from an earlier projection of 2.5 per cent to 3.5 per cent.

Despite the stronger overall performance, streets are dotted with shuttered shops while retailers and restaurant operators continue to struggle.

In a high-profile warning, real estate advocacy group Momentum 107 said the sharp decline in shop values in recent years had rapidly eroded the pool of available capital, undermining confidence in investment and consumption.

It noted that shop prices had fallen by more than 40 per cent from their 2018 peak, while the overall vacancy rate had reached a 40-year high of 12.5 per cent in late 2025.

The retail and food and catering sectors have also been hit by the continuing trend of Hongkongers crossing the border to spend their leisure time and money.

Meanwhile, inflation has been on the rise.

After war broke out in the Middle East on February 28 and triggered a global oil crisis, the city’s inflation rate jumped from 1.1 per cent year on year in January to 1.7 per cent in February and has hovered above 1.7 per cent as of August.

‘Companies are forced to change’

Vera Yuen Wing-han, a lecturer in economics at the University of Hong Kong, noted that looking solely at struggling high-street shops overlooked the bigger picture, as high-value sectors such as professional services and finance continued to drive the economy.

However, consumer-facing sectors are undergoing structural shifts as mainland competitors catch up and local consumers spend more elsewhere.

“Hong Kong’s local consumption market is relatively small, so retail and catering suffer from northbound spending and changing habits,” Yuen said.

“Conversely, high-end services, technology and finance are holding up strong. But across the board, businesses rely heavily on international trade and foreign clients, leaving them exposed to global geopolitical frictions.”

Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of Our Hong Kong Foundation think tank and executive director of its Public Policy Institute, said companies faced three main challenges – high operating costs, disruption to global supply chains and geopolitical risks and barriers to technological transformation caused by shortages of funding and skilled workers.

He said Hong Kong’s rents, wages and logistics costs were relatively high, placing pressure on companies’ cash flow, while AI was creating another divide.

Large corporations often had money to invest but struggled to integrate new technology with legacy systems and secure cooperation across departments. While smaller businesses could be more agile, they frequently lacked capital and technical expertise.

Shui cited a Productivity Council survey suggesting about 90 per cent of responding companies intended to increase their use of AI.

The problem, he said, was not a lack of interest but uncertainty over how to turn that intention into practical transformation.

“Many people think of technology or AI as something that can help companies reduce costs and save money,” he said.

“But what is more important is how they can use AI to upgrade and transform themselves, innovate their business models or open up new markets.”

Hong Kong appeared to be performing relatively well in adoption.

Shui cited a survey by Hong Kong University of Science and Technology that found that about 72 to 73 per cent of respondents used AI at work daily or weekly, compared with a global average of around 30 per cent.

Another study put AI adoption among Hong Kong firms at about 41 per cent compared with less than 30 per cent in Singapore, he said.

But widespread use did not mean that companies were applying the technology effectively.

Shui said the ideal outcome was “human-machine collaboration,” in which AI performed repetitive research, data processing and preliminary analysis, while employees devoted more time to decision-making and setting the company’s direction.

“If your competitor is already doing this while you are making very limited use of AI, it will be very difficult to catch up,” he said. “This is something that many companies and employees will need to learn.”

Yuen echoed this view, saying that true AI adoption required a complete overhaul of corporate workflows rather than superficial daily tasks.

“The real productivity boost from AI isn’t just using it to write an email or draft a report – it comes when companies reshape their entire workflow from top to bottom,” Yuen said, comparing the current transition with earlier technological shifts such as the invention of the printing press, personal computers and the internet.

“Legacy businesses face a dilemma because changing established processes while serving existing clients carries risk. It could take eight to 10 years for industries to truly integrate AI into their bottom line,” she added.

Shui said Hong Kong needed a coherent AI development blueprint and stronger cooperation between the government, universities and industry.

The planned Hong Kong Artificial Intelligence Research and Development Institute could provide a platform through which companies test applications, academics provide expertise and the government coordinates resources.

Transform, transform and transform

In Swire Coca-Cola’s case, So said transformation was robust across mindsets, strategies and business practices, pointing out that the 61-year-old business had in recent years embarked on a sweeping revolution.

“The future of our business lies in moving from reactive, manual operations towards proactive, data-driven ecosystems that respond to modern consumer habits,” she said.

The company’s “suggested order” system in Jiangsu province produced 20 per cent higher monthly sales volumes during a year-long pilot that ended earlier this year.

She said it would be gradually rolled out to other markets, but conceded that it would take time for staff to get used to the AI tool.

“Our employees need time to adapt to tools designed to change how they make decisions and approach customers,” So said.

The project forms a key part of a transformation at Swire Coca-Cola, whose franchise bottling and distribution operations reach more than 940 million consumers across the western United States, 11 mainland Chinese provinces and Shanghai, Hong Kong, Taiwan and four Southeast Asian countries.

The company’s transformation became more complicated as it expanded beyond its two main markets – Greater China and the US – into Southeast Asia.

It acquired Coca-Cola bottling businesses in Cambodia in 2022, in Vietnam in 2023 and in Thailand and Laos the following year.

“When we acquired businesses from local operators of Coca-Cola in Southeast Asia, they had their respective enterprise resource planning systems,” So said. “We faced a challenge but also an opportunity to form a consistent operating system.”

Even basic data definitions varied among markets, including what constituted a home market sales channel and how revenue was calculated.

The company had to clean up and standardise the information before it could perform reliable analysis to improve the decision-making process and help salespeople make more targeted calls.

“The data alignment will take two to three years,” So said.

Another tool transferred from the mainland to Southeast Asia was the smart cooler – a drinks refrigerator which customers unlock using an electronic payment code.

Scales and cameras identify which drinks are removed and customers are charged accordingly.

“The solution adapts technology and operating concepts proven in mainland China to the Hong Kong market, which combines digital payment and product-recognition capabilities to offer a seamless cashless purchasing experience,” So said.

In Hong Kong, the group has deployed 120 coolers across a broad mix of locations including sports and entertainment venues, workplaces, residential communities, educational institutions and industrial settings.

So said the company aimed to replace traditional vending machines with these smart coolers.

Swire Coca-Cola’s regional expansion has also helped Chinese suppliers go global.

Baosteel, China’s biggest listed steelmaker and a supplier of aluminium cans to Swire Coca-Cola on the mainland, established a factory in Ho Chi Minh City as the company expanded its presence there.

“It is a win-win situation – we have a stable supply of aluminium cans while Baosteel expands out of China for the first time,” So said.

“Hong Kong is where our ambition is set and our global system is run. A purpose-built solution developed in the Chinese mainland, and now ready to scale across the global markets we serve, shows the super value-added, superconnector role Hong Kong is positioned to play.”

Shui said Hong Kong could also turn the technological rivalry between China and the West into an opportunity by developing a “dual-model” environment in which businesses could access systems from both sides.

“Hong Kong has always been a bridge connecting mainland China with the rest of the world,” he said. “If both systems can be used here, companies coming to Hong Kong can choose the tools that best meet their needs or potentially use both.”

To raise efficiency and reduce manpower, Swire Coca-Cola has teamed up with a Hangzhou-based tech company, Seth Robotics, to develop its own AI-powered solution for its bottling plant in Zhengzhou, Henan province.

The plants boasts the world’s first AI-powered intelligent picking-and-sorting robot, according to So.

Capable of picking 600 pallets of drinks an hour with 100 per cent accuracy in executing orders, and handling loads as heavy as 40kg, the robot works at twice the speed of manual labour.

“Normally after the first hour of work, workers need to take a rest. The robotic deployment will enhance efficiency and minimise any work-related injuries of workers, too,” So said.

She added that Swire Coca-Cola’s technology development also showed what a Hong Kong-headquartered company could contribute to embodied intelligence.

Against the backdrop of these operational investments, the group reported solid financial results for the first half of the year – net profit rose 5.35 per cent to HK$846 million (US$107.9 million) while revenue increased 8.36 per cent to HK$23.3 billion, compared with the same period last year.

Yet, as economist Vera Yuen noted, the rising cost of uncertainty left businesses with little choice but to adapt their models or risk falling behind.

Ultimately, she said, the question was no longer simply whether companies adopted new technology, but whether they could restructure their core operations to deliver genuine value to consumers.

item.title: [SCMP] Thailand has had enough of foreign tourists behaving badly
item.description:
At a zoo a short drive south of Bangkok, Charoon Youngprapakorn has spent a lifetime taking the pulse of Thailand’s tourism industry from an unlikely vantage point: the open jaws of crocodiles.

Handlers at his Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm & Zoo have long thrilled onlookers by coaxing tips from the audience and carefully placing the money into the mouths of animals capable of taking off an entire hand.

The crocodiles at this open-air, fan-cooled throwback to 1980s showmanship still take their tips at the end of every show. But these days, the notes are almost all Thai baht, handed over by Thai visitors. The busloads of overseas tour groups have largely disappeared.
item.content:encoded:
At a zoo a short drive south of Bangkok, Charoon Youngprapakorn has spent a lifetime taking the pulse of Thailand’s tourism industry from an unlikely vantage point: the open jaws of crocodiles.

Handlers at his Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm & Zoo have long thrilled onlookers by coaxing tips from the audience and carefully placing the money into the mouths of animals capable of taking off an entire hand.

The crocodiles at this open-air, fan-cooled throwback to 1980s showmanship still take their tips at the end of every show. But these days, the notes are almost all Thai baht, handed over by Thai visitors. The busloads of overseas tour groups have largely disappeared.

Tourism accounts for roughly one-fifth of the Thai economy, from the five-star resorts of Phuket and Koh Samui to the jet-ski operators and massage parlours of Pattaya.

The industry has never been immune to external shocks, however – and Charoon, who is in his seventies, has felt each one register at the ticket office of a business his father founded nearly 90 years ago to sell crocodile leather to tourists.

Sars, bird flu and the global financial crisis of 2007-08 all took their toll on visitor numbers, interspersed with boom years as mass tourism from China, an emerging Russian middle class and increasingly affluent Southeast Asian travellers pushed up attendance.

Then came a three-year closure amid the Covid-19 pandemic and – as with so much else in this world – nothing at Charoon’s zoo has been quite the same since.

“We used to have maybe 100, 200 big tour buses a day,” he told This Week in Asia. “But they stopped and we had to close because of the lockdown.”

By the time the business was able to reopen, tourism trends had changed. “People stopped travelling as big groups and instead they came as FITs,” Charoon said, using the industry acronym for “free, independent tourists”.
