China vastly outproduces the United States in advanced industrial goods, such as EVs, solar power, wind power, advanced nuclear power, batteries, low-cost 5G and many other key technologies. China incorporates AI into advanced manufacturing processes more than the US.

Many European leaders feel that if they stick with the US against China and Russia, then maybe the Western hegemony will continue. This is delusional in my view, but nonetheless creates a lot of noise, friction and risks of conflict. None of it is a coherent strategy, however.

The US has no strategy to stay ahead of China. In fact, the US can’t succeed in that. We hear a lot of US sabre-rattling against China, Russia and the Brics countries. This is all dangerous. I think the heated rhetoric by itself can become a self-fulfilling prophecy of war. There are a lot of ignorant people in the US political leadership, and I worry very much about their naivety and delusions.

This, in my view, is essentially the origin of the “trade war”. The US decided during 2010-2015 that China is now a threat to US primacy. The US has tried a lot of things to block China’s continued rise, including: a military build-up in East Asia; export restrictions on hi-tech goods, especially advanced chips; economic sanctions on key Chinese companies; investment restrictions by US companies, and ownership restrictions on Chinese companies in the US; high tariffs against China’s exports; and others. But none of this stops China’s rise. China’s development results from hard work, ingenuity, high rates of saving, high rates of investment, very effective long-term planning and a very skilled, very entrepreneurial generation of business leaders, especially young business leaders. Those fundamental strengths continue despite America’s anti-China policies.

Trump’s policies are accelerating the move of top scientists to China. My overall view is that Trump is creating a lot of noise and some real dangers, but with no real strategy and no likelihood of success in holding back China’s rise. That’s a good thing. The rest of the world benefits from China’s economic success, including the US.

In your last Open Questions interview, you talked about “the deep state”, a complex vested interest group in industry, the military and other spheres. Does the deep state want military conflict with China? And do foreign governments – such as China and Russia – believe in the existence of a deep state, which many dismiss as a conspiracy theory?

The deep state means the permanent security system of the United States and its partners in Europe and in East Asia, including Japan, Korea and other places where the US has military bases and other security institutions. It includes the military, the CIA, the military contractors and the politicians who serve the military-industrial complex.

Does such a deep state exist? Yes. The US has around 750 overseas military bases and many of them are in East Asia. The US has many major military contractors with hundreds of billions of dollars of annual business with the US government. The US fights overt and covert wars pretty much non-stop, some of which are proxy wars (in which the US arms and funds Ukraine to fight Russia), and sometimes open conflicts with heavy US involvement, as in Iraq and Afghanistan. The US has the extensive global networks of the CIA and other intelligence and covert institutions. All of this constitutes the deep state. Presidents come and go but the underlying foreign policy is consistent and set largely out of view of the public, and without any reference to public opinion.

When Obama replaced [US president George] Bush Jnr, and Trump replaced Obama, and Biden replaced Trump, and Trump replaced Biden, on the PR level there was alleged to be change, but in fact very little policy change occurred. For example, how much foreign policy change was there when Obama succeeded Bush Jnr? Very little. Obama launched many wars, just as Bush had done. Obama’s team actively participated in the coup in Ukraine in 2014 that set the path for the Ukraine war. Obama went to war against Libya. Obama gave the CIA the order to overthrow the Syrian government. All of this was a continuation of the policies of the Bush period.

Trump continued most of the same policies. Trump continued to build up the Ukraine military. The Trump administration dismissed the Minsk 2 agreement that could have prevented the escalation of the Ukraine war. There was not any major change between Obama and Trump.

When Biden came in, their claim again was that there would be a new foreign policy, but it didn’t happen. What did Biden do with China? He continued Trump’s tariffs. He continued Trump’s hardline rhetoric. Biden absurdly divided the world between the so-called democracies and autocracies, which was an incredibly naive approach, as I said from the beginning.

Biden escalated the Ukraine war. He rejected all attempts at peace negotiations, including the Istanbul process that could have ended the Ukraine war in 2022. When it came to the Middle East, Biden was complicit in Israel’s ongoing genocide. So, Biden did very little different from Bush Jnr, Obama and Trump before him.

Now, Trump has returned. What’s the real difference? Trump is different in style, in his unpredictability, nastiness, self-dealing and endless flip-flops. Yet, in terms of basic foreign policy, Trump is not very different from his predecessors.

This is the sense in which deep state means an ongoing consistency of the US security institutions that run American foreign policy. American foreign policy is not determined by public opinion, or Congress, or even the president in large part. Look instead to the CIA, the Pentagon and the other parts of the deep state.

The deep state also determines the politics of US vassal states. Many observers consider Japan to be a US-occupied country, with Japan’s foreign policy basically subservient to the US. One can say the same about many other countries. Where the US has military bases, the host countries tend to act like occupied countries, bending their own foreign policy to that of the US.

The US deep state is profoundly arrogant, thinking that it can have its way around the world. The US deep state thinks that it can dominate not only US allies, which is typically true, but also China, Russia, Iran, Brazil and others. When US arrogance becomes too strong, we face the danger of disaster. That’s what happened in Ukraine. The US thought that it could push Russia around to its will. It could not. The attempt to assert US power in Ukraine led to war.

US arrogance deeply worries me. Trump certainly is not a strategist. There’s no long-term plan. The US is playing poker, but not very well or wisely. It often bluffs. The whole approach can lead to war.

China is now drafting its economic policies for the next five years. You have advised many countries before. What is your advice to China in the face of this tension and the global tariff war?

My main advice to China is look to the non-Western world for the strongest partnerships in trade, investment and diplomacy, at least for a while. The US-led alliance (US, Canada, Britain, EU, Japan, Korea, Australia and New Zealand) is around 13 per cent of the world population. China is another 17 per cent. The remaining 70 per cent of the world – in Asia, Africa and Latin America – wants good and strong economic and diplomatic relations with China. That 70 per cent of the world population wants to modernise, and China provides the means for those countries to achieve rapid growth and modernisation. China is key to the global energy transition to zero-carbon energy, especially in the markets outside the US and Europe.

The emerging and developing economies of Asia, Africa and Latin America will be the markets for China’s rapid export growth in the years ahead. China will play a vital global role in these economies in building advanced green and digital economies, using Chinese cutting-edge technologies.

This will be a great win-win for the world because China will continue to grow rapidly while also empowering rapid growth throughout the emerging and developing nations. Sadly, in my view, the US will not play much of a role in that modernisation in the next generation. The US under Trump is withdrawing from green technologies, and from global responsibility.

The US cannot compete with China for the global renewable energy market. The US can’t compete with China for the global digital connectivity market. The US can’t compete with China in fast rail or low-carbon ocean shipping. In all these sectors, Trump is handing world trade and leadership over to China.

Regarding the US markets, China should certainly attempt to make a suitable trade deal with the US but China should not fret too much either way. The US is already a small part of China’s exports – perhaps around 10-12 per cent. That share of China’s exports will most likely decline further.

I hope that I’m wrong and that the US regains some sense and rejoins the global effort for green transformation and re-establishes normal trade with China. Yet, I don’t think that’s going to happen for many years, and I don’t think that China can, or should, base its policies on a return to normal trade with the US.

More specifically, I advocate expanding [China’s] Belt and Road Initiative. I advocate that China should deal with regional groups, including Asean, the African Union, the Arab League and the Community of Latin America and Caribbean States (CELAC). China’s relations with these regional groups can be very strategic, as the regional groups can, and should, spur the interconnectivity of infrastructure among all the members of the group. For China, it will be easier to interact with regional plans rather than one country at a time.

In fact, no individual state in Asean, or the Middle East, or Latin America can modernise on its own without strong links with its neighbours through trade, finance and infrastructure. With Asean, for example, there really is the need for an Asean-wide energy system, not separate energy systems for Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia etc. These countries need an interconnected power grid, and China will play a key role in achieving an Asean-wide grid. Therefore, China-Asean diplomacy is strongly win-win.

I also believe that Hong Kong will have a huge and indeed unique leadership role in the global transformation. Hong Kong is vital for China’s growing links with Asean, the African Union, and beyond. The Greater Bay Area (GBA) combines Hong Kong’s world-class leadership in international finance, higher education and global management, with Shenzhen’s leadership in cutting-edge technologies, and the advanced manufacturing of Dongguan, Guangzhou and other GBA cities.

Put these strengths together, and the GBA becomes the beating heart of the global green transformation, in zero-carbon energy, robotics, AI-based manufacturing, digital connectivity and much more. All of this will help to fuel China’s – and Hong Kong’s – rapid growth for the next generation.

This year marks the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II. How is the post-war world order changing and what will the new world order look like?

There are three scenarios.

One is that we create a truly multilateral world. For that, we need a United Nations 2.0. We need an upgraded international system in which all the major powers agree to invest in the international rule of law and peaceful resolution of conflicts. This will require an upgrade of the UN Security Council, and UN institutions more generally.

I’d love to see a major UN campus in China, to help lead the green and digital transformation worldwide. I’d love to see China and India working together closely at the UN, including towards India’s seat in the UN Security Council. I’d like China to support the African Union to play a much larger role in global governance. I’d like to see China, Japan and Korea end the geopolitical divisions and form a strong alliance in northeast Asia. Most importantly in this scenario, the US and Europe accept the rising role of China, India and the rest of the non-Western world.

A second scenario is that the Western world hunkers down. It goes protectionist and the US tries to divide the world into camps. This is perhaps the likely US strategy, but I think it is significantly worse for the US and the rest of the world than the first scenario. I think the US absolutely should abandon the idea of building competing camps.

The third scenario is that we don’t have a global system at all, but rather increasing chaos from climate change, wars and geopolitical conflicts. This dire scenario is a real possibility.

Any of these three trajectories is possible. We should be aiming for the first. The United States and Europe should take a deep breath, sigh and welcome the non-Western world into a shared global leadership. The major powers – the US, Europe, Russia, China, India – should agree to prevent confrontations.

The US should stop Nato enlargement and should stop providing armaments to Taiwan. Such actions are provocative and lead to great-power conflicts that threaten the safety and security of the whole world.

In short, the West should stop asking “Who is Number One?” and instead ask, “How can the whole world work together for the global common good?” In my experience, China, Russia and other nations would enthusiastically back such a global, cooperative effort that is based on mutual respect and mutual security.

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines struggles to fill 20,000 teaching jobs: ‘we are facing a learning crisis’
item.description:
The Philippines has 20,000 teaching vacancies to fill, a budget hearing has revealed, with sector insiders warning that the gap signals a mounting education crisis.

Those in the industry are calling for transparency in the teacher hiring process, including clear figures on budget allocation and positions filled amid problems of mismatch and improper targeting of job applicants.

At a House of Representatives plenary session last week, Antonio Tinio from the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) grilled officials over the lack of urgency, arguing that thousands of qualified applicants in the registry were still waiting for jobs.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines has 20,000 teaching vacancies to fill, a budget hearing has revealed, with sector insiders warning that the gap signals a mounting education crisis.

Those in the industry are calling for transparency in the teacher hiring process, including clear figures on budget allocation and positions filled amid problems of mismatch and improper targeting of job applicants.

At a House of Representatives plenary session last week, Antonio Tinio from the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) grilled officials over the lack of urgency, arguing that thousands of qualified applicants in the registry were still waiting for jobs.

This Week in Asia has contacted the country’s Department of Education for comment. At the session, it said that some positions were “hard to fill” because they lacked qualified candidates for certain specialised roles.

The department is tipped to receive some 976 billion pesos (US$15.6 billion) under the 2027 budget, with more than 31 billion pesos allocated for filling teaching vacancies and 12 billion pesos to promote 135,000 existing teachers.

“The cost of delay falls on learners and on teachers already in service. We are facing a learning crisis; we cannot close learning gaps while leaving needed teaching positions vacant and asking existing teachers to carry additional classes and tasks,” said Ruby Bernardo, ACT chairwoman.

Bernardo urged the government to provide teachers with concrete support rather than another promise of positions that went unfilled, citing a World Bank report that found 91 per cent of Filipinos aged 10 could not read or understand age-appropriate texts.

“That makes timely hiring especially urgent,” she said.

Hanibal Camua, executive director of Philippine Business for Education, a non-profit advocacy group, said the hiring gap reflected both a workforce alignment problem and a problem with teacher quality.

“Some education graduates pursue opportunities abroad, where teaching can offer better compensation,” Camua said. “Others move to private schools or to sectors such as [outsourcing] and virtual assistance, which can offer competitive entry-level salaries and, in some cases, less administrative burden.”

Figures from the Second Congressional Commission on Education, a national body created by the government to evaluate the country’s education system, show that the pass rate for teacher qualification exams between 2009 and 2023 was 33 per cent for junior school teachers and 40 per cent for secondary school teachers.

“That tells us that we have to address both ends of the pipeline. We need to make teaching a career that can attract and retain good people, while also ensuring that the institutions preparing our teachers are producing graduates who meet the standards required in today’s classrooms,” Camua said.

Teachers at state-funded schools in the Philippines begin with a monthly salary of 31,705 pesos (US$506), yet they are often saddled with non-academic tasks and overcrowded classrooms.

But simply reducing the issue to quality “puts the burden of explanation on applicants without examining the system that recruits and retains them”, Bernardo said.

“The education department should publish how many qualified applicants there are for each vacancy, where applicants withdraw, and which subjects and locations are hardest to staff. That would show whether the obstacle is a shortage of qualified applicants, a mismatch in deployment, slow hiring, or poor retention,” she said.

Mismatched expectations

The enduring shortfall raises questions about the broader state of education in the Philippines, especially after the department received a “historic” budget of 1.015 trillion pesos in 2026 – marking the first time the country has met the Unesco benchmark for education spending, which requires allocating 4-6 per cent of gross domestic product or 15-20 per cent of public spending to the sector.

“We should acknowledge those allocations while asking a more important question: what has actually reached schools? How many teachers have been appointed and deployed? How many classrooms and materials are in use? Have class sizes, workloads and learning outcomes improved?” Bernardo said.

The word “historic” did not match many teachers’ daily experiences due to a long history of chronic underfunding, she said, calling for “transparent reporting on actual spending and results” and measuring commitments against completed hiring and facilities.

For Wilhelm Sheila A. Pineda, a top-tier educator known as a “master teacher” at the San Fernando South Central Integrated School in La Union province, Education Secretary Sonny Angara’s admission that budget cuts left his department unable to hire new teachers for next year is deeply concerning.

“On one hand, we have qualified teachers waiting for opportunities, while on the other hand, our schools continue to experience shortages,” she said.

“This is frustrating because teacher shortages are felt directly in schools. When there are not enough teachers, the workload does not simply disappear – it is absorbed by the teachers who are already there.”

Salve V. Calderon, a fellow master teacher in Bataan province, said the teacher shortage was especially alarming, with educators facing heavy levels of burnout as student populations and the number of schools continued to grow.

“Workload, burnout, compensation and too many non-teaching requirements are major factors. For me, teachers entered the profession to teach, but they are becoming exhausted by work that does not directly contribute to student learning,” Calderon said.

Actual school experiences also showed teachers constantly having to adjust to new programmes, requirements and changes being introduced, Pineda pointed out.

“Teachers are generally willing to contribute,” she said. “The concern is whether every new programme comes with adequate preparation, coordination, orientation, time and resources.”

Calderon, who teaches English, said technology was creating another set of problems for teachers: “In many ways it has created more documentation, submissions, reports, programmes and sudden tasks.”

The Philippines should not simply fill the 20,000 positions without addressing the underlying learning crisis, according to Camua of Philippine Business for Education, adding that it is equally important to provide teachers with the right support to help students learn effectively.

Bernardo suggested that education officials set a public hiring timetable, identify bottlenecks in every division, speed up appointments and deployment, and regularly report on vacancies actually filled.

“The goal is not merely to clear a vacancy count,” Bernardo said. “It is to ensure every learner has a teacher with the time, resources and support to teach well.”

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asia’s falling literacy: can cash and gamification fix it?
item.description:
Singaporean Najwa Alhabshi remembers spending her teenage years poring over literary classics such as F. Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby and George Orwell’s 1984. The books introduced her to ideologies, philosophies and the American dream while expanding her vocabulary.

But as work commitments grew, the pages of her books started yellowing. Finding time to read became harder, and her smartphone screen eventually took over. “I think I just fell out of reading,” the 35-year-old tutor said. “Life got in the way – it was work, a lack of time, and eventually, the phone screen.”

Across Southeast Asia, governments are stepping in to get people reading again. With screens reshaping how people consume information, concerns are growing over falling literacy rates, shortened attention spans and declining critical-thinking capabilities.
item.content:encoded:
Singaporean Najwa Alhabshi remembers spending her teenage years poring over literary classics such as F. Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby and George Orwell’s 1984. The books introduced her to ideologies, philosophies and the American dream while expanding her vocabulary.

But as work commitments grew, the pages of her books started yellowing. Finding time to read became harder, and her smartphone screen eventually took over. “I think I just fell out of reading,” the 35-year-old tutor said. “Life got in the way – it was work, a lack of time, and eventually, the phone screen.”

Across Southeast Asia, governments are stepping in to get people reading again. With screens reshaping how people consume information, concerns are growing over falling literacy rates, shortened attention spans and declining critical-thinking capabilities.

Singapore is one of those taking action. Earlier this month, the city state launched an initiative that pays citizens to read.

Under the scheme, users earn 20 virtual coins for every reading session lasting at least 15 minutes, logged via a government website. Recording one session a day for 50 days accumulates 1,000 coins, which can be exchanged for S$1 (US$0.78).

Developing a reading habit helped build the capacity to navigate an “increasingly complex” information landscape, said Melissa Tam, CEO of Singapore’s National Library Board.

“This is especially important for our children, who are growing up in a world where technological changes often outpace our ability to adapt,” Tam said.

The scheme relies on gamification to build daily reading streaks, according to Loh Chin Ee, an associate professor at the National Institute of Education.

“Sometimes it is helpful to have a little nudge or challenge to get one started,” Loh said. “Matching individuals to the right kinds of books they are interested in would be a good way to encourage people to get started on reading.”

But attaching financial value to reading could backfire by stripping away its intrinsic joy, said Ng Siew Chin, an early childhood lecturer at the Singapore University of Social Sciences.

She suggested using social media platforms to promote excerpts from books and texts. “The attention of readers is gained through bite-sized posts like these to intrigue their curiosity to potentially access the full article or book,” she said.

Rise of doomscrolling

Singapore is not alone in trying to revive reading habits. Other Southeast Asian countries have rolled out measures to raise literacy rates.

In July, Indonesia launched a countrywide distribution of more than 5.5 million books to primary and secondary schools. Jakarta said the 40.7 billion rupiah (US$2.27 million) project reflected its commitment to ensuring children have direct access to reading materials.

Neighbouring Malaysia is handing out 100 ringgit (US$24) vouchers to more than 2.2 million students to spend on its national digital book marketplace. The programme, which runs from July to October, expands on a 2024 initiative to include students across a wider age range.

At the launch of the Kuala Lumpur International Book Fair in May, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said books and education had to remain a priority despite fiscal constraints.

“If we want this country to become a truly civilised nation with a strong culture of knowledge and broad intellectual capacity, we must encourage reading,” he said.

He added that reading culture had become a problem, with many preferring to consume information from social media. “That is why I urge parents to monitor their children and ensure they start reading from tonight onwards.”

Researchers and experts share those concerns, particularly as artificial intelligence tools become increasingly widespread. A global study by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development released last month found that students are now reading at a level previously expected of students a year younger.

The study also found a decline in skills such as evaluating information, making connections across multiple sources and critical thinking, alongside an increase in hasty, superficial reading.

Overreliance on AI threatened the development of essential reading skills, said Portia Padilla, an associate professor in the College of Education at the University of the Philippines Diliman.

“If you do not think while reading, you are not truly reading,” Padilla said, adding that readers should use AI to challenge their assumptions rather than form judgments.

For Najwa, the battle begins at home. To instil a love for reading in her five-year-old son, she limits his screen time to just 15 minutes a month. Her son now reaches for short illustrated books when he wakes up, often pausing during walks to read words on road signs and pamphlets.

“Beyond just expanding vocabulary, reading does so much more for our children,” the tutor said. “Books are portals to a different world – through them, imagination lives.”

Finding community

While government intervention and incentives can nudge people to pick up a book, experts say they do little to build intrinsic motivation and cultivate lifelong habits.

Extra reading time did not automatically guarantee deeper understanding or critical thought, Padilla said. “Access and motivation are a starting point, not the finish line. True comprehension requires active engagement with the text. It goes beyond coins and vouchers.”

Reading should be viewed as a commitment rather than a short-term campaign, she added, urging support across the whole ecosystem – including public policy, language development programmes and supportive environments at home and in the community.

Providing dedicated spaces for reading – such as quiet public zones or after-hours book clubs – could offer another way to build momentum, said Loh from the National Institute of Education, pointing out that “silent book clubs” were gaining popularity in Singapore.

Community book groups have sprouted up across the region, meeting in places such as a park in Manila and an art cafe in Penang to a wine bar in Singapore.

On the second floor of a deli in Bangkok, two dozen people gather once a month to share their latest reads. Participants at the Books at Banter book club are free to bring any book they choose – a deliberate rule aimed at making the club accessible and less intimidating, said founder Kunatai Khunmuang.

“People don’t have to feel that they have to read classics, non-fiction or whatever book happens to be popular to be considered a ‘real reader’,” said Kunatai, who started the club in May.

“Someone else can interpret a story completely differently from you, notice something you missed or connect it to an experience you’ve never had. Reading is naturally a solitary activity, but a book club gives you somewhere for all those thoughts to go.”

item.title: [SCMP] Trump denies US arms offer to Xi but says China would ‘probably like to buy’ them
item.description:
US President Donald Trump denied discussing US arms sales with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping during their summit last week, though he noted that China would “probably like to buy” them.

Trump was asked by reporters on Monday about his recent meeting with Xi and US ambassador to China David Perdue’s remarks in an interview with Fox News a day earlier that Trump had proposed selling weapons to China.

“I never heard of that one,” Trump said. “I am gonna have to ask him. You mean we’re going to sell? No, they’d probably like to buy it because we do make better equipment than that, so maybe it’s a good idea. But we didn’t discuss.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump denied discussing US arms sales with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping during their summit last week, though he noted that China would “probably like to buy” them.

Trump was asked by reporters on Monday about his recent meeting with Xi and US ambassador to China David Perdue’s remarks in an interview with Fox News a day earlier that Trump had proposed selling weapons to China.

“I never heard of that one,” Trump said. “I am gonna have to ask him. You mean we’re going to sell? No, they’d probably like to buy it because we do make better equipment than that, so maybe it’s a good idea. But we didn’t discuss.

“He may have been talking about Taiwan,” Trump added, referring to Perdue’s interview.

Trump also spoke highly of his meeting with Xi, saying that out of a score of 10, “I would rate it at 12. Very respectful, very good, great meeting”.

Earlier, the US State Department ruled out any plan to sell arms to China, after Perdue said at the weekend that Trump had asked Xi whether Beijing wanted to buy American weapons.

There was no such “offer or plan”, the State Department said in an email response to the South China Morning Post on Monday.

Speaking to Fox News after the Chinese leader’s state visit to Washington, Perdue said: “[Trump] actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.”

Perdue did not say when Trump raised the question, what prompted it, or how Xi responded.

The State Department official in his response to the SCMP highlighted long-standing US policy. “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China,” the official wrote.

The swift clarification came as Perdue’s apparent disclosure ricocheted among Asia specialists, who noted the extraordinary contradiction between Trump reportedly raising the prospect of arming Beijing and his administration continuing to hold up a roughly US$14 billion weapons package for Taiwan.

Washington has for decades treated Beijing as a strategic rival, restricting military technology exports, strengthening security partnerships across the Indo-Pacific region and building its capacity to deter a potential conflict.

Beijing did not directly address the matter at Monday’s regular press briefing.

When asked about Perdue’s account of the exchange, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said only that China “consistently strengthens its national defence capabilities based on its own needs and remains committed to safeguarding world peace and stability”.

The US has not sold conventional weapons to Beijing for more than three decades and has spent much of that time building its military posture around deterring the Chinese military, not supplying it.

In the 1980s, the Reagan administration briefly expanded military cooperation with Beijing as both countries sought to counter the Soviet Union. Washington approved several military-related sales, including the roughly US$550 million Peace Pearl programme involving US avionics for Chinese J-8 fighter aircraft.

That relationship ended after the Tiananmen Square crackdown in June 1989. Then-president George H.W. Bush suspended military sales and exchanges with Beijing and Congress later codified restrictions on the transfer of US defence articles to the Chinese military.

US law permits a presidential waiver in the national interest, but no administration has used that authority to restore a conventional US arms pipeline to Beijing.

The strategic landscape has since changed dramatically. Successive US administrations have spent billions preparing for a possible military confrontation with Beijing and supplying weapons to Taiwan to help deter a potential attack.

Meanwhile, China has built the world’s largest navy by number of ships and rapidly expanded its missile, air and nuclear capabilities. The Pentagon has identified Beijing as the United States’ most consequential long-term strategic challenge.

That makes Perdue’s remarks particularly striking.

Zack Cooper, an Asia security fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and former Pentagon and White House official, wrote on social media that he was “underwhelmed when it looked like the big deliverable both sides actually announced at this Trump-Xi summit was the lease of two pandas”.

“But it never occurred to me that an American president might offer to sell American weapons to China,” he added.

Cooper later stressed that the remark came directly from Perdue, not an anonymous source.

“This wasn’t a leak, it was a comment by President Trump’s ambassador to China on Fox,” he wrote. “I’ll take him at his word until I’m told otherwise.”

He also highlighted the contrast with the stalled weapons deal with Taipei, saying it was “shocking that Trump is resisting authorising arms sales to Taiwan but at the same time offering them to China”.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Trump has previously signalled a willingness to use arms sales to Taiwan as diplomatic leverage with Beijing.

After meeting Xi in Beijing in May, Trump said he was holding the US$14 billion package “in abeyance”, calling it “a very good negotiating chip” and saying the decision “depends on China”.

Perdue offered no timetable on the sales in the interview aired on Sunday. “There are continuing conversations about other sales,” he said, adding that Trump “has a schedule of his own”.

Perdue also said that Trump and Xi discuss American arms sales to Taiwan “every time they meet” – a comment that drew attention to Washington’s pledge to Taipei in the 1982 Six Assurances not to consult Beijing on the issue.

Ryan Hass, who handled China policy at the National Security Council and now heads the China Centre at Brookings, said the disclosure would rattle US partners in Asia.

“Trump’s offer to sell weapons to China will be unsettling to American partners at the pointy edge of China’s spear,” Hass wrote on social media.

Taiwan’s de facto envoy in Washington, Alexander Yui Tah-ray, said on the CBS programme Face the Nation on Sunday that last week’s summit statements listed no Taiwan deliverable, even though Beijing called the issue “foundational”.

“It was foundational, but there was no reaction from the US side,” Yui said. On the stalled package, he added: “The United States has been our main supplier of weapons to Taiwan. We hope that we can get that weapons package in as soon as possible.”

Peace through strength, he argued, was “the best way to avoid any conflict”, adding that deterrence rested on the idea that Beijing would not attack if the island itself were strong.

The episode has left a simpler question hanging over Washington’s China policy debate: was Trump seriously floating the idea, or was he joking with Xi? And if it was a joke, why did Perdue feel it was worth mentioning on national television?

Denis Simon of the Quincy Institute said the key distinction was between Trump raising the idea and making a concrete arms offer.

“There is no evidence that Trump made a concrete offer for China to purchase a specific US weapons package, nor that China accepted or seriously negotiated such a deal,” Simon said.

“It appears to have been a rhetorical/negotiating manoeuvre rather than an actual arms-sales proposal.”

But this did not make the remark insignificant, Simon said, particularly given its connection to Taiwan.

“Trump’s logic appears to have been something like: ‘You object to our selling weapons to Taiwan. But America sells weapons to many countries. Why shouldn’t China be able to buy American weapons if it wants them?’,” he said.

“That is an intentionally provocative way of reframing the Taiwan issue.”

Simon said the episode pointed to a more transactional approach to Taiwan arms sales, in which the weapons package itself becomes leverage in the broader relationship between Washington and Beijing.

In his formulation, Trump’s approach is closer to this: Taiwan needs weapons, Beijing objects, so let us see what Beijing is willing to give in return.

He noted that Trump might also have been using the hypothetical sale to “tout the appeal of American military hardware”, suggesting that even Beijing might see US weapons as preferable to its own.

Scott Kennedy of the Centre for Strategic and International Studies had a more immediate reaction. “Wow! Not sure why Amb Perdue decided it’d be wise to share that comment with the world,” he said on social media.

Bonnie Glaser, who heads the Indo-Pacific programme at the German Marshall Fund, focused on another part of Perdue’s interview.

The ambassador said Trump and Xi discussed US arms sales to Taiwan “every time they meet” and that Washington “doesn’t support Taiwan independence and doesn’t support coercion”.

“Shouldn’t the US oppose coercion?” Glaser wrote.

Bill Bishop, author of the Sinocism newsletter, offered a different interpretation, calling it “just more Trump joking” while adding that he was “not sure why Perdue mentioned it”.

item.title: [SCMP] Scott Kennedy on China’s ‘slow tech dragon’ and 2 more Xi-Trump meetings
item.description:
Scott Kennedy is a senior adviser and trustee chair in Chinese business and economics at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. His areas of focus include China’s hi-tech drive, US-China relations and global economic governance.

Open Questions first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

How would you characterise the outcomes of the China-US summit compared to expectations going in? Is it largely a continuation of that track or do you see it moving the relationship a few steps forward?
item.content:encoded:
Scott Kennedy is a senior adviser and trustee chair in Chinese business and economics at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. His areas of focus include China’s hi-tech drive, US-China relations and global economic governance.

Open Questions first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

How would you characterise the outcomes of the China-US summit compared to expectations going in? Is it largely a continuation of that track or do you see it moving the relationship a few steps forward?

The summit continued the pathway set in May and, in terms of specific deliverables, met the low expectations that observers had going in. Most notably, they agreed to extend the economic ceasefire on tariffs and export controls, but only for two months, to January 10, 2027.

That will provide a little reassurance to financial markets and to businesses that trade and invest between the US and China and elsewhere. But that’s still just four months away, and as we get closer to January, if nothing is resolved by November or December, people will get more worried.

On the trade front, they agreed to cut tariffs on US$30 billion of products on each side and encourage trade of specific non-sensitive products, such as agricultural goods, fish and seafood, medical devices, and consumer goods.

They also agreed, according to the US side, to refer to artificial intelligence as “super intelligence” and create a notification system of serious incidents. [Chinese President] Xi [Jinping] emphasised the importance of keeping AI under human control in his opening remarks, views that were reaffirmed in subsequent Chinese statements.

The other significant outcome mentioned by both sides is their common commitment that Iran should not be permitted to have a nuclear weapon and that no one should be able to charge tolls for international waterways. Another point of emphasis during the discussions, though not mentioned in the fact sheets, was Taiwan, with Beijing trying to further pocket what they saw as adjustments in US language and actions coming out of the summit in Beijing.

But the summit’s deliverables were still quite modest. As with Beijing, there was much more pomp than substance.

US officials have said Beijing proposed a “bigger deal”. What do you think China means by that? And what would Beijing want in return?

We would need an explanation from either side, but one could hypothesise that the Chinese were looking to extend the commercial ceasefire to the end of the Trump administration, and in return would potentially offer larger and longer commitments to purchase American products, whether that would be commercial aircraft, agriculture, energy, or other goods. And they might have an offer to expand the amount of goods on each side that were tariffed at normal or below-normal levels.

China could also have proposed an investment arrangement with specific deals identified, pilots, or a mechanism to evaluate new Chinese investment. All of that could have been part of a larger deal. US President [Donald] Trump said that coming out of one of the meetings [with Xi], the two sides had made “tremendous strides”, but based on the fact sheets, no such big deal was reached.

You mentioned what China might want out of the summit. Are the two leaders just building momentum for when they meet again, say at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) or Group of 20 (G20) summits later this year to announce a bigger deal?

China may be holding back on some things for Apec and the G20, and President Trump may also be. But I think China would have been totally satisfied if they had made a big deal in Washington. China’s goal is to keep the current relationship in this form, for as long as they can. The kinds of things they are likely offering to keep the trade peace are not giant sacrifices to China. None would require China to make any adjustments whatsoever in economic strategy or industrial policy. No attention is being paid to the thorny issue of imbalances. So, China would be happy to make this kind of deal any time, whether it had been in Washington or on the sidelines of the Apec leaders’ meeting or the G20 summit.

So what limited the two sides from announcing a bigger deal in Washington?

At a minimum, it was the US side and their concerns about obstacles obtaining rare earths. Over the past year, China’s rare earth exports globally have risen but they have fallen towards the US by about 25 per cent and dropped dramatically with regard to Japan. The US wants to ensure that the flow of rare earths returns to normal levels in line with China’s commitment.

The US was also looking for support on Iran. Although we typically think of Iran as a security issue, a different bucket than on economics, we know that both sides in certain circumstances will connect different issues. It’s possible – although we don’t know – that the US made extending the ceasefire for a longer period conditional on greater Chinese support with regard to Iran, not just in word but in deed.

Both leaders have played up their personal rapport while deliverables look thin. Can a relationship this consequential rest on the chemistry between two leaders? Is that enough and is it sustainable?

People talk about a G2. The US and China do not have what is conventionally considered a G2, a group of two very powerful countries who collaborate in managing global affairs. That is not what they are doing.

President Trump’s version of a G2, based on his language and behaviour, is probably more like “two guys”. In his mind, he and Xi have a very strong personal relationship that is the key source of stable ties. It’s reflected in his praise of Xi, why he went out to personally greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews, had an extravagant welcoming ceremony and state dinner, and showed him the White House’s helipad and the East Wing construction site.

We have not seen Xi explicitly frame their relationship in personal terms. In his various remarks, he is respectful of President Trump and expresses appreciation for his graciousness, but it is clear he is representing the Communist Party and China, not framing this as a personal friendship. Xi tried to be pleasant, and he looked comfortable with Trump, but it’s clear he is not returning the same kinds of personal compliments that he receives. And so for him the G2 is “two governments”, not a bromance.

I don’t know whether Trump’s approach has something to do with a desire to be included among some of the world’s most powerful leaders or to develop friendships. He may be doing this strictly for utilitarian purposes or may be driven by something else. But he’s done this with several other political leaders. He may want to give Xi face, believing that will help keep the relationship stable and make Xi more amenable to making concessions aligned with US preferences.

It’s clear that Xi and other senior officials avoid directly offending Trump, and they showed him a lot of deference when they hosted him in Beijing in May. So both sides are careful in how they handle the interpersonal relationship and questions of respect and face.

You have been watching China for decades. Where does this moment in the US-China relationship rank against some past inflection points, including China’s accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the 2018 trade war?

For much of the past half-century, the US has been focused on trying to find ways to integrate China into the international system and have a stable relationship, and China has been interested in pursuing that path as well. That really describes much of the relationship through 2015, the last time Xi made a state visit to Washington.

But the promise of that state visit and other meetings during the [Barack] Obama administration were not realised, and what we’ve seen is the US becoming more frustrated with China’s trajectory, and going back and forth between different kinds of approaches to deal with the China challenge.

First, it tried under Trump’s first term to use unilateral pressure on China to push it to meet its bilateral and multilateral commitments. Then the [Joe] Biden administration concluded that China couldn’t be effectively integrated into the international order, and therefore its focus shifted to insulating the rest of the world from the problems that China’s economic system and foreign policy created for others.

Under the second Trump administration, the US has decided to abandon that original international order and build a relationship with China on a very different foundation, rooted solely in power politics and a very different conception of the global order – in many ways, an order which China’s current leadership is much more comfortable with and more familiar with than what was critical to the original project the US was pursuing. And so we’re dealing with each other on very different terms than how the US and China interacted with each other for much of the last half-century.

The US government is still grappling with finding the right framework. The label of “constructive strategic stability” – expanded with the modifier “on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity” in Washington – is more a slogan than a detailed concept and blueprint, but that’s where we are right now.

What we’re seeing is an allocation of resources tilted heavily towards advanced technologies and away from other potential investments in human capital, in the social safety net and other areas

Scott Kennedy

You talked about this new approach towards China in Trump’s second administration. For now, the relationship has some semblance of stability, with Trump and Xi meeting up to four times this year. How do you view this new stability and engagement? Is it a genuine recalibration of ties or is it a kind of managed truce that still has sticking points?

Those who are more optimistic about the potential endurance of stable ties believe that the US has essentially abandoned its mission to manage the world in line with the rules-based international order and instead be more pragmatic about how the world works and embrace realpolitik. As a result, that means being less concerned about the rules of the game and more about outcomes.

So, it’s still a competition, but not a competition of competing orders. In fact, there may also be some areas of cooperation, since some of the issues that generate tensions in a competition of those two systems and their underlying values and ideologies are being put to the side.

Those who think that the post-World War II, international rules-based order may have flaws but should be reformed and strengthened look at the current ceasefire as quite temporary and believe that there will eventually be a “snapback” and resumption of greater tensions.

Once the US reduces its vulnerabilities, it will go back on the offence again. I honestly don’t know what the right expectations should be because the US is still trying to figure out what kind of world it wants to have and the same with many other countries. There appears to be a shifting balance of power between China and the West, but we don’t know how durable that is because we’ve got a lot of different variables that we’re trying to assess.

Artificial intelligence has been repeatedly floated as an area where the US and China can cooperate. But the suggestion seems to be at odds with an escalating US campaign designed to slow China’s AI progress – and the two countries also view AI in fundamentally different terms. Is cooperation possible in a sector marked by deep differences and one in which the US is trying to contain China’s progress?

Certainly, if AI is viewed strictly as a race to get to AGI [artificial general intelligence] because of the economic and potential military benefits that accrue to the country that gets there first, then that makes cooperation extremely difficult. But I don’t think that’s really what has been occurring. There’s growing evidence that we’re not strictly in a race.

The US and China have different kinds of approaches to AI. There’s no certainty that there is some magical threshold that one crosses that differentiates yesterday from tomorrow. And there are significant risks from AI that are not a product of interstate competition, challenges that everyone faces from the technology and its potential consequences on the world – deepfakes, hallucinations, loss of control and military applications, and other kinds of risks. There’s also some amazing potential benefits that we could share that could help each other and the rest of the world.

Given the complexities of the technology, the various different countries and stakeholders involved, we’re still at a very early stage. This is like the late 1940s at the very beginning of the nuclear era. We’re at the very beginning of the AI era. It’s really up to us – and “us” meaning everyone on the planet, not just powerful governments – to define what AI means and how we should address this challenge. This is a moment when the clay is still quite wet.

In May, Xi and Trump struck a trade deal built on familiar terms: Chinese purchases of American soybeans and Boeing planes, similar to the phase one trade agreement reached in 2020. Given that history, can such trade deals really function as a stabiliser for the relationship? Or must real stability come from elsewhere?

In an era in which we are involved in great power competition, trade and investment are not going to be an obvious ballast in the relationship. Since the two countries’ comparative advantages are increasingly overlapping, they are competing for the same section of the pie in the global economy. The US also is focused heavily on “new quality productive forces”, just as the Chinese are.

And so, in an era when the two sides are inherently less competitive, interdependence is less problematic and serves as ballast. But in an era defined by rivalry, interdependence is viewed by both governments as a risk, and both have taken enormous steps to de-risk and hold the upper hand.

The agreements on capping tariffs and continuing to provide rare earths, deals on individual products like aeroplanes and agricultural goods, those are very superficial arrangements which don’t suggest a high level of trust.

If such transactions are the cornerstone of these summits, the two sides are just dealing with the most superficial elements of the relationship because the US and China are at fundamental loggerheads over the more serious challenges with no clear path to resolution.

If you don’t think stability in the relationship can come from economics, then where can it come from? Can anything anchor the relationship?

In this kind of world, with a shifting balance of power, competing visions of the global system and an unwillingness to anchor one’s actions on basic principles that should constrain the behaviour of everyone including themselves, instability is more likely to be the hallmark of the relationship.

Without other stabilisers, avoiding conflict requires greater dependence on leadership diplomacy, and the leaders’ depth of involvement will depend on where the other country fits in the views of those two leaders and the dynamics of domestic politics. But the chances of a more fundamental stability seem out of reach.

China’s hi-tech industries have become world-class, driving a narrative that it is overtaking the US. But China’s strengths in manufacturing, in exports and technology, coexist with weak consumption, high youth unemployment and a property slump. How should we understand this divergence, and does it complicate the story of Chinese strength?

I think of China as a “slow tech dragon”, where it is simultaneously achieving amazing technology breakthroughs, manufacturing at scale, diffusing those technologies widely – not just within China but far beyond – while at the same time having a very slow macroeconomic environment. Those two things are the product of a common source, which is the emphasis by China’s policymakers on investment in technology as the primary source of China’s growth trajectory, replacing investment in infrastructure.

As a result, what we’re seeing is an allocation of resources tilted heavily towards advanced technologies and away from other potential investments in human capital, the social safety net and other areas. In some ways, this is a misallocation of resources that is leading to a very imbalanced economy domestically, and therefore globally. China’s economy is at least one-fifth of the world’s economy, and any imbalances in China become global imbalances.

China’s economy has both impressive strengths and significant weaknesses, and it likely will be a slow tech dragon for some time to come. It is that challenge that the world faces. We face a country that is technologically quite advanced but is choosing to focus on the supply side of technology as opposed to the consumption side.

For China to continue with this growth model, by definition it needs the world to adjust and absorb the gap between what China produces and what it consumes. The rest of the world benefits in some ways, but on balance, it is going to be pushing back, aiming for China to rebalance domestically in order to address global imbalances. Of course, those global imbalances aren’t only created by China. The US overconsumes and has a massive amount of debt. In some ways these are mirrors of each other.

But China’s approach is, on its own terms, creating challenges for others, and managing a relationship with a slow tech dragon is quite difficult. The US is still struggling to figure out a way to do so, and China is increasingly encountering pushback – in Europe and Latin America, not just the US – from the consequences of its economic growth strategy.

How sustainable is this Chinese approach, especially when global pressure on China is building?

There are three different kinds of ways in which the Chinese economic model will run into obstacles that it can’t overcome and which will force it to change.

The first is debt, because China’s financial system is so inefficient and there has been a rapid build-up of debt to fuel investment. Even though China is a hi-tech power, many of its companies are not very profitable, and so China’s credit picture continues to worsen.

The second potential obstacle is the effect of an economic transition on labour in China. In some ways, these great advancements are requiring a lot less labour, and in some sectors different kinds of labour, generating a mismatch between the type of human capital China has and what its economy needs. The Communist Party was created on the foundation of labour protests, and if this mismatch continues to worsen, labour instability is a potential challenge, not just for China but for others.

The third obstacle is pushback from the rest of the world. Countries individually and collectively say they are not going to adjust any longer, and that instead they are going to make China adjust. Currently, because of the Trump administration’s approach, many countries in the world similarly view challenges emanating from China, but there’s no effective coordination among others.

We saw a statement from the G20 gathering in Asheville [in North Carolina] recently about concerns over non-market practices, but there’s no significant coordinated action. If international unhappiness coalesces into joint or aligned steps, limiting China’s ability to have large trade surpluses, this could become a more effective constraint on China’s approach.

Trade wars are no longer just a US-China story. The US is in an escalating one with Canada, and Beijing’s doing the same with the EU. If tariffs are becoming the default tool major economies use to settle disputes, what does this mean for the future of the global economy?

The US still has tariffs on China of roughly 30 per cent in total. And if the investigation into manufacturing overcapacity yields a verdict soon, the US could impose an additional 7.5 per cent on China. Total US tariffs are much higher than the 3 per cent level average tariffs that the US had before. Although tariffs on China are still extremely high, they’re also high on just about everyone else. The US is still using tariffs to try to lower its bilateral trade deficits, encourage manufacturing at home, and raise additional revenue. It’s not been hugely successful in those goals, but the [Trump] administration is not giving up.

US efforts are having a corrosive effect on the multilateral trading system because it’s clear that US actions violate its WTO commitments. But the US is not the lone bad actor. US protectionism is a reaction to changing terms of trade and a deep sense of unfairness by the US about its trading relationship with many countries, including China, and its view that industrial policy and non-tariff barriers have led to unfair changes in the commercial relationship, in market opportunities, bilaterally and globally.

And so, US policy is born out of frustration. The Trump administration’s approach to that frustration further erodes the multilateral order, but it’s part of the back-and-forth tit-for-tat that’s been occurring for over two decades.

Despite all of that, according to the WTO, 72 per cent of global trade still occurs on a most-favoured-nation basis. We see efforts by countries to push back on super high tariffs, and countries have cut bilateral and regional deals to expand their opportunities and sustain an open multilateral trading order. Having recently been in Geneva – in a Track 2 dialogue with Chinese counterparts – there is a lot of recognition at the WTO and by its members of these risks to the multilateral order in the context of growing great power competition.

Brics has been pushing harder to settle trade outside the US dollar, and the Netherlands recently pulled roughly US$10 billion in gold out of American vaults. With US allies hedging against the US dollar, what does it say about how secure the dollar’s central role is? And will this be the start of something structural?

Investors and governments are always making adjustments in their holdings of currency based on a variety of circumstances, including macroeconomic conditions across different economies and trends in exchange rates. We’ve seen significant adjustments in holdings of currencies, and we’ve also seen a shift towards shorter maturities recently.

This could be normal, short-term adjustments. The American stock market is performing at record levels, with investment pouring in from around the world. This trend is built largely on optimism about AI and America’s own version of “new quality, productive forces”, the cutting of taxes in the US, and what looks in many respects like still a relatively strong economy.

But there may be another story. Observers are concerned about growing geostrategic tensions, rising tariffs, and dangerous regional hotspots around the world. They’re worried about some of the foundations of the rule of law in the US, its democratic institutions, and the independence of the Federal Reserve.

These worries may signal a transition that is more structural and not just a short-term blip. At the end of the day, a lot will depend on people’s confidence in the US government’s ability to be a wise steward of its economy and the international order.

That said, even though there are worries about the US from a variety of quarters, there are not good alternatives to a dollar-based international monetary system. China is the world’s largest trader, but most of its trade still occurs in dollars, and most of its international financial transactions still occur in dollars. China still holds a lot of US Treasuries, and China’s capital account is still largely closed. China doesn’t have deep financial markets that are internationally open to serve as a significant alternative.

Even with the variety of experiments and initiatives it has pursued, central authorities prioritise domestic financial stability above all. Limited investment opportunities in renminbi, insufficient policy transparency and concerns about the rule of law together are constraints on the renminbi playing a larger international role.

Europe’s economy is growing very slowly. [There are] significant worries about Europe’s economy and European Union gridlock, concerns maybe even larger than those about the US. Hence, the euro is unlikely to be a clear, obvious alternative to the dollar.

And so, in a world where money needs to take some form, and investments are relative, even with concerns about the US and the dollar, it looks like we will continue to live in a dollar-based global economy for quite some time. There are obvious risks, but I don’t see us shifting significantly in a different direction in the near term.

item.title: [SCMP] Chickens in Malaysia are producing fewer eggs. Is haze a leading cause?
item.description:
This year’s haze crisis has added to the heat woes squeezing livestock farmers in Malaysia and Indonesia as they struggle to keep their animals cool, fed and productive.

While it is difficult to separately assess the effects of haze-related smoke from heat, water shortages, feed and disease, farmers and industry groups say the cumulative strain is severely affecting animal health, productivity and their finances.

In Selama, Perak, poultry keeper Zaiful Zakaria, 42, had begun installing ventilation fans at his open-sided chicken sheds before the haze hit Malaysia in August.
item.content:encoded:
This year’s haze crisis has added to the heat woes squeezing livestock farmers in Malaysia and Indonesia as they struggle to keep their animals cool, fed and productive.

While it is difficult to separately assess the effects of haze-related smoke from heat, water shortages, feed and disease, farmers and industry groups say the cumulative strain is severely affecting animal health, productivity and their finances.

In Selama, Perak, poultry keeper Zaiful Zakaria, 42, had begun installing ventilation fans at his open-sided chicken sheds before the haze hit Malaysia in August.

The fans were meant to draw out heat accumulating inside the sheds and protect the well-being of his mainly ornamental and heritage-breed chickens. Zaiful later also began installing a water-misting system.

For a basic fan-and-mister arrangement, Zaiful estimated he had spent about 500 ringgit (US$120) per shed.

Other refinements, such as solar panels and an automatic feeder, would cost more – up to 2,000 ringgit per shed, but these could save him money and effort in the long term.

Another breeder, Mohd Hazarulhizam Mohd Shafie, shared a photo of his newly renovated shelter for his heritage chickens in Alor Setar, Kedah. He estimated the total cost to be 50,000 ringgit, including built-in exhaust fans, solar panels and auto-misters.

“The figures are not final, but the haze and the weather were definitely reasons I rebuilt my reban [coops] to better protect my birds,” Mohd Hazarulhizam said.

The haze followed weeks of hot, dry weather across parts of the region, with forest and agricultural fires in Indonesia sending smoke billowing into Malaysia. The poor air quality, heat and lack of water and feed have all stressed livestock.

Against such a backdrop, it can be difficult for farmers and veterinarians to determine why an animal is ill, not putting on weight, or producing fewer eggs or less milk.

Farmers and industry groups have reported significant changes in animal health and productivity during the hot and hazy period.

Zaiful, who heads the newly established Malaysian Poultry Association, which focuses on heritage breeds and small-scale farms, said the association had received several reports of breeders losing large numbers of birds.

“There were no veterinary reports to establish whether it was the smoke, weather or other reasons for those deaths. Many might keep silent out of embarrassment,” Zaiful said.

Small-scale farmers with fewer than 500 birds, as well as backyard poultry keepers, were particularly exposed because their birds were often kept in basic, open-air sheds, he said, adding that these owners typically had less access to veterinary and animal husbandry advice than commercial producers, who had climate-controlled sheds, specialist consultants and tighter biosecurity.

Small-scale breeders are not required to register with Malaysia’s Department of Veterinary Services.

Livestock veterinarian Vijay Jayam said a similar divide existed among cattle, dairy and goat farms.

Larger dairies were generally better equipped in terms of ventilation and biosecurity, while smallholders might only be able to douse their animals with water to help them cool down, he said.

“Farmers should prioritise ventilation and clean drinking water,” Vijay said, adding that he would not attribute lower milk yields or slower growth to haze alone without considering other factors, such as feed, housing, disease and the animal’s stage of growth.

Ari Ramash Supramaniam, a dairy and goat farmer, said milk production from the five milking cows out of his 23 Australian Friesian-Jersey crossbreeds had fallen by four litres to six litres (8½ US pints to 12½ US pints) per day. He estimated that the lost milk output had reduced his daily earnings by up to 60 ringgit.

“For a small farmer, that is a lot,” said Ari, who started his farm about six years ago. He linked the decline to the cattle grazing less due to the daytime heat.

Ari said he was giving his animals clean water mixed with molasses and ice to help them regain their energy and beat the heat, as well as increasing the amount of concentrate feed and mineral supplements in their fodder.

Once the animals returned to the barn, they would finish their food and drink “within a few minutes”, he said.

The extra supplements needed to ride out current conditions can prove costly, as Ari uses about 5kg (11lbs) of molasses a day, at 1.80 ringgit per kilogram. The price of a 50kg bag of feed had risen by between 3 ringgit and 5 ringgit during the El Nino period, he said.

He also buys eight 30kg bags of fresh grass a day at 12 ringgit each to feed his animals at night, once temperatures have eased.

Ari, who built his shed above ground level to allow natural airflow without having to use fans or turbines, said he was working harder and spending more just to maintain productivity.

“Still, I have noticed saliva around the mouths of the goats and cows from the heat stress, and stressed animals will not contribute to expected results for farmers,” Ari said.

Jeffrey Ng, an adviser to the Federation of Livestock Farmers’ Associations of Malaysia, said the organisation had begun recording weaker production up to two months ago. Some broiler chicken producers reported that birds were taking up to an additional week to reach their normal sale weight.

The heat and haze were overlapping pressures, Ng said, adding that the federation had not received any reports of a rise in poultry mortality associated with the current haze.

Malaysia’s Ministry of Domestic Trade and Cost of Living has received reports of hot weather increasing mortality rates among laying hens, causing egg production to drop, deputy minister Fuziah Salleh told local media.

With demand unchanged, the tighter supply had contributed to higher egg prices, she said, adding that the increase remained under control.

Across the border in Mempawah regency, West Kalimantan, Sakiman has been struggling to cope with the drought. He said he had spent two whole weeks in August trying to find enough grass and water for his six animals.

The cattle farmer, who keeps six head of cattle and sells male calves and bulls for racing and meat, said much of the grass that was normally available had dried out, forcing him to look for fodder or buy it by the bundle early in the morning.

“They are not eating as much as they used to, but it’s enough to keep them going,” Sakiman said of his animals.

Water from the Mempawah River had also turned brackish and was no longer flowing strongly enough to reach the irrigation ditch he relied on, he said.

“Now I buy about two drums [of water] at a time – one for household use and another for the cattle. They last about five days, and each drum can cost about 150,000 rupiah,” Sakiman said.

Smoke particles may pose an additional risk, particularly in open-sided poultry sheds.

A modelling study by researchers at Thailand’s Chiang Mai Rajabhat University projected that three days of exposure to PM2.5 – particulate matter 2.5 micrometres or less in diameter – at 150 micrograms per cubic metre could reduce a broiler chicken’s average daily weight gain by 5.2 per cent.

But Kulisara Marupanthorn, a veterinarian and project supervisor for the research, stressed that these were “predictions, not observed farm losses”.

study currently being prepared for publication, her team measured PM2.5 levels at bird-breathing height across three 35-day broiler cycles. Birds in the higher-pollution cycle had poorer respiratory health, weaker immunity and lower egg production. However, the researchers could not attribute these outcomes to PM2.5 alone, as there were also variations in temperature, humidity and rainfall.

Marupanthorn advised small-scale farmers to keep their water clean and curb dust levels, but warned that closing curtains against smoke could backfire if it trapped heat and humidity.

Zaiful, meanwhile, said he was worried about mounting financial losses because of lower production.

“Sometimes some breeders only have 500 ringgit to start their breeding business with and if they lose their chickens to heat stress or illnesses, that is a lot of money to them,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] The porcupine dilemma: why US-China diplomacy is about distance, not deals
item.description:
Arthur Schopenhauer’s classic parable of relationships may help us understand today’s China-US ties.

The reclusive German philosopher famously described how wintering porcupines need to cluster together to survive the biting cold, but hurt one another with their quills if they get too close. In the end, the porcupines must learn to balance the need for shared warmth against the pain of pricking each other.

Chinese President Xi Jinping received an unprecedentedly lavish reception from Donald Trump this week – one that would make America’s staunchest allies envious. On his second state visit to the US, a first for a Chinese president, Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan schmoozed with the American first couple like old friends. Both presidents heaped praise on one another and pledged to do more to further the friendship of the two peoples.
item.content:encoded:
Arthur Schopenhauer’s classic parable of relationships may help us understand today’s China-US ties.

The reclusive German philosopher famously described how wintering porcupines need to cluster together to survive the biting cold, but hurt one another with their quills if they get too close. In the end, the porcupines must learn to balance the need for shared warmth against the pain of pricking each other.

Chinese President Xi Jinping received an unprecedentedly lavish reception from Donald Trump this week – one that would make America’s staunchest allies envious. On his second state visit to the US, a first for a Chinese president, Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan schmoozed with the American first couple like old friends. Both presidents heaped praise on one another and pledged to do more to further the friendship of the two peoples.

They will meet again in Shenzhen and Miami before the year is out: three presidential summits in four months set another record.

Yet the warmth between the two leaders could not conceal the tensions sizzling beneath.

The fact that the two sides only agreed to extend the truce in their costly trade war by two more months, after an unscheduled, eleventh-hour negotiation ahead of the summit, is telling.

Expectations for any breakthrough on critical minerals or chip controls are low. Observers also doubt whether Washington is willing to fundamentally shift its policy on Taiwan, even though Trump did postpone an approved arms sale and was careful about public comments on the issue, mindful of Beijing’s sensitivities.

To some, the three-day summit seemed heavy on pageantry but light on substance. One former US diplomat called it “theatrical pageantry” that “papered over real problems”.

Yet often in diplomacy – and especially in this case – form is substance. Protocols and rituals function in human society as a way of setting the right distance.

It is unrealistic to expect the two sides to reach any substantial breakthrough, given the sharp spikes these two “porcupines” carry on their backs.

While Xi was given the highest honours by his host, the trip was overshadowed by domestic American political turmoil and Trump’s feud with the mainstream media.

Most Americans saw little footage of the actual summit, as major television networks did not provide live coverage – a consequence of Trump’s ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House.

When the visit was covered, the narrative was often coloured by the networks’ anger at the president. Trump was relentlessly criticised by liberal media for warming up to Communist China, and the tirades against Beijing often bordered on hysteria.

We are where we are because neither side could land a knockout punch, and both hold enough leverage to make the winter hard for the other

The underlying sentiment seems to be that Washington simply needs to “act tough” to strong-arm Beijing into submission.

That script has been tried before, and it has never worked. Before this week’s meeting, the US and China had already settled into nine years of intense rivalry, fighting trade wars, tech wars, financial wars and narrative wars.

We are where we are because neither side could land a knockout punch, and both hold enough leverage to make the winter hard for the other.

It is fitting, if ironic, that it’s Marco Rubio – still on Beijing’s sanctions list – who offers the sharpest rebuttal to that view, now wearing his Secretary of State hat.

“The United States and China are the two largest economies in the world. The United States and China are probably the two most powerful militaries in the world. The relationship between the United States and China will define the 21st century,” Secretary Rubio said. “The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible. It’s outrageous. We have to. That doesn’t mean we don’t have strong disagreements. Of course, we do.”

The present entente between China and the US is hardly, as some commentators believe, the result of Trump’s tendency to cosy up to authoritarian strongmen. The two sides are being driven together by the need for “shared warmth” in the face of pressing internal and external urgencies.

Unlike the Soviet Union and the US during the Cold War, there is no Iron Curtain separating the two sides in today’s globalised world. For all the efforts to decouple or de-risk, Chinese and American national interests remain deeply intertwined.

A study released by the Peterson Institute for International Economics last month found that despite all the tariffs and trade restrictions imposed on Beijing by Trump and his predecessor Joe Biden, China’s share of total value added in American imports dropped by only 2 per cent. Chinese supply chains remain deeply embedded in the American economy.

At the same time, the need for cooperation on issues like the regulation of artificial intelligence – or “superintelligence” in President Trump’s terminology – is real and pressing.

The danger of artificial intelligence lies not so much in machines replacing humans, but in the disproportionate power it hands to those with access to advanced AI over those without. That imbalance opens the door to every kind of abuse and misuse.

It also sharply raises the risk of miscalculated nuclear warfare.
