During the Cold War, a strategic missile launched from Soviet or American soil would take roughly an hour to hit its target. Today, hypersonic technology has cut that window to under 20 minutes, and sophisticated stealth technology makes early detection far harder.

Cold War-era generals had time to assess intelligence and call each other for clarification in an extreme emergency. Today, no human being can do all of that in 8 to 20 minutes.

Inevitably, this may mean ceding control of the nuclear button to AI – unless the two sides can reach some comprehensive agreement first.

These are just some of the cold realities both sides must face. No matter how much you dislike the “spiky porcupine” across the room, you have to learn how to get close enough to survive the winter.

This, in a roundabout way, is my explanation of what Xi means by “strategic stability” between the two sides. The term, first raised last October when the two leaders met in Busan, South Korea, describes how China and the US might find the “Goldilocks distance” – close enough to cooperate, far enough to compete, without risking bringing down the house.

Seen this way, the success of this week’s summit should not be measured by the deals signed or missed, but by whether the two sides have established the right distance to contain their differences and allow controlled cooperation – one step at a time.

item.title: [SCMP] In Malaysia, a mother’s love offers her trans daughter refuge
item.description:
In a village on the outskirts of Kota Bharu, in Malaysia’s deeply conservative northeastern state of Kelantan, Rozi* has learned to ignore what people say about her daughter.

She had known for years that Hana* was different. As a child, Hana preferred girls’ clothes and spent most of her time with girls. Later, after leaving Kelantan to study, she began transitioning and eventually returned home, living openly as a woman.

Rozi, 58, struggled to accept it at first, but what troubled her more was the thought that rejecting Hana might push her out of the family altogether.
item.content:encoded:
In a village on the outskirts of Kota Bharu, in Malaysia’s deeply conservative northeastern state of Kelantan, Rozi* has learned to ignore what people say about her daughter.

She had known for years that Hana* was different. As a child, Hana preferred girls’ clothes and spent most of her time with girls. Later, after leaving Kelantan to study, she began transitioning and eventually returned home, living openly as a woman.

Rozi, 58, struggled to accept it at first, but what troubled her more was the thought that rejecting Hana might push her out of the family altogether.

“When you see your own child’s face, what mother does not love her child?” Rozi told This Week in Asia. “No matter how bad people may think your child is, she is still your child. If I didn’t accept her, she would go further and further away from me. I don’t want her to be far away.”

That acceptance has turned home into a refuge for Hana, at a time when other transgender Muslims in Kelantan say they have had to become increasingly cautious in public.

Kelantan, where 95.5 per cent of the population is Muslim, is the political stronghold of the Islamist Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party, which has governed the state since 1990.

The state’s sharia laws penalise gender transition and cross-dressing among Muslims, and recent prosecutions have heightened concerns within the local transgender community over intensifying state scrutiny.

Against that backdrop, Rozi said her initial resistance to her daughter’s transition had gradually given way to a quiet acceptance she once thought unlikely.

Hana, 27, now regularly returns home, joins family gatherings and brings transgender friends over for meals, while her mother happily fusses over the food.

“They are human, too. They want to eat like us, they want to feel loved,” said Rozi, a mother of three who works at a local mosque. “They don’t want to be thrown away by their families.”

Private sanctuary

Hana began taking hormones around 2019 while living away from Kelantan. By the time she returned, her hair was longer and her appearance had changed enough that her father, picking her up at the station, was taken aback.

“My mother said, ‘Whatever people want to say, let them. Just don’t stop coming home’,” Hana said.

There are boundaries. The interior designer dresses more conservatively in Kelantan than she does in Kuala Lumpur, where she occasionally travels for work, and says her mother would object if a friend turned up at the family home in revealing clothing.

Still, Hana is free to be herself at home – a privilege she knows many of her peers do not share.

“As long as my family accepts me, that’s enough,” she said. “What outsiders want to say, I don’t really care.”

Hana thinks carefully about what she wears before going out in Kelantan, favouring loose or unisex clothing and understated make-up to avoid drawing the attention of religious enforcement officers.

“If you go out, go out for something important,” she said. “We try to avoid making the issue hot again. If there is nothing to do, it’s better to stay home.”

Most Kelantanese she encountered were not overtly hostile, Hana said – the uglier reactions tended to appear online, where videos circulated rapidly and social media users tagged religious authorities to demand enforcement action.

Another member of Kelantan’s transgender community shared a similar account, saying that while transgender people could still run shops and deal with customers in daily life, public social spaces had noticeably shrunk.

“Before, [trans] people would still go out to eat, hang out and meet in public. Now it’s very different. People don’t really do that any more, and even when we gather, it’s usually in small groups, maybe four or five people,” the person said, asking not to be named.

“There is fear. Social media is where some of us make money, but at the same time it makes people know where we are and what we are doing.”

Shrinking public spaces

The growing sense of unease has coincided with a series of recent legal actions.

In February, local news outlet Malaysiakini reported that Kelantan had recorded its first prosecution under Section 18 of its 2019 sharia criminal code – which criminalises changing one’s gender – since the law was gazetted in 2020. It was believed to be the first prosecution of its kind in Malaysia.

Then, last month, Kelantan lawmakers unanimously passed a revised sharia criminal offences bill, after Malaysia’s Federal Court struck down 16 provisions of the earlier enactment in 2024 for intruding on federal jurisdiction.

The updated law retains strict penalties for Muslims who change their gender, help another person to do so or induce someone to transition without a reason permitted under Islamic law.

On September 8, a 25-year-old transgender person pleaded not guilty in a Kota Bharu sharia court to “posing as a woman” by wearing women’s clothing. The charge carries a maximum fine of 3,000 ringgit (US$730), up to two years in prison, or both.

Kelantan’s leaders have taken a hard line. Deputy chief minister Mohamed Fadzli Hassan said last year that the state “does not recognise deviant cultures that go against Islamic teachings”, describing LGBT practices as “a clear transgression of human nature”.

Thilaga Sulathireh, co-founder of the human rights group Justice for Sisters, said the recent cases reflected “a clear clampdown on the visibility of trans people” across the state.

Transgender entrepreneurs and social media personalities are particularly exposed, as the same platforms they rely on for income make them visible to religious authorities.

“These laws completely disrupt all areas of a trans person’s life: [their ability] to work, move around freely, socialise and be who they are,” Thilaga said. “There is a lot of self-censorship. Movements are restricted. Many only go out at selected hours due to fear of arrest.”

Justice for Sisters had documented instances of transgender women losing income after curtailing their online presence, Thilaga said, while others avoided shopping centres, beaches and other public spaces known for religious raids.

The Kelantan Islamic Religious Affairs Department did not respond to a request for comment from This Week in Asia regarding its enforcement operations.

Back in their village, Rozi continues to pray for her daughter, viewing matters of faith as something Hana must ultimately answer for herself.

“That is between her and Allah,” she said. “It is not for humans to judge.”

What matters most for her is closer to home.

“As long as my child is safe,” Rozi said, with teary eyes. “She is still my child.”

*Names changed to protect interviewees’ identities

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s animal welfare laws fail to meet modern demands, experts say
item.description:
Hong Kong’s existing animal welfare laws are no longer “fit for purpose” to deal with issues around pet abandonment and strays, legal experts have said, urging authorities to expedite long-delayed reforms to the city’s ordinances following a spate of dog attacks.

The calls echo comments by Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan, who said on Wednesday that authorities would look at whether existing penalties for pet abandonment should be strengthened and bring suggestions to the Legislative Council by the end of the year.

Hong Kong’s animal welfare laws – namely the Protection of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance and Dangerous Dogs Regulations – have drawn intense public scrutiny following a string of recent incidents, including the suspected fatal mauling of a woman by stray dogs in Yuen Long last Saturday night.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong’s existing animal welfare laws are no longer “fit for purpose” to deal with issues around pet abandonment and strays, legal experts have said, urging authorities to expedite long-delayed reforms to the city’s ordinances following a spate of dog attacks.

The calls echo comments by Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan, who said on Wednesday that authorities would look at whether existing penalties for pet abandonment should be strengthened and bring suggestions to the Legislative Council by the end of the year.

Hong Kong’s animal welfare laws – namely the Protection of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance and Dangerous Dogs Regulations – have drawn intense public scrutiny following a string of recent incidents, including the suspected fatal mauling of a woman by stray dogs in Yuen Long last Saturday night.

“Hong Kong’s Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance … remains fundamentally focused on prohibiting acts of cruelty,” said Kim McCoy, a practising barrister and founder of the Hong Kong Animal Law and Protection Organisation.

“It is an outdated and fundamentally flawed framework, no longer fit for purpose and wholly incapable of meeting the demands of modern society.”

Stray dogs have caused increasing concern as land clearance for the Northern Metropolis megaproject has led to a surge in abandoned animals.

Preparatory land resumption for the megaproject in the New Territories has triggered a growing animal welfare crisis, as many residents and business operators abandon pets or guard dogs ahead of government clearance deadlines.

Despite these concerns, the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) previously told the South China Morning Post that no prosecutions had been brought against people for abandoning animals under the Rabies Ordinance – the law governing such matters – between 2023 and 2025.

In his recent policy address, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the government would amend the city’s laws on animal care by the end of 2027 while also reviewing pet ownership and control regulations.

Speaking to lawmakers on Wednesday, Tse said authorities would bring suggestions to the Legislative Council by the end of 2026.

But animal law reform has been an ongoing discussion in the city for years, with the government submitting a paper to the Legislative Council in 2022 outlining proposed amendments to the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance.

The proposals, which received support from 88 per cent of respondents during a public consultation exercise in 2019, included increasing the maximum penalties for animal cruelty offences and strengthening rules around animal abandonment.

They also introduced a positive “duty of care” provision, long sought by animal welfare advocates and legal experts, requiring owners to ensure their pets’ safety and fulfil basic care obligations.

Such requirements would include ensuring animals have a suitable diet and living environment, exhibit normal behaviour patterns, and are protected from pain, suffering and injury.

While the 2022 paper suggested the bill amendments would be put before lawmakers that year, it was never formally introduced. In subsequent responses to lawmakers’ questions on the lack of progress, the government as recently as this February cited “divergent views” among stakeholders on the need for “duty of care” provisions and the extent of penalties.

It is not yet clear whether the government’s new round of proposed amendments will match those introduced in 2022.

Animal welfare advocates have argued that existing laws make it difficult to prosecute owners who fail to microchip or properly secure their pets, while allowing them to deny that an abandoned animal belongs to them.

McCoy said introducing “duty of care” rules would define responsible ownership, and a person who acquired an animal would need to accept the responsibilities that came with their decision.

“In the context of these recent incidents, a properly drafted ‘duty of care’ could help prevent neglect and abandonment, improve standards of supervision and enable earlier intervention where an animal’s welfare is being compromised,” he said.

He also called for a comprehensive review of the city’s Rabies Ordinance.

“While rabies prevention remains important, we should not be relying on disease-control legislation to address fundamental issues such as animal abandonment, irresponsible ownership and the humane management of stray animals,” he said.

Amanda Whitfort, an associate professor at the University of Hong Kong specialising in animal law, said there was a need to introduce welfare standards for animals, prosecute abandonment, and introduce humane population control of strays in certain areas.

Whitfort co-wrote a landmark animal law reform report in 2010 which, among a number of recommendations, called for the implementation of a new Animal Welfare Ordinance containing “duty of care” provisions.

“Rather than take a holistic view of solving these problems, the [AFCD’s] policy has been to collect and pass on their responsibility for unwanted dogs to overburdened shelters. This policy has not been sustainable for some time,” she said.

She noted that the department had not brought any prosecutions for animal abandonment in recent years, which she argued “sends the public the message that they may give up their responsibilities to their pets without significant repercussions”.

Whitfort said it was too easy for people to keep dogs without obtaining licences under existing rules, and suggested that laws could be altered to reward those who spay or neuter their dogs with lower licence fees.

She also called on authorities to follow Macau’s example, where failing to report the loss of a dog within a specific time period was an offence.

In a reply to the SCMP, the AFCD said that pet owners had a responsibility not only to care for their pets but also to control them.

“While ‘duty of care’ focuses primarily on the animal’s welfare needs, the concept of ‘pet owner responsibility’ encompasses welfare, safety, environmental considerations and public health,” it said.

“We will encourage pet owners to understand and fulfil their responsibilities through reviewing regulations and conducting public education and publicity campaigns.”

The department also reiterated that the government would consult the Legislative Council on proposals to step up efforts to combat cruelty to animals, and that it would work to complete the amendment exercise in 2027.

item.title: [SCMP] Trump asked Xi if Beijing wanted US weapons: a joke, a gambit or something more?
item.description:
Donald Trump asked President Xi Jinping whether Beijing wanted to buy American weapons, the US ambassador to China said on Sunday, prompting the State Department to quickly rule out any such deal with Washington’s principal strategic competitor.

“He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point,” the ambassador David Perdue said on Fox News after Xi’s state visit to the White House last week. He did not say when Trump raised the question, what prompted it, or how the Chinese leader responded.

A State Department official, speaking on background to the South China Morning Post, said: “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.”
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump asked President Xi Jinping whether Beijing wanted to buy American weapons, the US ambassador to China said on Sunday, prompting the State Department to quickly rule out any such deal with Washington’s principal strategic competitor.

“He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point,” the ambassador David Perdue said on Fox News after Xi’s state visit to the White House last week. He did not say when Trump raised the question, what prompted it, or how the Chinese leader responded.

A State Department official, speaking on background to the South China Morning Post, said: “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.”

The swift clarification came as the disclosure ricocheted among Asia specialists, who noted the extraordinary contrast between Trump reportedly raising the prospect of arming Beijing and his administration continuing to hold up a roughly US$14 billion weapons package for Taiwan.

Washington has spent decades treating Beijing as a strategic rival, restricting military technology exports, strengthening security partnerships across the Indo-Pacific region and building its capacity to deter a potential conflict.

That is what makes Trump’s reported offer so extraordinary: the US has not sold conventional weapons to Beijing for more than three decades and has spent much of that time building its military posture around deterring the Chinese military, not supplying it.

In the 1980s, the Reagan administration briefly expanded military cooperation with Beijing as both countries sought to counter the Soviet Union. Washington approved several military related sales, including the roughly $550 million Peace Pearl programme involving US avionics for Chinese J-8 fighter aircraft.

That relationship ended after the Tiananmen Square crackdown in June 1989. Then-president George H.W. Bush suspended military sales and exchanges with Beijing. Congress later codified restrictions on the transfer of US defence articles to the Chinese military.

US law permits a presidential waiver in the national interest, but no administration has used that authority to restore a conventional US arms pipeline to Beijing.

The strategic landscape has since changed dramatically. Successive US administrations have spent billions preparing for a possible military confrontation with Beijing and supplying weapons to Taiwan to help deter a potential attack.

Meanwhile, China has built the world’s largest navy by number of ships and rapidly expanded its missile, air and nuclear capabilities. The Pentagon has identified Beijing as the United States’ most consequential long term strategic challenge.

That makes Perdue’s disclosure particularly striking.

Zack Cooper, an Asia security fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and former Pentagon and White House official, wrote on social media that he was “underwhelmed when it looked like the big deliverable both sides actually announced at this Trump-Xi summit was the lease of two pandas”.

“But it never occurred to me that an American president might offer to sell American weapons to China, he added.

Cooper later stressed that the remark came directly from Perdue, not an anonymous source. “This wasn’t a leak, it was a comment by President Trump’s ambassador to China on Fox,” he wrote. “I’ll take him at his word until I’m told otherwise.”

He also highlighted the contrast with the stalled weapons deal with Taipei, saying it was “shocking that Trump is resisting authorising arms sales to Taiwan but at the same time offering them to China”.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

After meeting Xi in Beijing in May, Trump said he was holding the package “in abeyance”, calling it “a very good negotiating chip” and saying the decision “depends on China”.

Perdue offered no timetable on the sales in the interview on Sunday. “There are continuing conversations about other sales,” he said, adding that Trump “has a schedule of his own”.

Perdue also said that Trump and Xi discuss American arms sales to Taiwan “every time they meet” – a comment that drew attention to Washington’s pledge to Taipei in the 1982 Six Assurances not to consult Beijing on the issue.

Ryan Hass, who handled China policy at the National Security Council and now heads the China Centre at Brookings, said the disclosure would unsettle US partners in Asia.

“Trump’s offer to sell weapons to China will be unsettling to American partners at the pointy edge of China’s spear,” Hass wrote on social media.

Taiwan’s de facto envoy in Washington, Alexander Tah-ray Yui, said on the CBS programme Face the Nation on Sunday that last week’s summit statements listed no Taiwan deliverable, even though Beijing called the issue “foundational”.

“It was foundational, but there was no reaction from the US side,” Yui said. On the stalled package, he added: “The United States has been our main supplier of weapons to Taiwan. We hope that we can get that weapons package in as soon as possible.”

Peace through strength, he argued, was “the best way to avoid any conflict”, adding that deterrence rested on the idea that Beijing would not attack if the island itself were strong.

The episode has left a simpler question hanging over Washington’s China policy debate: was Trump seriously floating the idea, or was he joking with Xi? And if it was a joke, why did Perdue feel it was worth mentioning on national television?

Denis Simon of the Quincy Institute said the key distinction was between Trump raising the idea and making a concrete arms offer.

“There is no evidence that Trump made a concrete offer for China to purchase a specific US weapons package, nor that China accepted or seriously negotiated such a deal,” Simon said.

“It appears to have been a rhetorical/negotiating manoeuvre rather than an actual arms-sales proposal.”

But Simon said that this did not make the remark insignificant, particularly given its connection to Taiwan.

“Trump’s logic appears to have been something like: ‘You object to our selling weapons to Taiwan. But America sells weapons to many countries. Why shouldn’t China be able to buy American weapons if it wants them?’,” he said.

“That is an intentionally provocative way of reframing the Taiwan issue.”

Simon said the episode pointed to a more transactional approach to Taiwan arms sales, in which the weapons package itself becomes leverage in the broader relationship between Washington and Beijing.

In his formulation, Trump’s approach is closer to this: Taiwan needs weapons, Beijing objects, so let’s see what Beijing is willing to give in return.

He noted that Trump may also have been using the hypothetical sale to “tout the appeal of American military hardware”, suggesting that even Beijing might see US weapons as preferable to its own.

Scott Kennedy of the Centre for Strategic and International Studies had a more immediate reaction. “Wow! Not sure why Amb Perdue decided it’d be wise to share that comment with the world,” he said.

Bonnie Glaser, who heads the Indo-Pacific programme at the German Marshall Fund, focused on another part of Perdue’s interview.

The ambassador said Trump and Xi discuss US arms sales to Taiwan “every time they meet” and that Washington “doesn’t support Taiwan independence and doesn’t support coercion”.

“Shouldn’t the US oppose coercion?” Glaser wrote.

Bill Bishop, author of the Sinocism newsletter, offered a different interpretation, calling it “just more Trump joking” while adding that he was “not sure why Perdue mentioned it”.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Southeast Asia feels relief and caution after the Xi-Trump summit
item.description:
Southeast Asia welcomes the continued thaw in US-China ties after the Xi-Trump summit, with analysts saying that less friction between the two powers over issues such as the South China Sea could lower the pressure on the region.

Yet, caution persists as the summit left deeper disputes unresolved.

“Stable great-power relations – competitive but with sturdy guardrails – will create more legroom for third countries to navigate an increasingly complex world,” according to Lucio Blanco Pitlo III, a research fellow at the Manila-based Asia Pacific Pathways to Progress Foundation.
item.content:encoded:
Southeast Asia welcomes the continued thaw in US-China ties after the Xi-Trump summit, with analysts saying that less friction between the two powers over issues such as the South China Sea could lower the pressure on the region.

Yet, caution persists as the summit left deeper disputes unresolved.

“Stable great-power relations – competitive but with sturdy guardrails – will create more legroom for third countries to navigate an increasingly complex world,” according to Lucio Blanco Pitlo III, a research fellow at the Manila-based Asia Pacific Pathways to Progress Foundation.

Such stability, he said, could ease pressure on countries of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to pick a side, slow supply-chain disintegration and reduce the intensity of great-power competition in long-standing flashpoints like the Taiwan Strait and South China Sea.

Beijing described Xi’s visit, his second summit with Trump in five months, as a step towards a “constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability”, emphasising continued economic engagement, dialogue on artificial intelligence and the need for Washington to handle the issue of Taiwan cautiously.

Trump’s lavish treatment of Xi suggested that both sought to avoid escalation, as “the language and tone coming out of the summit suggest a continuation of interest in stability on both sides”, said Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore and a non-resident scholar at Carnegie China.

On the other hand, better US-China relations could revive concerns in the region about a “G2” dynamic in which major powers make decisions affecting the region without meaningful Southeast Asian input.

“A sustained thaw would give Southeast Asia more breathing space, particularly economies such as Vietnam that connect Chinese supply chains with American consumers,” said Nguyen Khac Giang, a visiting fellow at the Vietnam studies programme at Singapore’s ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute.

“But no one in the region wants a ‘G2’ deciding everyone else’s interests over their heads. One Cold War was enough.”

Chong expressed similar concerns, saying any US-China arrangement that made decisions about Southeast Asia without regional participation would curtail the agency of Asean states.

Such new momentum across the Pacific may also draw their attention to how the two powers are handling issues over Taiwan and the South China Sea in the absence of a reference to the highly contested waters in the Chinese read-out.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Instead of mentioning the South China Sea in its read-out, the White House simply stated that the US military’s presence has “preserved a free and open Indo-Pacific” since World War II.

According to Zhu Junwei, director of the Horizon Insights Centre consulting firm, while the disputed sea falls directly within the US definition of the “Indo-Pacific”, it was not a main agenda item and required no explicit mention.

Its absence signalled an intent to avoid public friction given the two sides’ shared commitment to build towards the “constructive, strategically stable relationship”, Zhu noted.

“Their differences on issues like the South China Sea should be managed and handled through consultation,” she added. “Unilaterally criticising the other party in the read-out does not help manage these differences.

“Nevertheless, this will not stop the US State Department or the [American] military from continuing to speak out on the South China Sea in the future.”

Such an approach might even be welcomed in some regional capitals, Giang said.

“From that perspective, the absence of Southeast Asia and the South China Sea from the public read-outs may be welcome,” Giang added. “Southeast Asian capitals are not naive enough to mistake silence for indifference. But Beijing’s emphasis on Taiwan signals its priorities, at least in the short term.”

Even as leaders spoke of regional stability in Washington, tensions flared again in the South China Sea.

The Philippine Coast Guard accused China on Friday of obstructing a resupply mission to Second Thomas Shoal, known as Renai Jiao in China and Ayungin Shoal in the Philippines.

The China Coast Guard said it had lawfully monitored and warned a Philippine vessel delivering supplies to what Beijing described as an “illegally grounded” ship at the shoal.

On Sunday, China carried out a joint air and naval exercise near Scarborough Shoal, calling the drill a “necessary action” to counter efforts by “individual countries undermining regional peace and stability”.

The coral atoll, known as Huangyan Dao in China and Panatag Shoal in the Philippines, has been a persistent source of friction between Beijing and Manila. Having controlled the feature since 2012, China has stepped up scientific research and geological surveys on the shoal this year.

As for Taiwan, it remains a significant concern for Southeast Asia because of the large number of its citizens living and working there and the broader security and economic implications of any conflict.

“Over a million Asean nationals live and work in Taiwan, so a contingency there portends a serious human and economic tragedy for regional countries,” Pitlo said, referring to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

“Constructive dialogue between China and the US may help avert a crisis over these hotspots. That said, US allies and partners hope that a modus vivendi will not come at their expense.”

Meanwhile, the two-month trade truce extension between the US and China and their proposed economic arrangements could provide some immediate relief for businesses. But the longer-term impact on Southeast Asia will depend on how Washington and Beijing implement their commitments.

Asean exporters have been concerned about transshipment risks and the spillover effects of a prolonged US-China trade war, particularly for those relying on Chinese inputs to manufacture goods for the US market.

“Progress on the trade front is a welcome respite,” Pitlo said.

Still, analysts cautioned that a more cooperative tone was unlikely to reverse continuing efforts by Washington and Beijing to secure supply chains and restrict sensitive technology transfers. Trump’s unpredictability also remains a risk factor.

“Under the Trump administration, predictability still has a short shelf life,” Giang said.

Southeast Asian countries therefore needed to compete on infrastructure, skills and local suppliers regardless of the direction of US-China relations, he said.

That could make it increasingly difficult for Southeast Asian economies to continue benefiting from their traditional role as intermediaries between the US and Chinese markets, Giang added.

On the proposed dialogue on artificial intelligence, Pitlo said a China-US understanding could help “assuage fears that great-power strife may lead to technology fragmentation” at a time when Washington and Beijing were advancing competing visions for future cutting-edge technologies.

But Giang argued that an AI dialogue alone was unlikely to overcome deeper structural divides or resolve the region’s technology dilemma.

“On AI and advanced technology, dialogue could help manage risks, but it does not automatically open access to advanced chips or bridge competing technological ecosystems,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Xi Jinping skipped the UN after his Trump summit
item.description:
Han Zheng, China’s vice-president, called on “major countries” to respect the sovereignty and security of Middle Eastern nations and bring about a two-state solution for the “Palestinian question” on Saturday at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in an implicit dig at the US and Israel.

This came as some analysts questioned why Chinese President Xi Jinping opted not to address the global body given his three-day summit in Washington with US President Donald Trump this week – despite the short distance between New York and Washington, Beijing’s long-standing assertions on the UN’s importance and active campaign to build soft power and promote its global initiatives.

“Many months ago, Chinese officials said that Xi wouldn’t go to the UN unless it was to mark a major anniversary,” said Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the German Marshall Fund of the United States. “Seems like a missed opportunity.”
item.content:encoded:
Han Zheng, China’s vice-president, called on “major countries” to respect the sovereignty and security of Middle Eastern nations and bring about a two-state solution for the “Palestinian question” on Saturday at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in an implicit dig at the US and Israel.

This came as some analysts questioned why Chinese President Xi Jinping opted not to address the global body given his three-day summit in Washington with US President Donald Trump this week – despite the short distance between New York and Washington, Beijing’s long-standing assertions on the UN’s importance and active campaign to build soft power and promote its global initiatives.

“Many months ago, Chinese officials said that Xi wouldn’t go to the UN unless it was to mark a major anniversary,” said Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the German Marshall Fund of the United States. “Seems like a missed opportunity.”

Since coming to power in 2012, Xi has addressed the annual General Assembly gathering once in person, in 2015 for the 70th anniversary. He appeared by video in 2020 and 2021 during the pandemic but missed the 80th anniversary last year when Premier Li Qiang spoke. In other years, China has generally been represented by other senior officials, including Han and Foreign Minister Wang Yi.

China has also placed significantly more importance on Washington relations than on multilateral issues, analysts said.

This week’s summit mirrored its counterpart hosted by China for Trump in May – limited to 48 hours with no side trips or multilateral events – to underscore the geopolitical parity Beijing sees as its due.

“He’s not giving America any more honour than Trump gave to the Chinese,” said Jeffrey Moon, principal at China Moon Strategies, a former US consul general in Chengdu. “In the Chinese psyche, that was more important than attending UNGA. Somebody else can do the speech.”

“Protocol-wise, [Xi’s appearance] would get slightly more benefit. But not appearing to be anything less than equal to the US would be probably more important.”

Among the initiatives China has promoted at the UN in recent years, touted by Han on Saturday, are its vaguely worded global development, security, civilisation and governance initiatives aimed at promoting prosperity, stability, mutual trust and procedural justice.

These dovetail with China’s growing global reputation.

A Pew Research Centre survey released this month found that US favourability across 20 countries was 36 per cent in 2026, down from 58 per cent in 2023, while China’s rose to 46 from 32 during the same period.

A Global Soft Power Index released in January saw the US maintain its No 1 ranking with a score of 74.9 out of 100 but it recorded the largest decline among the 193 countries ranked, while China strengthened its No 2 position modestly with a score of 73.5.

“It is difficult not to make a connection between some of the ‘America first’ policies and the negative turn of the US perceptions internationally,” the survey said, adding that China’s “soft power gains are underpinned by a long-term policy-led programme”.

Some wonder how much of the change is due to China’s actions, however, and how much to Trump’s deeply unpopular foreign policy, damaging tariffs, military adventurism and threats against long-standing allies.

While it has strongly supported multilateralism and the UN Charter, China has not always walked the walk, some argue.

“To fill the lane that America’s retreat has opened … China will need to put forward resources, not just rhetoric,” said Ryan Hass, a director at the Brookings Institution and former US National Security Council official. “Beijing clearly has ambition. I’m not clear that they’ll be able to realise it.”

Analysts say China attributes the Soviet Union’s demise and what it sees as America’s inexorable decline to being overstretched, including the US actions in the Middle East.

“Historically, global leaders have spent pretty generously to realise their vision of revising the international system. Beijing has not,” added Hass, a former US diplomat in Beijing, citing reduced Belt and Road Initiative largesse, perhaps given economic weakness and high youth unemployment at home.

While nations welcome Chinese infrastructure projects and preferential lending, few appear keen to follow its governance model, Hass said.

“They’ve been very tight-fisted,” he added. “It is striking how little progress Beijing is making in attracting followers to its vision. It reflects the limits in Beijing’s ability to attract support.”

Others said it may be unrealistic to expect China to fill the US void.

“The US has burned so many bridges and China has taken over so completely,” said Marc Limon, executive director of Universal Rights Group, a civic group based in Geneva. “They’re very good at coalition building with countries of the Global South. They have a huge number of friends. They really do try to help.”

Han’s speech on Saturday comes as the Iran war started by Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nears its seventh month. Earlier in the week, in a fiery exchange, Netanyahu accused UN diplomats of “mind-blowing hypocrisy” over protests as he addressed the assembly on Thursday.

Envoys booed loudly and many walked out during his speech, prompting him to accuse those leaving the cavernous hall of being “moral cowards”, claiming that many of their same nations had “privately thanked us for taking out Iran’s nukes”.

Relations between Trump and Netanyahu have also grown notably cooler recently. Trump chose not to meet Netanyahu earlier this week when they overlapped in New York.

The death toll now exceeds 73,600 Palestinians in Gaza since the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel that killed some 1,200 people and saw 251 others taken hostage, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, as Netanyahu revs up campaigning for his late October re-election bid.

Han on Saturday called on the international community to respect the sovereignty and security of Middle Eastern nations.

At a thinly attended Saturday morning session, Han called on the international community to “reject the Cold War mindset and bloc confrontation”.

“We should settle differences and disputes through dialogue and consultation, and oppose unilateral military actions that violate the UN Charter and circumvent Security Council authorisation.”

He also called for efforts to safeguard peace, rebuild trust and reject unilateralism at the expense of multilateralism, echoing themes voiced this week by Wang.

China’s vice-president did not join Xi during the Washington summit that saw Trump meet Xi on the tarmac when he arrived Wednesday evening. The Chinese president did not bestow the same honour on Trump when he landed in Beijing in May, a role he delegated to Han.

item.title: [SCMP] Why US chip controls took a back seat at the Xi-Trump summit
item.description:
There is little question that Jensen Huang and Lisa Su, the heads of US semiconductor chip giants Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), had secured two of the best seats in the house at the White House state dinner on Thursday evening: at the head table alongside the two presidents and their wives.

But what remains unclear is how much progress they were able to make on their primary goal of restoring access to the Chinese market, amid entrenched opposition to that happening in both China and the US.

That is because US semiconductor chip export controls do not seem to have been a major sticking point during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s historic state visit to Washington this week, despite most of the restrictions still being in place.
item.content:encoded:
There is little question that Jensen Huang and Lisa Su, the heads of US semiconductor chip giants Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), had secured two of the best seats in the house at the White House state dinner on Thursday evening: at the head table alongside the two presidents and their wives.

But what remains unclear is how much progress they were able to make on their primary goal of restoring access to the Chinese market, amid entrenched opposition to that happening in both China and the US.

That is because US semiconductor chip export controls do not seem to have been a major sticking point during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s historic state visit to Washington this week, despite most of the restrictions still being in place.

Early indications suggest that export controls were not a significant topic of debate during the talks, with no direct mention of them in the readouts so far from both Beijing and Washington summarising the achievements of the Xi–Trump summit.

“This is especially strange considering that export controls were brought up regularly by Xi during his talks with [President Joe] Biden,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at Washington think tank Brookings specialising in Chinese technology.

On Friday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC that the US side had taken “off the table” all the export controls “that are national security issues” during trade talks this week. China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Saturday did not mention export controls or Beijing’s usual references to US tech restrictions in its announcement of eight deliverables from the summit, including the launch of a China-US dialogue on AI risks.

But if export controls have become less of a sticking point, it is not because they have gone away. The Trump administration has largely kept intact restrictions first introduced by the Biden administration in October 2022 on China’s ability to obtain advanced chips and chipmaking equipment.

Some areas were even tightened at the start of Trump’s second term, including a ban on exporting Nvidia’s H20 chip to China, which the company had developed specifically to comply with US rules.

According to Chan, Beijing has likely grown more comfortable with the export controls already in place as it looks to deepen its technological self-reliance campaign to reduce its reliance on US tech.

“The biggest thing that’s changed is China’s growing confidence in its chip self-reliance efforts,” he said. “While the 2022 export controls may have surprised Beijing at the time, China has made real progress on building a domestic supply chain for advanced semiconductors in the years since”.

A temporary stalemate

When Washington first imposed sweeping export controls on China in 2022, Beijing treated them as a direct attack on China’s technological and economic rise and began regularly calling for their removal in talks with the US.

The controls became a wedge issue in US-China relations. At China-US talks on AI safety in Geneva in May 2024, Chinese officials tied progress on AI safety to the US unwinding those controls, former Biden administration officials have said.

This was not an issue this time around. Export controls were not brought up during the AI safety related talks between Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last Sunday in New York, according to Greer, who also attended the meeting.

The AI talks, which also resulted in the launch of a “bilateral communication channel” for AI incidents, were “candid, in-depth and constructive”, Beijing said.

Paul Triolo, a partner and technology policy lead at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, said Beijing is likely “pleased with progress that the domestic semiconductor industry has made despite the [US] controls”.

Chinese chip manufacturers are taking a greater share of the domestic market. According to TrendForce, Chinese chip suppliers led by Huawei Technologies and Cambricon Technologies are set to capture nearly 80 per cent of the domestic AI server market this year.

Nvidia, AMD and other foreign suppliers’ share is set to fall to 21 per cent in 2026 from 34 per cent last year, according to the Taipei-based research firm.

Domestic chip substitution is expected to further ramp up in the coming years as tech self-reliance remains a central pillar of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan. Earlier this year, Beijing resisted efforts by both President Donald Trump and Nvidia’s Huang to push for the US chip giant’s less powerful H200 chips to be allowed back into the Chinese market.

Beijing has since allowed a small number of Chinese tech companies to purchase the chip with the quantities capped, as it continues to promote domestic chip adoption instead. Meanwhile, the delayed approval caused Nvidia to take a US$400 million charge due to excess H200 inventory in the first half of the year.

Spanner in the works

Still, talk of an export control impasse might still be premature. That is because Beijing is likely to push back forcefully against any new restrictions the US introduces, with some already on the horizon, according to Triolo.

A major area of concern is US congressional efforts to bolster its export controls regime. One of these is the Match Act, which would require US allies such as Japan and the Netherlands to more closely align with US restrictions on selling advanced semiconductor equipment to China, such as Dutch firm ASML’s deep ultraviolet (DUV) immersion lithography machines.

The bill has been folded into the National Defence Authorisation Act (NDAA) in the US Senate, improving its chances of becoming law.

“Chinese officials view any new controls as a violation of the Busan agreement, and [would] retaliate strongly via expanded controls on rare earths and related production equipment,” said Triolo, referring to the economic detente reached in October 2025 between the two countries that paused escalating tit-for-tat tariffs and export controls, which the two leaders agreed to extend to January.

“Beijing likely sought assurances on this [this week],” he said.

Even as the official readouts of the two presidents’ meeting have largely focused on trade and investment, senior Chinese officials have referenced US technological restrictions on China in statements elsewhere.

On Saturday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said in a post-meeting statement that China and the US should not “adopt a defensive posture towards each other” in the emerging field of AI.

The relative quiet on export controls this week might therefore reflect strong domestic pressure on both sides not to concede ground, Triolo said, with powerful contingents in the US pushing for tighter controls and those in China for greater self-reliance.

“Neither side will acknowledge progress on any of these issues, given domestic sensitivities around anything that could be perceived as a concession,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] How Kenya’s sacred Mrima Hill became new front in US-China minerals rivalry
item.description:
Mrima Hill, a sacred site about 65km (40 miles) southwest of Mombasa on Kenya’s Indian Ocean coast, is emerging as a new front in the US-China rivalry for critical minerals.

US-led and Chinese bidders are competing for rights to develop the site, which is rich in rare earths and niobium, a metal used to make steel stronger and lighter.

American officials have offered to support Kenya’s development of its domestic critical minerals processing industry as Washington seeks to challenge Beijing’s dominance of global rare earth refining.
item.content:encoded:
Mrima Hill, a sacred site about 65km (40 miles) southwest of Mombasa on Kenya’s Indian Ocean coast, is emerging as a new front in the US-China rivalry for critical minerals.

US-led and Chinese bidders are competing for rights to develop the site, which is rich in rare earths and niobium, a metal used to make steel stronger and lighter.

American officials have offered to support Kenya’s development of its domestic critical minerals processing industry as Washington seeks to challenge Beijing’s dominance of global rare earth refining.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Kenyan President William Ruto on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last week. They discussed how Kenya’s critical minerals resources could “position the country as a key player in the sector while presenting opportunities for US firms to provide value addition”.

A senior US delegation also made the case for such American participation at the AmCham Business Summit in Nairobi on September 9. It included Frank Garcia, assistant secretary of state for African affairs, and Chris Kulukundis, acting deputy assistant secretary of state for Southern Africa, foreign assistance and critical minerals.

Washington is trying to reduce its reliance on China for processed rare earths. China accounted for about 85 per cent of global rare earth refining in 2025, according to the International Energy Agency.

Aly-Khan Satchu, a geoeconomic analyst focused on sub-Saharan Africa, said the US-China contest went beyond simply securing mineral deposits.

“Ultimately, the US-China competition around critical minerals is less about access to those minerals and more about the refining infrastructure,” he said.

“China holds a decade’s worth of advantage,” Satchu added. Kenya, he said, should assess competing offers with that wider strategic context in mind.

Garcia said Washington was prepared to support Kenya’s efforts to build its mining and processing industries. “Critical minerals are a top priority for President Donald Trump,” he said. “We are ready to work with Kenya as it becomes a regional leader in this space.”

In remarks that appeared to take a thinly veiled swipe at China, Garcia said: “American companies are not here to extract and ship. That is not a partnership. That is extraction.” Garcia added that US involvement would include investment in communities, workforce development and technology transfer.

He said Washington wanted more processing to take place in Kenya, creating local jobs and allowing the host country to capture more of the minerals’ value.

At the same event, Kulukundis said two US-led consortiums were among the bidders seeking development rights at Mrima Hill, where historical studies indicate the presence of about 105 million tonnes of mineralised ore.

Kenya launched an international tender in March to select a developer for the deposit, whose rare earth and niobium resources have been valued at US$62.4 billion.

Mining principal secretary Harry Kimtai said six candidates remained in contention, down from 13 groups that initially showed interest. Two of the remaining bidders were Chinese, he said.

“The deal has not been closed,” Kimtai said.

The Mrima Earth Limited Consortium, led by New York-listed Critical Metals Corp, said in July that it had advanced in the tender. Australian companies RareX and Iluka Resources had formed a consortium and sought prospecting rights over Mrima Hill before the international competition began. The identities of the other bidders have not been publicly disclosed.

Chris Berry, head of US-based commodities advisory firm House Mountain Partners, said the US government had proven to be aggressive when funding domestic rare earth projects such as MP Materials and USA Rare Earth. “The US presence in this bidding war indicates that Western interests are looking to diversify supply chains and bolster allied efforts to counter China’s grip on critical mineral supply chains both in Africa and globally,” Berry said.

On whether US-backed processing in producing countries could compete with China, Berry said: “Absolutely, but the timing here is crucial. The US isn’t competitive today, but that can change with continued investment and offtake agreements.”

He cautioned that reducing dependence on China would take years. “Japan has been working to minimise its dependence on Chinese materials for 15 years and is still perhaps 60 per cent dependent on Chinese imports, down from 90 per cent originally. Untangling supply chains is a long, hard slog.”

US interest in Mrima Hill was apparent by June last year, when Marc Dillard, who was then serving as charge d’affaires at the US embassy in Kenya, visited the site. Agence France-Presse later reported, citing a community guard, that Chinese nationals had also tried to enter the area but were turned away.

Local residents have resisted previous plans to mine Mrima Hill, which is a “Kaya”, a sacred forest and ancestral site for the Digo, a coastal people belonging to the nine-group Mijikenda community. The forest was designated a national monument in 1992.

Residents fear mining would damage shrines and wildlife habitat, lead to evictions, and threaten farming and access to forest resources.

Washington is also pursuing mineral agreements elsewhere in Africa. In December last year, the US signed an agreement giving qualifying American investors preferential access to selected mining projects in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Washington has since backed US-based Virtus Minerals’ acquisition of Chemaf, a local operator of copper and cobalt projects. The deal followed the collapse of a planned sale to a unit of Chinese state-owned Norinco after Kinshasa withheld approval, reportedly following US pressure. The outcome marked a direct US gain at China’s expense in the contest for Congolese minerals.

The US is also seeking a larger role in Nigeria, where lithium, nickel, copper and rare earth prospects have been identified.

Last month, solid minerals minister Dele Alake said he led a delegation to the White House to discuss American investment in Nigeria’s minerals sector. “We talked about moving beyond simple extraction and working together across the entire supply chain, from exploration and mining to local processing and refining,” Alake said after talks with National Security Council official David Copley.

Washington is entering a sector where Chinese companies already have a sizeable presence. Chinese firms had invested more than US$1.3 billion in lithium processing since late 2023, including a US$250 million plant commissioned in Nasarawa state in July, according to the Nigerian government.

item.title: [SCMP] 3 top reasons Trump will face a stronger Xi Jinping at November Apec forum in China
item.description:
When Donald Trump arrives in Shenzhen for the November Apec summit, he will face a Chinese leader even more confident than the one who left Washington this week after a state visit heavy on pageantry but light on concrete deliverables.

Experts attributed this confidence to three key factors – a newly upgraded bilateral framework seeking a “constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity”, the warmer tone during Xi’s three-day visit, and – crucially – the significant leverage of host diplomacy.

In southern China’s Shenzhen – home to technological giants Huawei, BYD and Tencent – President Xi Jinping will have greater control over the agenda and showcase Beijing’s growing diplomatic clout in ways impossible during a bilateral summit.
item.content:encoded:
When Donald Trump arrives in Shenzhen for the November Apec summit, he will face a Chinese leader even more confident than the one who left Washington this week after a state visit heavy on pageantry but light on concrete deliverables.

Experts attributed this confidence to three key factors – a newly upgraded bilateral framework seeking a “constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity”, the warmer tone during Xi’s three-day visit, and – crucially – the significant leverage of host diplomacy.

In southern China’s Shenzhen – home to technological giants Huawei, BYD and Tencent – President Xi Jinping will have greater control over the agenda and showcase Beijing’s growing diplomatic clout in ways impossible during a bilateral summit.

Meanwhile, the Washington spectacle will reverberate with US allies and middle powers, who experts said would need to reassess their China strategies.

“As the Apec host, China will clearly possess far more autonomy in agenda-setting, topic selection, and preparatory work than it did during the Washington summit, where the US controlled the choreography while China held only participation and discussion rights,” said Chen Qi, director of the Centre for US-China Relations at Tsinghua University.

The shift in leverage would be particularly evident in the multilateral setting, he added.

“Beijing could also showcase its diplomatic influence and leadership far more effectively than in bilateral encounters.”

Statements released by both countries on Saturday confirmed that Trump intended to travel to Shenzhen in November to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, setting up a third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.

Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations at the International Crisis Group, said the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting would help Xi highlight “China’s growing economic and diplomatic sway – including with several US allies and partners” shortly after midterm elections likely to be bruising for Trump’s Republican Party.

“Xi appreciates how greatly Trump values opportunities to convey that the two leaders enjoy a strong rapport … Their Washington summit this week demonstrated his willingness to reverse or weaken US measures that might risk his meetings with Xi,” Wyne added.

Zhang Chi, senior researcher at the University of Hong Kong’s Centre on Contemporary China and the World (CCCW), called the upgraded relationship “a very successful strategic convergence” that placed Beijing and Washington on a fairer footing.

“Equally important is that China has demonstrated that attempts by Washington to reshape the bilateral power balance through ‘maximum pressure’ are ineffective and create uncontrollable problems,” he said.

Marking his second state visit to the US since 2015, Xi arrived to a rare tarmac greeting from President Donald Trump – a courtesy usually delegated to lower-level officials.

The 42 hours of summitry that followed saw both leaders hold up China as an equal or near-equal power to the United States. Trump spoke warmly of an emerging “great friendship”, while Xi portrayed the bilateral bond as a “river that never stops flowing” as its leaders work to “steer the giant ship” of relations forward.

Saturday’s statements by both countries further indicated a fourth Xi-Trump meeting this year, at the December Group of 20 summit in Miami. The pair last met in May, when Trump travelled to Beijing on a state visit.

Just ahead of the Washington summit, the two sides agreed to extend the bilateral trade truce set to expire in November by two months. As part of the truce, Washington has pledged to pause new tariffs while Beijing will suspend some rare earth export controls.

The unprecedented frequency of head-of-state interaction – four summits in eight months – signals a window of relative stability, according to Chinese experts.

The high-frequency meetings this year make policy continuity “both a promise and an inertia”, said Zhang Zhizhou, from the school of international relations and diplomacy at Beijing Foreign Studies University.

This would potentially help to shield Beijing from disruptive unilateral actions by Washington in the interim, he said, while identifying several factors contributing to China’s increased confidence heading into the Apec summit. These include China’s rising technological strength, growing influence in the Global South and Belt and Road Initiative partner nations.

All of this would make the Chinese side – which excels at host diplomacy – “more confident and bolster their negotiating position”, Zhang in Beijing said.

Shortly after Trump and Xi wrapped up their Washington summit, the White House announced that both sides had recommended reciprocal tariff relief covering US$30 billion worth of non-sensitive trade moving in each direction.

US exports slated for preferential treatment under the proposed framework include agricultural produce, seafood, timber, cosmetics and medical equipment.

The reciprocal Chinese list covers consumer goods such as small household appliances, toys, festive decorations and children’s car seats.

But experts also urged caution on long-term predictability, noting that the present strategy remained tied to Trump personally and domestic pressures and geopolitics could test the diplomatic momentum.

“Going forward, there are two key factors to watch: whether Trump can still honour his commitments once his hands are free, as upcoming midterm elections and the quagmire in Iran are currently draining his attention; and second, any provocative moves on Taiwan arms sales,” Zhang from CCCW said.

Trump, who has described arms sales to Taiwan as a negotiating tool with Beijing, postponed a planned US$14 billion package following his May summit with Xi.

The South China Morning Post reported this month that the US was considering postponing the announcement of arms sales to Taiwan until the end of the year, pointing to the potential Apec and G20 summits.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise self-ruled Taiwan as an independent state. But Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Ma Bo, associate professor at Nanjing University, said Washington was operating on two parallel tracks. While the White House projects cordiality at the top, the US security apparatus – aligning with its allies – continues to press ahead.

“Detente at the leader level does not bind Congress, technological export controls, or the actions of America’s regional allies,” Ma warned.

The current equilibrium is also seen as likely to prompt uneasy recalibration among middle powers and traditional US allies who watched Xi’s visit with a mix of relief and trepidation.

Xin Qiang, deputy director of the Centre for US Studies at Fudan University, noted that Washington’s regional partners – from Tokyo to Manila – were increasingly anxious about the potential erosion of US strategic support.

“As [US-China] ties stabilise, the backing these countries can extract from Washington will inevitably erode,” Xin said.

“If they attempt to use America to confront Beijing, they may find themselves without US endorsement, or even risk being left out in the cold.”

According to Zhang from CCCW, Europe is in an “embarrassing” position, as the progress in US-China ties will make Europe’s own escalation of trade pressure on Beijing look increasingly discordant.

Meanwhile, countries that recognise Beijing’s playbook in handling Washington – “those convinced that caving in to Trump brings no tangible benefit, will be the first to pivot towards Beijing with a more proactive and pragmatic posture”, he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Pakistan’s endless war on militants fails to break the cycle
item.description:
For over two decades, Pakistan has waged countless counterterrorism campaigns against Taliban and Baloch insurgents in its western regions bordering Afghanistan and Iran, yet remains mired in a cycle of violence it cannot break.

Scores of soldiers, policemen and civilians are killed every month in Pakistan’s northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and southwestern Balochistan provinces, where near-daily attacks on security personnel, government officials and other prominent figures are carried out by militants to undermine the state’s authority and credibility.

Insurgents target patrols, checkpoints, police stations and administrative centres with roadside bombs, explosive-laden drones, coordinated ambushes, suicide attacks, large-scale raids, assassinations and kidnappings.
item.content:encoded:
For over two decades, Pakistan has waged countless counterterrorism campaigns against Taliban and Baloch insurgents in its western regions bordering Afghanistan and Iran, yet remains mired in a cycle of violence it cannot break.

Scores of soldiers, policemen and civilians are killed every month in Pakistan’s northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and southwestern Balochistan provinces, where near-daily attacks on security personnel, government officials and other prominent figures are carried out by militants to undermine the state’s authority and credibility.

Insurgents target patrols, checkpoints, police stations and administrative centres with roadside bombs, explosive-laden drones, coordinated ambushes, suicide attacks, large-scale raids, assassinations and kidnappings.

Pakistan’s military regularly hails the success of its counterterrorism operations, touting the eradication of hundreds of perpetrators each month. Its press releases often read like scoreboards, listing the number of insurgents “sent to hell” – with only a handful surviving to be interrogated.

Yet these tactical victories have not translated into the strategic success Islamabad has long yearned for, analysts say.

“Force alone won’t help in curbing security issues long term,” said Farwa Aamer, director of South Asia initiatives at the Asia Society Policy Institute in New York. “Force will continue to meet force, keeping the loop alive. There has to be some political solution and dialogue.”

Such a solution would not appear overnight, she said, but without one – or at least a viable strategy to combat insurgency – Pakistan faced the prospect of continued instability deterring foreign investment, not least in its critical minerals sector.

Border escalations

Armed groups have long exploited the porous Pakistan-Afghanistan border to seek sanctuary, smuggle goods and provide logistical support.

In recent years, months-long terrorist campaigns have driven up casualty numbers and prompted Pakistan to launch retaliatory air strikes against insurgents based in eastern Afghanistan.

The latest came on Monday, when military jets struck Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) “terrorist camps and safe havens” in Afghanistan’s Paktika and Kunar provinces, killing 28 militants, Pakistan’s information ministry said, including what it said were suicide bombers in training.

Monday’s air strikes followed an assault on a mosque on September 18 that left at least 31 people dead and more than 100 injured at a police compound in the northwestern town of Kohat, Pakistan.

Zabihullah Mujahid, chief spokesman for Afghanistan’s Taliban regime, has repeatedly denied the existence of terrorist camps in his country and claimed in a statement that Pakistan’s air strikes killed three civilians.

After he vowed revenge, border skirmishes intensified, culminating on Thursday in eight “rudimentary” drones being launched from Afghan territory into Pakistani airspace, security officials said. All were shot down, four of them near Kohat.

Mujahid again denied responsibility for the drone incursions, though Pakistani officials view them as further evidence that Kabul is actively supporting the TTP, not merely tolerating its presence.

Pakistan retaliated in the early hours of Thursday with “precision aerial and drone strikes” on 10 locations in Afghanistan “used for launching and storing these drones”, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar announced in a social media post.

Officials in Islamabad have made clear they believe the Taliban government in Kabul has been feigning interest in recent diplomatic efforts by China, Turkey and Qatar to de-escalate tensions, following a previous cycle of insurgent violence that ended with Pakistan carrying out cross-border air strikes in June.

At a meeting in Belarus this summer, officials discussed potential compromises, including a joint mechanism to monitor the cross-border movement of TTP militants, according to Islamabad-based security analyst Iftikhar Firdous, who disclosed details of the talks in a social media post on September 16.

The meeting reportedly failed to produce a breakthrough because Kabul refused to compel the TTP to halt its attacks on Pakistan or relocate militants away from the border.

The day before the Kohat attack, Qatar’s National Security Council deputy secretary general Hamad Khamis al-Kubaisi and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalın had visited Kabul in a renewed attempt to broker further talks between Afghan and Pakistani officials.

Analysts see the repeated cycles of violence as proof that Islamabad’s largely reactive approach to counterterrorism, built around retaliatory counter-attacks, is not working.

Riccardo Valle, a researcher tracking militancy across South and Central Asia, called the strategy “incomplete and limited”.

Local grievances and poor governance constrained the effectiveness of counterterrorism operations in violence-hit areas, he said, adding that local security forces in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan – especially the police – were ill-equipped to confront “full-fledged insurgencies”.

The reactive, rather than preventive, nature of intelligence-based operations is another limiting factor, according to Valle.

“Thus, tactical success cannot compensate for a broader strategic deficiency, which fuels a circle of instability” in the affected provinces, he said, with the twin insurgencies becoming a “multigenerational issue”, drawing in new cohorts of young militants.

As such, Valle said a holistic approach that accounted for both Pakistan’s domestic concerns and the wider conflict’s international dimensions would be essential.

Converging insurgencies

Signs have also emerged of increasing collaboration between the radical Islamist TTP and ethno-nationalist Baloch separatist groups in Balochistan.

The vast and sparsely populated province, bordering southern Afghanistan and eastern Iran, recorded a marked rise in attacks over the summer. In one instance this July, the TTP and the Balochistan Liberation Army carried out separate attacks in the province’s Pishin and Ziarat districts within hours of each other.

Muhammad Faisal, a South Asia security researcher based at the University of Technology Sydney, said tactical coordination between the TTP and Baloch insurgents was “increasingly documented”, including reports of joint training and logistical links.

However, he doubts this will amount to a “durable strategic coalition” given the two groups’ different ideologies and aims – the TTP seeks to overthrow the government of Pakistan and establish an Islamist political order, while Baloch groups are more concerned with achieving independence.

Linguistic, cultural and geographic differences further limit each group’s ability to operate in the other’s core territory, likely confining cooperation to an exchange of tactics and targets, according to Faisal.

Meanwhile, Pakistan’s ties with Iran have improved since the two countries exchanged air strikes against militants based on the other’s soil in January 2024.

Islamabad helped broker talks earlier this year aimed at ending the US-Israel war on Iran, but Faisal said that widening conflict and residual Pakistan-Iran mistrust would continue to hamstring relations.

Pakistan has also accused India, with which it fought a brief air war in May last year, of covertly supporting Baloch separatists as proxies.

However, Faisal said Islamabad would be better off closely monitoring the separatist networks involved instead of treating every one of their attacks as proof of foreign backing.

The more immediate danger was the effect the Iran conflict might have on border security if it created a power vacuum filled with more militancy and foreign intelligence operatives, he said.

“This is a serious security risk, but one best managed through intelligence cooperation and sustained diplomacy,” Faisal added.

item.title: [SCMP] India’s ‘cockroach’ movement targets election chief in political pivot
item.description:
India’s “cockroach” youth movement is testing whether it can turn anger over education and jobs into a broader challenge to the country’s political establishment, two months after its protests helped force an education minister to resign over alleged entrance exam leaks.

Its latest target is another powerful institution: the country’s election watchdog. The shift marks a transition for the movement from high-profile demonstrations in New Delhi to a more diffuse campaign of school audits, meetings with authorities and demands for electoral reform.

Leaders of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) on Thursday demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after a local newspaper reported allegations that his handling of voter-list revisions could disenfranchise eligible voters and undermine confidence in India’s electoral process.
item.content:encoded:
India’s “cockroach” youth movement is testing whether it can turn anger over education and jobs into a broader challenge to the country’s political establishment, two months after its protests helped force an education minister to resign over alleged entrance exam leaks.

Its latest target is another powerful institution: the country’s election watchdog. The shift marks a transition for the movement from high-profile demonstrations in New Delhi to a more diffuse campaign of school audits, meetings with authorities and demands for electoral reform.

Leaders of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) on Thursday demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after a local newspaper reported allegations that his handling of voter-list revisions could disenfranchise eligible voters and undermine confidence in India’s electoral process.

The Indian Express reported on Wednesday that two election commissioners had raised questions or expressed concern to Kumar at least 14 times in 10 months, mostly over the process of updating voter lists that began last year.

The report alleged that Kumar repeatedly bypassed the two other election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi – who had formally raised objections – making critical decisions regarding voter lists, registration and deletions without their knowledge or consent.

The dispute has heightened scrutiny of a large-scale exercise to revise electoral rolls, with critics questioning whether voters excluded from draft lists will have adequate safeguards and opportunities to challenge their removal.

“When millions of names can disappear from draft rolls, the burden is on the commission to establish that every exclusion is lawful, transparent and subject to meaningful reviews,” said CJP National Convenor Abhijeet Dipke.

If Kumar did not resign by Saturday, the CJP would launch a nationwide protest, Dipke said.

Anjali, a national executive member of the All India Students Association, said 300 to 400 young people representing different backgrounds had already launched protests demanding Kumar’s resignation.

“We believe this [the chief election commissioner’s actions] weakens democracy to the core. So along with civil society and concerned citizens, we have staged a protest at Jantar Mantar,” she said, referring to the venue in the capital that was the focal point for earlier demonstrations. She added that they had been detained by the police.

The CJP began in May as a satirical online campaign after Chief Justice of India Surya Kant referred to unemployed young people as “cockroaches”. It then turned its attention to alleged irregularities in the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) – a nationwide medical examination – and other grievances with the education system.

Its protests at Jantar Mantar in Delhi helped force the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July. But the movement has since shifted from high-decibel demonstrations in the capital to less prominent school audits and meetings with authorities across at least six states.

The non-political movement, which has given voice to middle-class anxieties over opportunities for young people, highlights a growing challenge for political leaders trying to respond to one of the largest sections of India’s electorate.

“There is a definite Generation Z factor coming up. That Generation Z factor is largely anti-establishment,” said Yashwant Deshmukh, an independent political commentator and founder of C-Voter, a public opinion research firm.

The younger generation’s grievances had exposed a cross-party challenge that all political parties were struggling with, Deshmukh said: connecting with young people’s hearts and minds.

India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which is now in its third successive term – this time at the head of a multiparty coalition – has gradually recovered ground in state elections after losing its outright majority in 2024.

The BJP’s dominance has only grown amid a fragmented opposition led by the Congress party, which held sway for decades following India’s independence in 1947.

Analysts say it is too early to predict whether the cockroach movement could trigger broader political changes ahead of a string of elections next year in Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Manipur, Himachal Pradesh and Gujarat.

“It is going to create problems for anybody in power in those states. It is not one-way traffic,” Deshmukh said, referring to the BJP’s political fortunes.

On Friday, Congress was set to stage protest marches at state election offices across India to demand Kumar’s arrest.

“No matter what narrative is created by the opposition and Congress, eventually it will come down to what kind of party infrastructure they have to turn that traction from Gen Z into votes against the BJP,” Deshmukh added.

Young voters’ challenge

The cockroach movement’s expansion beyond education has coincided with what independent political commentator Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay described as a change in India’s “political drift”.
