Demanding the removal of the chief election commissioner was likely to catalyse that change further, Mukhopadhyay said.

“What has happened is that the movement has triggered the erasure of fear from the minds of youngsters,” he said, pointing to a protest against the gang-rape of a 17-year-old girl on Thursday by students from Lady Shri Ram College for Women in Delhi as an example.

But Mukhopadhyay warned that the protests did not mean the BJP was facing an electoral rout, saying next year’s state elections would provide a clearer test of its popularity.

Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi of Congress has also been seeking to connect with Gen Z voters through a nationwide student outreach programme called Chhatron Ki Goonj (Echo of Students), aimed at amplifying grievances over the education and examination systems.

The initiative had given Gandhi greater credibility among young people, Mukhopadhyay said.

Meanwhile, a high-powered panel led by technology entrepreneur Nandan Nilekani is examining structural reforms to the NEET.

The panel was announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi after weeks of protests against alleged irregularities in the exam, which culminated in Pradhan’s resignation and the government agreeing to several of the movement’s demands. Its report is due by the end of this month.

Suhruda Dasyam, who graduated from the London School of Economics in December and currently works in London, said she took part in solidarity protests in the city in July to express her support for the movement.

“I think there is a larger issue that needs to be addressed. People are unemployed and struggling to get by. I sought education in a country that is not mine because I feel that I don’t have the same opportunities in India,” she said. “I feel so many people share the same sentiment. I just hope that we can get there some day.”

Dasyam said the movement had not lost momentum, although its focus had shifted since Pradhan’s resignation.

The cockroach movement had also been trying to build a presence beyond the capital, with its leaders personally inspecting facilities in government schools across different states, said Harsh Ramaswamy, an independent political commentator.

“Their network is growing well. What they have not been able to do is attract more people to do the job in a decentralised way,” he said, pointing out that visiting India’s roughly 1 million state schools would be physically impossible without support from other groups.

The audits had struggled to capture national attention, partly because the CJP’s founders had refused to align with any political party, reducing local media interest, Ramaswamy said.

Pradhan’s resignation also appeared to reduce the movement’s momentum, he added, as many young supporters felt the job was done.

item.title: [SCMP] Pacing problem: can AI fears overcome US-China race dynamics and force a slowdown?
item.description:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the sixth part of a series, Chong Ming Lee and Vincent Chow examine what’s behind the call for “pacing” by American AI giants – effectively a slowdown in development – and how the phenomenon is being viewed in China.

After years of rapid development, leading US AI executives are proposing what would have been unthinkable even a year earlier: that it may be time to slow down.

In recent weeks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk have all called for “pacing” the development of frontier artificial intelligence over purported fears that its capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards designed to control them.
item.content:encoded:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the sixth part of a series, Chong Ming Lee and Vincent Chow examine what’s behind the call for “pacing” by American AI giants – effectively a slowdown in development – and how the phenomenon is being viewed in China.

After years of rapid development, leading US AI executives are proposing what would have been unthinkable even a year earlier: that it may be time to slow down.

In recent weeks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk have all called for “pacing” the development of frontier artificial intelligence over purported fears that its capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards designed to control them.

On Wednesday, Amodei pushed further for a slowdown when he addressed the UN Security Council by video link, warning that mismanaged AI posed an existential threat to humanity and urging nations to unite on global safety standards.

These public statements come ahead of a highly anticipated summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday, after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng met in New York City on the weekend to discuss AI safety, among other issues.

Yet despite converging on the language of restraint, Silicon Valley’s AI leaders remain locked in a high-stakes and costly tech race against each other – and with China – with no clear winner in sight.

These dynamics, both domestically between industry players and globally between the world’s two AI superpowers, make it highly unlikely that a slowdown will happen any time soon, analysts told the South China Morning Post.

“Even the US companies themselves cannot agree on that,” said Victor Shih, a professor at the University of California San Diego and an expert on Chinese elite politics. “So certainly the US and China will not agree on that.”

It has been four years since Washington imposed wide-ranging controls on the export of advanced semiconductor technology to China, citing national security concerns. Yet Chinese AI models from the likes of DeepSeek and Moonshot AI continue to be competitive with their US counterparts in price and capability.

This, in turn, threatens the trillion-dollar valuations of OpenAI and Anthropic as they head towards initial public offerings, as well as challenging US claims of global AI leadership – an explicit priority of US President Donald Trump, who outright dismissed the calls for a slow down in AI development.

“AI taking over the world, destroying humanity, and all other things bad, is a hoax,” he wrote on social media last week, raising questions about whether the world can pace AI without the support of one of its most powerful leaders.

The more pacing is framed as a way to win geopolitical competition, the harder it becomes to cooperate on the risks both sides share

Oskar Galeev, Concordia AI

What is driving calls to slow down?

There have long been concerns about the existential risks of AI. Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, winners of the Turing Award computer science prize and widely regarded as the “Godfathers” of AI, have both warned that the technology could eventually displace all humans, with Hinton saying earlier this month that a 10 per cent chance of AI killing all humans within a decade was not an “unreasonable” estimate.

While such concerns are legitimate, what sets apart the recent statements by industry leaders such as Amodei and Altman was that their AI safety proposals also served commercial and geopolitical ends, said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy in Beijing.

Sun pointed to Amodei’s recent essay “We Must Pace the Frontier”, in which the Anthropic founder warned that a swarm of AI agents could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months, potentially causing “hundreds of billions of dollars in damage”.

While the essay laid out why Amodei believes pacing is needed, it also devoted a large part to advocating for tighter restrictions on China’s AI industry. These included US semiconductor chip export controls and a “crackdown on unauthorised distillation by companies” in “autocratic” China.

“Amodei explicitly connects pacing with preserving a US lead over China,” Sun said. That made it “difficult” for Chinese policymakers to view the move as “politically neutral”, the Tsinghua fellow added, even if Amodei acknowledged that “[global] pacing will require cooperation with China”.

Reaction in China to Amodei’s essay was dismissive, with many accusing the tech CEO of using the guise of AI safety to shape the rules governing the sector and to entrench Anthropic’s position as an industry leader.

Last week, the official newspaper of the Communist Party, People’s Daily, published a commentary accusing the US of seeking to monopolise frontier AI development, while a DeepSeek engineer invoked Nazi Germany in a blog post that criticised OpenAI and Anthropic for their latest pacing calls.

China was likely to draw a sharp distinction between AI safety and efforts it viewed as “AI containment”, according to Wei Sun, principal analyst for AI at Counterpoint Research. Beijing has recently unveiled new AI initiatives that call for greater AI safety measures and international cooperation on AI governance, including a new “AI Safety Governance Framework” standards document for the industry released last week.

Oskar Galeev, a researcher at Beijing-based AI safety consultancy Concordia AI, said the Chinese government had demonstrated that it increasingly cared about AI safety. But it would still require the US to deal with it on an “equal footing”, he said, rather than as a subordinate being dictated to by a stronger power.

“The more pacing is framed as a way to win geopolitical competition, the harder it becomes to cooperate on the risks both sides share,” he said.

Existential risks, practical realities

Geopolitics aside, even getting the US to pace its own industry would be a challenge, according to UC San Diego’s Shih. While the Anthropic and OpenAI founders have raised alarms about the existential risks of AI, they have also been rebuffed by fellow industry titans including Meta Platforms’ Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who dismissed such worries as “complete nonsense” at an event last week.

Huang dismissed such “doomerism” while on a New York Times podcast on Wednesday , arguing that fearmongering only slowed down industry adoption.

There are questions over how a pacing mechanism would be enforced given high levels of mistrust between US AI companies.

As Karen Hao chronicled in her award-winning 2025 book Empire of AI, Altman and Musk helped found OpenAI in 2015 because they did not trust Google to develop AI safely. Six years later, Amodei and other former OpenAI executives and researchers left to start Anthropic after losing trust in Altman to develop AI safely.

Musk, founder of Grok model developer SpaceXAI – formerly xAI – took Altman to court earlier this year after having long accused the OpenAI CEO of prioritising profits over AI safety.

Qian Zilan, a research scholar at the independent AI governance think tank GovAI, said US AI leaders claimed that they wanted to build safe AI but did not trust others to do the same. This created pressure to continue building powerful AI systems, driven by fears that slowing down would cede ground to a rival who would deploy a system with far fewer safeguards.

Further intensifying these dynamics are the massive investments being made by US and Chinese companies in underlying AI infrastructure, such as chips and data centres, with the pace of spending not slowing down.

According to a Morgan Stanley report published earlier this month, capital expenditure by Chinese AI hyperscalers was forecast to jump 121 per cent year on year in 2026 to 995 billion yuan (US$142 billion), outpacing the 41 per cent growth among US peers.

China has long been a laggard in terms of AI investment, but recent successes, including DeepSeek’s breakthrough moment in January 2025 and growing policy support from Beijing, have spiked investment levels.

Still, even as the gap narrowed, China was set to spend only around 17 per cent as much as the US on AI infrastructure over the five years to 2030, Morgan Stanley estimated. Given that China’s AI spending was a much smaller share of its economy than the US, it would not likely slow down its investment momentum, Lu Ting, managing director and chief China economist at Nomura Securities, said at a Fortune event in Guangzhou last week.

“I think the key question in China is whether it can obtain chips, how many chips it can get, and how many Nvidia chips it can buy,” he said.

With China not showing signs of slowing down, the US want to maintain its pace over fears of China fully catching up, said Shan Hui, chief China economist at Goldman Sachs, at the same event. “The next 12 to 18 months will not slow down, and may even accelerate, especially in terms of AI infrastructure,” she said.

Adding to investor frenzy is the rush from both leading American and Chinese AI companies to go public. Despite its high-profile safety warnings, Anthropic itself was still expected to go public later this year, with a targeted valuation of around US$2 trillion, Axios reported earlier this month, citing multiple sources.

In China, Kimi developer Moonshot AI has reportedly been valued at US$50 billion in an ongoing funding round and confidentially filed for a Hong Kong initial public offering, people with knowledge of the matter told SCMP earlier this month.

Meanwhile, GLM developer Z.ai, which is listed in Hong Kong, announced plans earlier this month to raise an additional US$5 billion through a combination of new shares and convertible bonds, just two months after raising US$4 billion in a share placement.

According to Tsinghua’s Sun, the new influx of capital and unprecedented investor interest made a collective slowdown difficult. “If one frontier company deliberately slows the development of its most capable models while its competitors continue to move ahead, it risks losing market share, capital, talent and technological leadership,” he said, adding that this also applies to countries.

Genuine safety fears

While there were legitimate concerns about the feasibility of pacing AI development, recent incidents involving AI agents demonstrating unprecedented cyber hacking capabilities had “captured the attention of both policymakers and the public”, said Scott Singer, co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic have in recent months released details about how their models hacked into other companies’ internal systems through “agentic swarms” that went undetected for weeks.

Besides industry warnings, calls for greater safeguards have also intensified among US and European politicians after former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from his role at Anthropic earlier this month and accused the companies of “gambling with our lives” with their plans to accelerate AI development.

Central to their plans was recursive self-improvement (RSI), Coxon warned, which involved automating the AI research and development process itself with the use of AI – a controversial practice that some experts say could lead to humans losing control of AI entirely.

Still, both American and Chinese AI industry leaders have in recent months described RSI as imminent. Given the AI hacking incidents, calls for restraint from industry should not be dismissed as “regulatory theatre,” said Counterpoint Research’s Sun, as the arguments for AI safety had become “much more concrete.”

According to Singer, AI’s growing threat to both US and Chinese interests and humanity as a whole could ultimately be what overrides geopolitical and commercial incentives to continue racing ahead.

“At this stage, voluntary pacing isn’t just feasible, it’s pragmatic [in] the face of serious risks,” Singer said. “Regardless of whether a model is developed in San Francisco or Shanghai, they can create risks that transcend borders.”

Even in its attacks on Amodei and Washington’s hawkish tech policy towards China, the People’s Daily commentary nonetheless called on Washington to work with Beijing to “manage risks through dialogue and communication” and “promote AI to benefit mankind”.

Wang Shengyu, a research assistant at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Centre for China Analysis, said China’s dominant national security apparatus may be more sympathetic to calls for a slow down given the risks of AI expanding from cyberattacks to bioweapon development.

Last week, China’s top intelligence official Chen Yixin called for robust risk prevention frameworks and stronger global governance of the emerging technology in an article published in a journal run by the country’s Cyberspace Administration.

“Once the benefits and risks of frontier AI become concrete enough to create real policy trade-offs, the final judgment is likely to rest with President Xi [whether to slow down AI development]”, Wang said.

As the Xi-Trump meeting nears, experts cautioned against expecting a sweeping agreement on AI, saying any breakthrough would focus on narrower areas where US and Chinese interests overlapped.

A good deliverable from the summit would be for the two sides to agree to have more AI dialogue in future, while finding out what the common concerns over AI risks were, said Tsinghua’s Sun.

There are early signs that this may be possible. Following Sunday’s meeting, US Treasury Secretary Bessent said that the US and China had discussed a “US-China AI dialogue” mechanism and further meetings to discuss AI-related issues.

He added that the US side would “want a shared vision of common goals and threats” with China, including a proposed “notification mechanism” between the two countries.

“Just like any cross-border activity, moving from opaque to more transparency between the No 1 and No 2 AI powers in the world is very important,” Bessent said.

item.title: [SCMP] Escape Manila’s heat for northern Luzon’s pine-scented hills, hanging coffins and other hidden wonders
item.description:
Travellers rolling north through Metro Manila along the Skyway are treated to an elevated perspective of the Philippine capital. The land is pancake flat but the buildings – from bric-a-brac slums to gilded high-rises – reach for the heavens.

My partner and I, too, are headed higher. Our aim is simple – to escape the city heat and exchange the pervasive congestion for nights that aren’t polluted by light, and days by smog. The most obvious solution would be to take a ferry to some exotic isle – after all, the Philippines has 7,000 of them – but we’ve resolved to head in the opposite direction to the Boracay-bound sun-seekers, to the pine-scented hills of Luzon.

The first quarter of the day is spent on a Victory Liner coach, staring at an undulating sea of rice, with only the volcanic profile of Mount Arayat suggesting there may be mountains ahead.
item.content:encoded:
Travellers rolling north through Metro Manila along the Skyway are treated to an elevated perspective of the Philippine capital. The land is pancake flat but the buildings – from bric-a-brac slums to gilded high-rises – reach for the heavens.

My partner and I, too, are headed higher. Our aim is simple – to escape the city heat and exchange the pervasive congestion for nights that aren’t polluted by light, and days by smog. The most obvious solution would be to take a ferry to some exotic isle – after all, the Philippines has 7,000 of them – but we’ve resolved to head in the opposite direction to the Boracay-bound sun-seekers, to the pine-scented hills of Luzon.

The first quarter of the day is spent on a Victory Liner coach, staring at an undulating sea of rice, with only the volcanic profile of Mount Arayat suggesting there may be mountains ahead.

Once we pass the city of Tarlac, lowland farms begin to submit to hill country, as the coach lurches from a cane-straight highway to a winding road that traces the contours of the land. The temperature cools with the altitude and the natural world evolves in tandem. Brilliant wildflowers line the passage north and menacing raptors circle overhead.

Eventually, we encounter the strangest of things in the tropics – forests of conifers, which dominate the slopes on the outskirts of what’s been aptly dubbed the City of Pines. Baguio, where we plan to spend the night, is a little over 200km (124 miles) from Manila. But it’s the altitude, not distance, that distinguishes it most from the capital.

At 1,400 metres (4,600 feet) above sea level, the Americans found a cool spot on a former Spanish ranchería to build a summer capital in the vogue of Shimla, in British India, and duly designed one of the country’s most pleasant cities. Lungfuls of pine-scented air explain why administrators from Boston and Chicago chose to escape here from the muggy oppressiveness of Manila during the worst months of the year.

As we circumvent Burnham Park – a public lake garden designed by architect Daniel Hudson Burnham that remains the city centrepiece – the laid-back atmosphere of Baguio eases our work-frenzied minds. Although many of the finest old houses have been lost to war and the catastrophic earthquake of 1990, a few period buildings – log and stone constructions designed to blend with the mountainous pine forest – still dot the neighbourhood.

Drawn northwest of the park by the imposing City Hall, we stumble upon Café by the Ruins, an American house bombed during World War II only to be reconstructed by local artists using indigenous materials such as bamboo and nipa, the sense of place enhanced by photographs of mountain tribes on the wall and a menu that mixes classic Filipino fare with international dishes. Tortang talong (grilled aubergine omelette with carabao cheese and tomatoes) washed down with tapuey – the local rocket fuel, made with rice, roots and ginger – kindles a satisfied glee at the end of a hard day’s travel.

About 1.5km (one mile) to the north, the Baguio Village Inn is a prim wooden lodge overlooking the city suburbs, which carpet a series of steep hills, resulting in topsy-turvy, chaotic little districts catering to a quickly expanding population.

The following day, morning light is creeping over the hills when we hop a Jeepney to the City Market in search of breakfast. We get more than we bargained for; mountain-grown strawberries are piled outside shop fronts throughout the labyrinthine bazaar, where peanut brittle, sweet wine and honey are offered for sale along with textiles from the ethnically diverse mountains stretching ahead of us for more than 320km (200 miles) and over six provinces.

A brass band appears, and marches through the throng, the trumpets and drums cultivating the feel of a fiesta, recalling the Spanish influence in the Philippine cultural mosaic. However, Iberian colonists didn’t make it far into the cordilleras and mountain peoples were largely spared the corrupting influences of the outside world until the completion of the American-made Halsema Highway, in 1930.

It is along this 96-year-old road that we embark on the next leg of the journey. You can’t pre-book, we just have to wait for a minivan ride at the Sto. Niño Bus Terminal.

Although, not for long; we’re soon travelling through villages in eyeshot of the terraced hills that turn whole mountainsides into a laddered patchwork of rice fields. It’s a stunning vista, but our driver – a 20-something heavy smoker with a novelty skull dangling from the rear-view mirror – handles the minivan as though he’s driving in the Macau Grand Prix. It’s a roller-coaster trip that ends only after six hours of bouncing and clinging on for dear life, when we’re unceremoniously deposited roadside in Sagada.

This remote mountain settlement found its way onto the hippie trail with the arrival of electricity, in the early 1970s, after which intellectuals flocked here to write, paint and make merry on tapuey. Western beatniks followed, “and the artistic influence has left its mark in the form of little boho cafes and inns and a distinctly laid-back atmosphere”, according to my guidebook.

Grandma’s Yellow House is not quite “boho”, but homely and convivial nonetheless. Members of the owning family are cooking and offer us food when we arrive. We have a second-floor room with thick blankets on the beds – it gets cold at night – and our own bathroom, with running hot water some of the time. It’s not the Ritz, but not bad given the remoteness of Sagada.

The town, it turns out, is no longer the getaway for scribes and bohemians it once was. What Sagada can claim to be, though, is blissful, the alpine cool and whispering pines a balm for travellers with stiff limbs and sore buttocks. The town is dotted with weaving houses - selling everything from traditional scarves to guitar straps - and cafes serving local specialities, notably lemon pie.

As the sun sets, the plummeting temperature impels us to return to Grandma’s Yellow House for an early night.

The following day, having risen with the cock crow – literally – we rendezvous with Wihlis Talanay on the terrace of the building that houses Saga Tours a little after sunrise. Inside, our guide for the day offers us a variety of hikes, cave tours and terraced mountain viewings. We opt for a tour to Echo Valley and its famous hanging coffins.

After compulsory registration with the tourist office, he walks us to the church that overlooks Sagada, a not uncommon sight in a Catholic country, except that this one, the Church of Saint Mary the Virgin, “is Anglican, the Spanish never got here”, explains Talanay.

“It’s the Americans who introduced Christianity, this church was built in 1904.”

A Protestant church might be out of the ordinary but the traditional burial sites set on the cliffs of Echo Valley are truly extraordinary.

“The hanging coffins were hung up high as it was believed the higher the dead were placed, the greater chance of their spirits reaching a higher nature in the afterlife,” Talanay explains of a tradition that is fast disappearing.

The coffins are those of distinguished members of the Kankanaey (an ethnic grouping of the Igorot people) and are in various states of repair. They are jammed into crevices, roped to outcroppings and balanced on brackets on sheer cliff faces as if floating. Some have been broken into by foraging animals, the skulls and bones visible as if the dead were preparing to rise.

Our walk across the rooftop of the Philippines proceeds along a mountain track deep in the forest, which is home to cloud rats, forest mice, warty pigs and deer, according to Talanay. Hunting and timber were the economic mainstays in Sagada but recent decades have seen the introduction of cash crops, most notably coffee.

“Welcome to Sagada’s Starbucks,” says Talanay, pointing to the thatch-roofed Baw-eng Coffee Shop, which has a backdrop of vegetation, stands on a coffee farm and serves mountain-grown brews to thirsty hikers. We pair ours with lemon-cream cookies.

Fortified with caffeine, we trek on into the forest. The path climbs then descends to follow a stream, leading through dark caves and patches of upland meadow until it opens onto a clearing drenched in midday sunlight. Butterflies flit everywhere, birdsong chorusing from the tree canopy.

We could walk indefinitely in temperatures this conducive and surroundings this seductive, the pull of nature impelling us towards wherever it is Talanay is leading us, for we have no destination in mind. The act of walking is enough.

Like so many Filipinos, Talanay once travelled overseas to find work, in his case to Britain. No doubt it was hard to make a living in Sagada but, as the last leg of the hike takes us out of the forest to cultivated land marked by a wooden fence, the mud path becoming a narrow stone road, I begin to understand why he returned to this pristine corner of Earth.

We conclude our hike, as all good hikes should end, in a pool beneath a waterfall – feeling a lot farther from Manila than the 400km a crow would fly.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong bar trends in 2026: comfort, classics and mindful drinking
item.description:
Hong Kong’s drinks scene is one of the world’s best – but also one of the world’s most diverse and volatile. Every year, the city has had to navigate – to varying degrees of success – trends and shifts in what bargoers enjoy, resulting in celebrated openings and sombre closures alike. Speakeasies (The Old Man, Please Don’t Tell, Room 309, Stockton) in the 2010s gave way to neighbourhood bars in the 2020s. Publications like Time magazine, Fortune and Drinks International all note that Gen Z drinks less overall than their predecessors, swapping evening bar crawls for daytime coffee raves.

As we ease into 2026, we sat down with some of Hong Kong’s leading mixologists to explore the latest trends shaping the industry – showing how our bars are adapting to the way we drink and how that, in turn, is redefining our nights out.

Neighbourhood bars are still in, so keep it simple
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong’s drinks scene is one of the world’s best – but also one of the world’s most diverse and volatile. Every year, the city has had to navigate – to varying degrees of success – trends and shifts in what bargoers enjoy, resulting in celebrated openings and sombre closures alike. Speakeasies (The Old Man, Please Don’t Tell, Room 309, Stockton) in the 2010s gave way to neighbourhood bars in the 2020s. Publications like Time magazine, Fortune and Drinks International all note that Gen Z drinks less overall than their predecessors, swapping evening bar crawls for daytime coffee raves.

As we ease into 2026, we sat down with some of Hong Kong’s leading mixologists to explore the latest trends shaping the industry – showing how our bars are adapting to the way we drink and how that, in turn, is redefining our nights out.

Neighbourhood bars are still in, so keep it simple

“I think of neighbourhood bars as focusing on simplicity and character, with an interior design that isn’t too elaborate,” says Antonio Lai, co-owner of Tastings Group, whose bars include Quinary, The Opposites and Draft Land.

A significant portion of bars that opened in the last two to three years have embraced some blend of relaxed atmosphere, simple drinks and a focus on community – think Socio, which upcycles surplus and waste ingredients from other venues, or Sugar King with its standing-room-only approach to Cuban-inspired cocktails. Hong Kong’s biggest success on the world stage, 2025 World’s Best Bar, Bar Leone is founded on similar tenets: accessible drinks and a convivial, casual atmosphere.

“Neighbourhood bars, to me, are places to have a drink in comfort,” says Samuel Kwok, who co-founded The Opposites with Lai. “Some places, like hotels, give the impression that you have to dress up a bit, or act or sit in a certain way,” he adds. “Sugar King and Mius [founded by Shelley Tai] have an atmosphere where you can just go in and have a drink, and the staff won’t bother you too frequently.”

Timeless, refined and classic flavours are in

If keeping it simple is at the root of the neighbourhood bar movement, classics are just one of the ways to get started. “People have always been wowed by bold, boundary-pushing innovation,” Singular Concepts and Tell Camellia co-founder Gagan Gurung says, “and we love serving [that need], but there’s been a noticeable shift to where guests are craving comfort. They’re reaching for those everyday, go-to cocktails that feel familiar, timeless and satisfying.”

Many of Hong Kong’s bars have pared back some part of their service to this effect. Both Sugar King and Montana opened on the strength of their daiquiris, also known as the “bartender’s handshake” (the cocktail represents a test of skill in producing the perfect balance of rum, lime and sweetness). Likewise, Kwok cites Bar Leone’s selection of classically inspired drinks as key to its success: “They are cocktails you could probably make at home and understand easily. Younger, newer bartenders these days are increasingly interested in the classics – a sort of return to form.”

“Trends come and go,” Gurung continues, “but the truth is everyone needs their all-time favourite, whether it’s a negroni, a daiquiri or a perfectly balanced Old Fashioned. Innovation excites, but comfort keeps people coming back.”

Less is more – comfort and moderation are key

For Ajit Gurung (no relation to Gagan Gurung), co-founder of The Savory Project, a part of this comfort lies in the way drinks are presented – especially when it comes to bars like his, which continue to find success with bold and innovative flavours. “I think tasting menu-style cocktails will dominate a lot of markets,” he says. “Small portions of multiple courses for cocktails is a great way to showcase new ideas and flavours without overwhelming guests.”

Draft Land and Bar Oasis are two examples of bars boasting exceptional cocktails on tap, allowing guests to sample before they order. “We’ve already pushed the boundaries of food and cocktail innovation – the real differentiator is in how we make people feel,” Gagan Gurung says. “It’s about the entire guest experience.”

Guests are becoming more selective when it comes to those experiences, seeking out spots they trust for drinks they are comfortable with. “Refined drinking is the way forward,” says Ajit Gurung. “Guests are more health conscious and are drinking less. They are selective about where they drink, how much sugar is in their drink, what spirits are used. They are following the bartenders as each has a different style of experiences they provide.”

“The younger generation may prefer to drink quality over quantity, just sipping a couple of glasses at any one bar,” Lai says. “They may also bar hop or prefer a low- or no-ABV style of drinking, and may start earlier in the day with coffee. The earlier they start, the earlier they can sleep, and the less they’ll be affected the next day.”

“People today are far more health conscious,” Gagan Gurung notes. “Whether it’s about wellness, mindfulness or just opting for a more balanced lifestyle, drinking habits are clearly shifting.”

Local ingredients for well-travelled guests

If bargoers are to step outside their comfort zone, it may well be to try a local ingredient far from home. “Guests now are well travelled and constantly looking for new experiences,” Ajit Gurung says. “Bold, culinary-driven ideas are the perfect category of cocktail for guests with more sophisticated palates.”

He is referring mainly to the resurgence of savoury cocktails, but Lai and Kwok see the same spirit of exploration extending to greater interaction with China. For Lai, Chinese-produced wines and spirits, including non-alcoholic sparkling spirits, will be more ubiquitous. Kwok adds that more bartenders from mainland China will go overseas for guest shifts.

“The new generation of [Chinese] bartenders is getting better in terms of language and communication, which has always been the biggest barrier,” he says. “China also has a lot more to show the world in terms of techniques and ingredients.” Kwok points out that China’s eight great cuisines are distinct and ripe for discovery. “Yunnan has great teas. Some areas have great herbs, while others have great spices and chillies. Every time I go to China, I see things I’ve never seen before thanks to this diversity.”

The reverse is also increasingly true – over the last few years, Bar Leone, Coa and Penicillin have opened branches in Shanghai. Lai hopes to open a branch of Quinary on the mainland, but obstacles remain.

“A surprising barrier is toilets, especially in second- and third-tier cities – even Hongkongers don’t know how to navigate the situation,” Kwok says. “We went to Chengdu once and every toilet was a squat toilet. If you’re hosting guests in China, taking them to truly local places requires them to navigate those toilets.”

“If I open a bar in China,” Lai says emphatically, “I will require sitting toilets!”

item.title: [SCMP] How Japan’s innovative Nakagin Capsule Tower is finding new life
item.description:
In 1988, upon moving to Tokyo, British architect Mark Dytham made a pilgrimage to Ginza to see one building he believed encapsulated everything he had imagined Japan to be: Nakagin Capsule Tower. “It was one of the first proper hi-tech buildings in the world, like a machine or a robot, and represented a vision where things don’t have to be static,” the co-founder of Klein Dytham architecture says. “I thought it was the future.”

So in 2022, it was with mixed feelings that Dytham stood on a street in the Japanese capital and watched the Metabolist building come down. After cranes gingerly hoisted capsules off the two interconnected towers that accommodated them, roughly one in five were loaded onto trucks destined for temporary shelters, where they would be rehabilitated and shipped to new homes.

Given that Metabolism was an architectural movement founded on the ability of buildings to move with the times, its radical poster child seemed to be exhibiting normal vital functions. Or was it metastasis? In the past two years, newly revitalised since the dismantling of their 50-year-old mother ship, Nakagin cells have spread throughout Japan and beyond. Hong Kong is part of that advance.
item.content:encoded:
In 1988, upon moving to Tokyo, British architect Mark Dytham made a pilgrimage to Ginza to see one building he believed encapsulated everything he had imagined Japan to be: Nakagin Capsule Tower. “It was one of the first proper hi-tech buildings in the world, like a machine or a robot, and represented a vision where things don’t have to be static,” the co-founder of Klein Dytham architecture says. “I thought it was the future.”

So in 2022, it was with mixed feelings that Dytham stood on a street in the Japanese capital and watched the Metabolist building come down. After cranes gingerly hoisted capsules off the two interconnected towers that accommodated them, roughly one in five were loaded onto trucks destined for temporary shelters, where they would be rehabilitated and shipped to new homes.

Given that Metabolism was an architectural movement founded on the ability of buildings to move with the times, its radical poster child seemed to be exhibiting normal vital functions. Or was it metastasis? In the past two years, newly revitalised since the dismantling of their 50-year-old mother ship, Nakagin cells have spread throughout Japan and beyond. Hong Kong is part of that advance.

Nakagin’s scattered course would have pleased its avant-garde architect Kisho Kurokawa (1934-2007), who conceived the design to emancipate what he called Homo movens (mobile humans). Many fans still demonstrate their unbridled enthusiasm for the building by donning zany get-ups inspired by its form – often described as a stack of front-loading washing machines.

In my mind’s eye, however, Nakagin had always been a colony of barnacles. That analogy borrows from the free movement of these crustaceans before anchoring themselves in place. But unfortunately, it was the unexpected immobility of Kurokawa’s capsules during their first phase of life that ultimately thwarted his vision that they be modular, interchangeable and recyclable.

That idea of impermanent permanence remains irresistible, however – at least in Japan. Which was one reason Metabolism captured the imagination of many during the country’s buoyant post-war expansion, making its name and ethos heard at the 1960 World Design Conference in Tokyo. Adaptable buildings and cities – with renewable nodes fed by circulation systems – sparked interest. Adding excitement was the promise of Expo ’70, whose theme was “progress and harmony for mankind”.

At that landmark event in Osaka, futuristic pavilions, including several by Kurokawa, allowed the forward-thinking to see for themselves the biomimetic potential of a movement whose proponents included other eminent architects, Kenzo Tange and Fumihiko Maki among them.

Nakagin, however, earned the kind of cult status accorded few other buildings in Japan. One reason was the charisma of Kurokawa, also a media personality and, towards the end of his career, a politician. His building was among the few examples of Metabolist architecture ever realised.

In late 2022, Ikko Yokoyama visited a warehouse in Chiba, near Tokyo, where salvaged Nakagin capsules, resembling pet Cyclops, awaited adoption. As lead curator of design and architecture at M+, she was there to see one of 23 pods that had been saved by the Nakagin Capsule Tower Preservation and Restoration Project, founded by former resident Tatsuyuki Maeda.

Hong Kong’s museum of contemporary visual culture was prepared for this inevitable moment, according to Yokoyama. Debate had raged for years about whether to preserve Nakagin whole, with Kurokawa himself shifting from yes to no. Ultimately, land value outweighed legacy, says Dytham, who had tried without success to persuade developers and hospitality groups to turn Nakagin into a boutique hotel. “It wasn’t sustainable to keep it there,” he says.

The decision to tear it down was made despite its uniqueness. Unlike anything the West had produced – except, perhaps, in the minds of Britain’s Archigram group of architects – Nakagin consisted of capsules “plugged” into the building’s towers, or cores, one 11 storeys high, the other two floors taller. Tight spaces between each pod impeded access and meant that repairs were difficult because “you couldn’t get in”, says Dytham. Worse, owners were unwilling to pay the high cost of detaching their capsules for upkeep every 25 years, as Kurokawa had warned they must. Decay set in, leaks appeared and damage from Japan’s frequent earthquakes saw the building’s exterior netted for safety. Additionally, the presence of asbestos complicated matters.

But M+’s capsule speaks volumes about their enduring appeal. A806 now stands beside another of the museum’s inspired acquisitions, Kiyotomo (1988), the sushi bar designed by Shiro Kuramata. Unlike that 656 sq ft restaurant – which was disassembled in Japan, shipped to Hong Kong and later put together again by the original contractors and an M+ team of restorers – Kurokawa’s capsule was purchased fully reconditioned.

The 2.78 metre x 2.69 metre x 4.21 metre capsule in the East Galleries is one of six standard units, complete with their famous round window at one end accommodating a circular blind that folds open like a hand fan. Also included within the 121.9 sq ft space are mod cons and a dinky unit bath, those tiny waterproof rooms sold as a single product in Japan.

“Like organ donation”, as Yokoyama puts it, parts for the capsule were harvested from others in the building because none of the pods survived with all of its original fittings intact. Kiyotomo’s neighbour now also boasts a new blue carpet and mattress, in addition to a fold-down desk, television and reel-to-reel tape deck, among other integrated features. Combine the service and payload modules of a spaceship and you get the idea.

Of the capsules plucked to safety by Maeda’s group, 14 have been sold to companies and museums, including M+ and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, which purchased Kurokawa’s prized personal unit. Of the nine remaining, he says, four are to stay in Japan while five will head abroad.

Some have already been turned into display modules and mobile units and, next year, hotel-room conversions are expected, which should come as no surprise: in 1979, Kurokawa’s ideas also gave birth to the world’s first capsule hotel. New Japan Umeda continues to offer budget accommodation in Osaka.

Maeda’s is not the only group intent on giving the (in) famous corner building a second life. The Nakagin Capsule Tower A606 Project is named after the pod that another ex-resident helped restore several years before the building came down. This group, which owns seven units, has even more ambitious, albeit firmly parochial, aims.

“We plan to reconstruct a mini-tower using several capsules we own,” the group reveals via core member, architect Akiko Ishimaru.

“We aim to keep the reconstructed ones for 50 years [100 years after their completion] by continuing to use them ourselves. We want to utilise the capsules that were born in Japan and rebuild them in Japan.”

Crowdfunding has helped pay for the work so far. “The cost of asbestos control and investigation during the survey and dismantling, transportation and storage of seven capsules, storage of original parts, printing of a book with records, restoration of the interior of capsule A606, crowdfunding gifts [such as the aforementioned book], and fees consumed most of the total 8,673,000 yen [HK$443,000],” the group says.

Ishimaru’s efforts to keep Nakagin from history’s scrapheap underscores the passion in the project. But that’s not to say she fully enjoyed her year living in the building (and seven more working in two other capsules).

“One of my fond memories is drawing the actual survey plan for Nakagin Capsule Tower on my laptop at the original desk of Capsule A606 in August 2021,” she recalls, adding, “The 1.3-metre-diameter round window meant that the small room didn’t feel cramped.”

Having been designed as “hotel-like second homes” – or crash pads for salarymen – none of the capsules came with a kitchen. It was “very quiet”, Ishimaru recalls. The prefabricated steel modules didn’t share walls and, by 2013, when she moved in, there were only a few residents left. “Since it was so old and there was no hot water, I couldn’t even take a shower inside the capsule, so I stopped living there and used it as a shared office.”

Other assessments were bleaker. “From outside, the tower looked like a dying animal, sweating and greasy in the heat, trapped inside its wire netting,” reads an account by The Paris Review of Nakagin’s condition in 2016. “Looking up, you could see that some capsules had been half-filled with rotting garbage, a rippling line of trash drawn across their single windows. Inside, panels peel from the ceilings and mold crawls underneath; grime and seepage scorches the concrete with strange, bubbling forms.”

The reviewer added: “Kurokawa’s masterpiece was an utter, unsalvageable failure.”

And there’s the rub.

On whether Metabolism remains relevant in the 21st century, few can deny the importance of urban development that hews closely to principles of sustainability and flexibility. “The idea that buildings can change, grow and regenerate over time within a city may be increasingly needed to adapt to urban population growth and environmental issues,” the A606 group argue.

But how to label Kurokawa’s achievement remains as polarising as the fractious debates about whether the building should have been protected for posterity.

“It was an amazing success because he made it happen,” says Yokoyama, referring to how Kurokawa turned theory into reality and created a prototype. “It wasn’t just imagination.”

Dytham also believes Kurokawa got it “pretty right”, explaining that Nakagin was an early model. “If you’re building 10 of them, you get it. That was the first one.”

He adds that, for him, the building’s success had much to do with a design so simple that even a child could read and recognise it. “That would be a totally protected building if it was in the UK,” he posits. “Traditionally, here [in Japan], things are built in a temporary way.”

However, the recent wide dispersal of Nakagin capsules underscores the fact that Kurokawa’s vision has come to fruition. As Dytham says, “How many buildings have been taken apart and put all around the world?

“Taking [Nakagin] to the rest of the world is as important as just being all in one place.”

Metabolism was simply operating at its own pace.

item.title: [SCMP] Xi-Trump Washington summit aimed at putting US-China ties on equal footing: Wang Yi
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States was crucial to maintaining the overall stability of China-US relations and aimed at putting the relationship on an equal footing.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who accompanied Xi on the three-day trip to Washington, gave the assessment on Saturday, expanding on relations between the two countries.

According to state news agency Xinhua, Wang said Xi’s visit “maintained the overall stability of Sino-US relations” and “will have a deep impact on the world’s peace and development”.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States was crucial to maintaining the overall stability of China-US relations and aimed at putting the relationship on an equal footing.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who accompanied Xi on the three-day trip to Washington, gave the assessment on Saturday, expanding on relations between the two countries.

According to state news agency Xinhua, Wang said Xi’s visit “maintained the overall stability of Sino-US relations” and “will have a deep impact on the world’s peace and development”.

The Chinese foreign minister also expanded on one of the eight outcomes of the trip – an agreement between the two leaders to build a “constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity”.

“It means the two countries have equal sovereignty and no one is more superior than the other. None is domineering or abusive and they should resolve their own concerns on an equal footing,” Wang said.

“Respect” referred to respect for each other’s sovereignty, territory and core interests, while “fairness” meant rejection of the “zero-sum mindset”, he added.

Wang said the exceptional reception given to Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan, including the personal welcome US President Donald Trump and his wife Melania gave on the tarmac on arrival, reflected respect for Xi and the importance of China-US relations to the United States.

After the trip, China and the United States issued separate statements about the outcomes, saying they had agreed to improve cooperation on artificial intelligence, tariffs and chemical precursor control.

The two countries agreed that their leaders would also support each other in hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum and Group of 20 summits later this year, signalling their intent to attend the meetings in person.

The agreement means that Trump plans to travel to the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen in November, while Xi is scheduled to go to Miami in December, making this year unusual in terms of the number of face-to-face meetings between the two men.

Also unusual was the mention in both statements about the leaders’ references to the US-China alliance during World War II, a partnership that Xi and Trump highlighted several times during the trip.

Xi, also accompanied by chief of staff Cai Qi and Vice-Premier He Lifeng, left Beijing for Washington on Wednesday and returned to the Chinese capital on Saturday afternoon.

The Chinese statement about the trip said both sides agreed to open a communication channel on incidents involving “artificial intelligence”. The US statement said they agreed to rename AI as “super intelligence”, a campaign Trump has been pushing in recent weeks.

The two leaders also formally endorsed a US$30 billion reciprocal tariff reduction arrangement reached earlier by the Chinese and US trade teams, as well as an extension of their trade truce.

The two countries affirmed the establishment of the Board of Investment. The US said the board would discuss “potential investment opportunities and investment-related impediments”.

On geopolitics, both countries said they agreed that Iran should not have nuclear weapons and that no country or institution should impose tolls on international waterways.

They also lauded the arrest in August of 21 Chinese citizens for making and distributing precursor chemicals for illicit drug producers in North America, saying the action was the fruit of China-US cooperation on fentanyl.

While neither statement mentioned Taiwan, a sticking point of bilateral relations, Wang said the issue was brought up during the meetings.

“President Xi Jinping set out China’s principled position on the Taiwan issue, stressing that China is firmly committed to safeguarding national reunification and territorial integrity,” Wang said.

“[Xi] urged the US side to maintain the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’, handle the Taiwan issue prudently, and remove obstacles to China-US strategic cooperation and the development of bilateral relations.”

In a veiled reference to Japan, Wang said Xi also urged the US to share the “responsibility to uphold the post-war international order and prevent the revival of militarism”, with this year marking the 80th anniversary of the start of the Tokyo war crimes trials.

There were also differences between the statements from the two countries, which has become the norm in recent years since they stopped issuing joint statements.

The US said China had agreed to import at least 10 million tonnes of coal from the United States next year and again in 2028 – a commitment that Beijing did not refer to.

The US also said the two sides would “continue to work on” US concerns about China’s exports of rare earths and critical minerals to the US, “with the goal of ensuring shipment levels return to appropriate levels”. Again, the Chinese statement was silent on the issue.

In addition, the White House said the next meeting of the newly formed US-China Super Intelligence Dialogue would take place by November.

China’s Ministry of Commerce confirmed on Thursday that its senior trade negotiators had already held their first talks with the US on artificial intelligence.

One of the biggest differences was over the American presence in Asia.

Although the US highlighted its alliance with China during WWII, it nevertheless implied that it would remain a force in the region, which Beijing has repeatedly condemned as US hegemony.

“Since World War II, the United States’ forward military presence has preserved a free and open Indo-Pacific, contributing to generations of American prosperity,” the US statement said.

The Chinese statement instead highlighted potential improvements in military-to-military communication.

“The Chinese and US militaries agreed to sign as soon as possible a memorandum of understanding on strengthening crisis communication and prevention,” it said, adding both sides also agreed to continue their cooperation to search for the remains of missing US servicemembers in China.

The statementconfirmed an exclusive that the Post reported earlier this month that the two sides might announce measures to improve military-to-military communication.

In the meantime, Iran continued to wait for an official US response to its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the US ending its sanctions.

The proposal was made at the UN General Assembly and conveyed to the Americans via Qatari mediators, Iran said.

Trump and Xi also discussed concerns about Russia and North Korea, saying the US “advocated” for trilateral arms-control negotiations between the US, Russia, and China.

Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, said the affirmation of the investment board exceeded expectations as differences within the US had stalled progress.

“The US statement said specifically that the investment board will discuss potential investment opportunities and investment-related impediments, and that is going towards the direction that China has hoped for. And the work of this board is one thing we need to look out for,” Wu said.

He said the historical alliances during WWII mentioned by both sides was particularly interesting and it was not expected, especially as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi spoke to Trump in New York before Xi’s visit.

“Trump is different from [his predecessor Joe] Biden. Biden has a strong ideological orientation and when he talked about these things, he would certainly talk about the shared values of the United States and its allies – things like democracy,” Wu said.

“Trump is a nationalist, so he has a strong memory of Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbour. You can see that he likes to bring up Pearl Harbour from time to time. So for him, as a nationalist, there is nothing unusual about talking about World War II.”

Chen Qi, professor of international relations at Tsinghua University, said there was room for further discussion on trade and hopes for trade relations to stabilise with the Apec and G20 meetings later this year.

“The trade truce extension until January will [also] give more room for imagination for the rest of the world,” Chen said.

“When they are meeting so frequently, in November and December, do you think it is possible to upend the trade relationship and reopen the door to additional tariffs? I don’t think there is any room for that,” he said.

Daniel Kritenbrink, a former US assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, said the frequent meetings between the two leaders this year meant there was less pressure for deliverables during this trip.

“I think we have to keep in mind that we are in this extraordinary period right now where two presidents are meeting so frequently that I think the amount of pressure on each interaction is slightly less than would traditionally be the case,” said Kritenbrink, now a partner at Washington-based strategic advisory firm The Asia Group.

Additional reporting by Alyssa Chen

item.title: [SCMP] Trump, Takaichi reaffirm US-Japan ties in phone call after Xi state visit
item.description:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said she and Donald Trump had reaffirmed their collaboration on issues relating to Beijing in a phone call on Saturday.

The call followed the US president’s nostalgic invocation of the World War II alliance with China during his summit with Xi Jinping, remarks that sent shock waves through Tokyo.

Trump made the references as he welcomed the Chinese president to the White House on Thursday for his first state visit to Washington in over a decade.
item.content:encoded:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said she and Donald Trump had reaffirmed their collaboration on issues relating to Beijing in a phone call on Saturday.

The call followed the US president’s nostalgic invocation of the World War II alliance with China during his summit with Xi Jinping, remarks that sent shock waves through Tokyo.

Trump made the references as he welcomed the Chinese president to the White House on Thursday for his first state visit to Washington in over a decade.

In a social media post on Saturday, Takaichi said Trump provided detailed explanations regarding the recent US-China summit during the call starting at 9pm Tokyo time. They exchanged views centred on various issues surrounding China, including the economy and security, and confirmed the Japan-US collaboration, she wrote.

Takaichi met Trump in person on Tuesday in New York, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. Two exchanges with the US leader within one week “truly demonstrates the strength of the Japan-US alliance”, her post read.

“Japan and the United States have now become the most trusted allied nations, and we confirmed our commitment to jointly contribute to peace and stability in the region and the world.

“In order to elevate our unwavering Japan-US alliance to even greater heights, I will closely collaborate with President Trump,” she pledged.

Both Trump and Xi repeatedly invoked their nations’ wartime alliance against Japan in their remarks in Washington – an unusual historical reference that immediately unsettled Tokyo.

Such bonds were also reflected in statements released by the two countries following Xi’s visit.

“The two leaders recalled that United States and China were allies in World War II and fought side by side to win the war,” both statements said.

However, the White House statement added a paragraph to justify US presence in the region.

“Since World War II, the United States’ forward military presence has preserved a free and open Indo-Pacific, contributing to generations of American prosperity,” it said.

Takaichi said on Friday that Tokyo and Washington were “allies bound by very strong ties” based on mutual trust. But she pointedly declined to comment on the Trump-Xi summit.

To avoid being sidelined completely, Takaichi had rescheduled her address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, moving it up by two days to secure a 35-minute meeting with Trump on Tuesday.

Japanese analysts warned that the wartime nostalgia boded poorly for Japan, though they cautioned against reading too much into the rhetoric.

Chinese observers, meanwhile, argued that the moment should prompt Tokyo to rethink its approach towards Beijing.

Shin Kawashima, professor of international relations at the University of Tokyo, said the main question was why Washington was embracing the wartime framing now.

“Trump’s remarks could easily be interpreted by China as indicating that the US and China are in agreement on issues of historical perception and that the US supports China’s rhetoric condemning the [Takaichi] administration as a form of ‘new militarism’,” Kawashima said.

Hotaka Machida, a visiting senior research fellow at the Institute of Geoeconomics in Tokyo, said Japan would find Trump’s historical references “surprising and awkward”, but noted that the remarks were made in the context of the US-China relationship.

Still, he cautioned: “Japan needs to be careful about the possibility of the Chinese side taking advantage of the amicable atmosphere presented this time as a propaganda tool.”

Kenichi Doi, senior research fellow at the same institute, called Trump’s description of wartime China as an ally “striking”.

But the bigger question was whether that shared history would be used to cast doubt on present-day Japan. It would be a mistake to assume that Trump had endorsed Beijing’s criticism of Tokyo, he said.

Rintaro Nishimura, a senior associate at The Asia Group strategic advisory firm, said that though worrying, the single statement was unlikely to weaken the US-Japan alliance.

Tokyo was also less concerned because Takaichi coordinated with Trump on issues related to China ahead of the Xi-Trump summit, he added.

“[But] it does not bode well for Tokyo that Washington and Beijing are both emphasising the fact that the two countries were wartime allies,” Nishimura said.

Beijing and Tokyo have remained largely out of official contact since November, when Takaichi suggested that a blockade of Taiwan would be a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan.

Official relations went into a tailspin but Japanese business and legislative delegations have made sustained efforts to visit Beijing to gauge Chinese thinking.

Another business delegation, led by former Japanese foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya, will go to China on Sunday in the latest attempt to bridge the diplomatic impasse.

Nishimura expected Tokyo to “stay the course” when engaging with Beijing, using legislative and commercial dialogue to tease out potential openings for government-level talks, with an end goal of securing a Takaichi-Xi meeting at the Apec summit in Shenzhen in November.

“Japan will be looking to see if there are any signs that Washington is ready to compromise regional security for a deal, perhaps economic, with Beijing.”

Meanwhile, Tokyo’s discomfort is seen as an inevitable consequence of stabilising US-China ties, with analysts saying the warm tone from the summit should prompt Tokyo to reassess its own approach to Beijing.

Kawashima noted that Japan-China relations would “grow more tenuous” if US-China ministerial engagement deepened and might prompt Tokyo to conclude that it was better to improve relations with China to some extent.

Wang Guangtao, deputy director of the Centre for Japanese Studies at Fudan University, said Japan’s anxiety was an inevitable result of further stabilisation between Beijing and Washington.

“The sheer fact that Chinese and American leaders can have such frequent interactions this year should serve as a prompt for Tokyo to change its perceptions towards China and rethink its posture,” Wang said.

Zhang Yun, professor of international relations at Nanjing University, said Tokyo harboured deep concern about the prospect of another 1972 “Nixon shock”, when the US normalised ties with China without consulting its closest East Asian ally.

Takaichi’s push to meet Trump ahead of his talks with Xi reflected this anxiety, he said.

“Compounded by Trump’s transactional approach towards its traditional alliances and tariff actions, these dynamics are fuelling deep-seated anxieties in Tokyo over Washington’s reliability, leaving Japan’s position adrift,” Zhang said.

According to Cho Sung-min, associate professor of international relations at Sungkyunkwan University in Seoul, the memory of US-China military cooperation against Japan has long been a Chinese talking point.

“Trump’s reference to America’s past partnership with China against Japan, a US ally in the present, suggests how far he was willing to go to maintain a cordial relationship with Xi,” Cho said.

item.title: [SCMP] China-based Brics bank set for lead role in hunger alliance this year, Brazil says
item.description:
The Brics-founded New Development Bank could help launch a fund by the end of the year to guarantee cheap loans for poor families in Africa and Latin America, Brazil’s social development minister said.

The scheme would be the Shanghai-based lender’s first financial commitment to Brazil’s global anti-hunger alliance, an initiative sidelined by Washington’s presidency of the G20 this year.

Wellington Dias told the South China Morning Post on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York that the chances of a first pilot programme, worth as little as US$200 million, getting off the ground by December were “very big”. The bank is designing the scheme with four other development lenders, he added, and each still has to run its compliance checks.
item.content:encoded:
The Brics-founded New Development Bank could help launch a fund by the end of the year to guarantee cheap loans for poor families in Africa and Latin America, Brazil’s social development minister said.

The scheme would be the Shanghai-based lender’s first financial commitment to Brazil’s global anti-hunger alliance, an initiative sidelined by Washington’s presidency of the G20 this year.

Wellington Dias told the South China Morning Post on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York that the chances of a first pilot programme, worth as little as US$200 million, getting off the ground by December were “very big”. The bank is designing the scheme with four other development lenders, he added, and each still has to run its compliance checks.

The money would go to Brazil’s Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty, launched at the G20 summit Brazil hosted in Rio de Janeiro in November 2024 but dropped from the group’s agenda after the United States took over the rotating presidency in December last year.

The Trump administration, which boycotted last year’s summit in Johannesburg, has narrowed the G20 agenda to deregulation, energy, technology and trade, leaving out priorities of Brazil’s 2024 presidency such as inequality and hunger.

Dias, who co-chairs the alliance, said Washington had become “somewhat isolated” on hunger, but admitted that its reduction in aid was a “hard problem” for the group’s objective.

This is because even though it has 215 members (including over 107 countries and 14 international financial institutions), the alliance has no money of its own and relies on members to fund the programmes it brokers.

Much of the money so far has come from the Inter-American Development Bank, which pledged up to US$25 billion between 2025 and 2030. It approved US$4.1 billion in alliance-aligned operations last year and expects to approve US$5.8 billion this year.

Dias acknowledged that neither the New Development Bank nor the Beijing-based Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank had financed any alliance programme so far, but added that the Brics’ bank contribution would come through the guarantee fund.

That would be new territory for a lender set up in 2015 by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa to finance mostly infrastructure. When it joined the alliance in October 2024, the bank offered help with water, sanitation, housing and irrigation projects, without naming a funding figure.

In the model he described, local banks would lend to poor borrowers and the guarantee fund would absorb any defaults.

“This will allow a poor person in the country being supported to walk into a bank and get financing,” Dias said.

“The poorest are seen by banks as high risk, and the interest is very high. With the guarantee fund, that goes away. The rate collapses, and that matters for financing in both rural and urban areas.”

The idea draws on Brazil’s Acredita programme, which offers microcredit to low-income families backed by a one billion reais (US$194 million) government guarantee fund. By October last year it had lent 1.7 billion reais, with a default rate of 0.36 per cent, according to the social development ministry.

China steps up global anti-hunger alliance involvement

The fund would also add a financial dimension to China’s involvement in the alliance, which it has lacked so far.

When President Xi Jinping announced China would join the Rio summit in November 2024, Beijing’s statement of commitment covered domestic policy and knowledge sharing but left out the section on financial support that members can choose to sign.

Its pledges were largely domestic, including a 50-million tonne increase in grain production capacity by 2030.

Abroad, China offered advice on 13 types of policy, among them microcredit for poverty alleviation through the International Poverty Reduction Centre in China.

That state-backed centre says it has trained nearly 15,000 officials from 140 countries and runs a poverty reduction forum with the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States. Its deputy director general, Li Xin, sits on the alliance’s Board of Champions as one of its vice-chairs.

Asked what Beijing had contributed since joining the alliance, Dias began with China’s success in reducing poverty at home before turning to its investment in developing countries.

“China is also one of the countries investing the most in Africa and South America, and with that it contributes, even if in a traditional way, to opening up opportunities for jobs and work,” he said. “It invests in infrastructure and so on.”

On the alliance itself, Dias said Chinese financial support has been focused on family farming in African countries, alongside other donors.

The minister also cited larger Chinese purchases from small producers’ cooperatives in Brazil, Africa and South America, including organic honey from Brazil’s north and northeast.

Countries contribute “with knowledge, with money, but also with investment”, he said, and “in this field, China is a prominent partner”.

Dias said Beijing could help fill the space left by US aid cuts, though as part of “a pact among several countries” rather than alone. But talks on that between the Brics bloc, the European Union and other forums were disrupted by the Iran war early this year, according to the minister.

Cuba’s isolation and armed conflicts worldwide

Alliance members have sent food to Cuba, mainly milk, and are backing better seeds, irrigation and fishing projects to help the island produce more of its own, Dias said.

Cuba has suffered repeated nationwide blackouts since Venezuelan oil shipments stopped after US forces captured Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in January, and Washington has since blocked tankers bound for the island.

Dias described the positions of China, Brazil, Mexico and Spain on Cuba as “very firm”, and mentioned a Cuban target of 3.5 gigawatts of solar power.

With 42 countries at war or in armed conflict by his count, Dias asked richer economies, China among them, to avoid further aid cuts or to compensate where they had happened. He framed it as self-interest.

“When wars proliferate, when hunger and poverty are not dealt with, the richest also pay,” he said.

“Look at disorderly migration. All countries pay, whether it is the United States, countries in Europe or Brazil.”

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines’ short-lived Discord ban exposes cracks in online safety strategy
item.description:
The Philippines’ decision to block messaging platform Discord for less than a day following a series of school shootings has raised questions about the government’s response to child safety online, with analysts describing the move as a show of regulatory muscle that did little to address underlying problems.

The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) announced on Thursday that it had lifted the ban after what officials described as successful negotiations with Discord over compliance with child safety measures.

The government’s action came days after a shooting on September 18 at Banga National High School in South Cotabato, where a student opened fire on classmates, killing two students and himself, and injuring eight others.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines’ decision to block messaging platform Discord for less than a day following a series of school shootings has raised questions about the government’s response to child safety online, with analysts describing the move as a show of regulatory muscle that did little to address underlying problems.

The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) announced on Thursday that it had lifted the ban after what officials described as successful negotiations with Discord over compliance with child safety measures.

The government’s action came days after a shooting on September 18 at Banga National High School in South Cotabato, where a student opened fire on classmates, killing two students and himself, and injuring eight others.

Authorities said they were investigating whether the student had been influenced by online conversations, while the government also raised concerns about online communities being used to groom or radicalise minors and potentially encourage real-world violence.

On Wednesday, the government gave Discord and Reddit 24 hours to establish a physical office or assign a resident agent, alongside detailed explanations of their safety protocols, rapid-response mechanisms and age-assurance systems.

The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Centre (CICC) said Discord had servers associated with nihilistic violent extremism and grooming, but stopped short of blaming either Discord or Reddit for the recent shootings.

Reddit was given an extension to comply, while Discord was blocked after failing to meet the government’s deadline.

‘Performative’ governance?

The move drew widespread public criticism, as it disrupted communications for enterprises, workers and students who use the platform.

“People use Discord for work meetings, school and running small businesses. Block it and they all get hit, while bad actors just move to another app,” Filipino actor Paulo Avelino wrote on social media. “Child safety matters. So fix the actual problem, not just the easiest target.”

“We now live in a world of super powerful AI swarms,” said Carl Javier, executive director of ethics organisation Data and AI Ethics PH, describing their ability to “hack into government systems and cause catastrophic harm to key digital infrastructure”.

“And the department that wants to be at the head of dealing with these threats … does not know how Discord works?”

The CICC apologised for the inconvenience caused by the hours-long ban.

“Please don’t worry, as we are already working to resolve everything,” Renato Paraiso, undersecretary and executive director of the CICC, said at a press conference.

The CICC was also responsible for banning the video game GoreBox, which was part of officials’ investigation into a school shooting in Tacloban City in June.

Beyond the immediate disruption, digital rights and child safety advocates said the incident highlighted a lack of foresight in creating coherent and feasible regulatory systems.

“When access to a platform can disappear abruptly, the consequences reach far beyond a single app,” volunteer-led civic technology initiative BetterGov said in a petition to protect digital democracy. “Work can be interrupted, learning disrupted and communities cut off. People deserve to know who made the decision, what evidence supports it, how long it will last and how it can be challenged.”

The government likely banned Discord to flex its regulatory muscle and look like it was tackling online harm, but the decision ultimately proved to be “careless”, said Jason Torres, a tech consultant and founder of BetterGov.

“I don’t think they properly consulted the people affected. We use Discord to organise volunteers and get work done. Others depend on it for school and income. You can’t ignore that impact just because you want a platform’s attention,” Torres said.

Javier shared similar views regarding the government’s approach.

“Performative governance allows them to seem like they are taking steps to ‘protect us’, threatening bans on platforms when these don’t actually fix the root causes of the problems,” Javier said.

Torres added that the incident showed the Philippines’ lack of capacity to address online harm properly, despite rising cases.

Ysrael Diloy, a child protection specialist at the Manila-based non-profit organisation Stairway Foundation, said the “more useful way of looking at this is not whether a 24-hour directive by itself inspires trust, but whether we are developing a coherent, realistic and sustainable system for holding platforms accountable”.

The CICC’s requirement for platforms to designate local representation was legitimate, Diloy said.

“When there is an immediate threat to a child – sexual exploitation, grooming, a credible threat of violence or digital evidence that needs to be preserved – authorities should not have to spend critical time figuring out whom to contact in another jurisdiction,” he said. “However, regulatory demands also have to be realistic and feasible.”

Setting up in a new physical office within a 24-hour time frame was unrealistic, Diloy said, even with the alternative of appointing a local representative.

“That naturally raises an important question: why 24 hours, and what exactly is expected to be realistically accomplished within that period?”

Constitutional questions

Digital creators and advocates said targeting platforms such as Discord and Reddit also raised concerns over free and protected speech.

“Blanket blocking raises constitutional questions, especially when the legal basis and due process are unclear,” Torres said.

“When I was undersecretary of the DICT … pressures were coming in from Congress for us to block websites, apps, and even to take down critics’ posts,” former DICT Undersecretary Jeffrey Ian Dy told ABS-CBN News on Friday.

“But we didn’t do it because, number one, it is unconstitutional.
