There was already a ruling by the Supreme Court that there shouldn’t be unilateral blocking of any websites except those that are clearly defined to be blockable under the law,” Dy added. “Last time I checked, we’re still a democracy so they should work within the boundaries of the law.”

Speaking on a podcast hosted by tech founder Ann Cuisia on Thursday, Dy accused Congress of holding the DICT’s budget hostage in exchange for action against posts critical of public officials.

He said he suspected the issue of child safety was being “used” by congressmen as a smokescreen to get negative posts about themselves taken down.

“If you look at the transcripts of Congress hearings regarding DICT’s budget. Congressmen were asking why DICT was unable to take down posts negative to them … They’re talking about child safety and ‘fake news,’” Dy said.

“The real reason why our politicians want to regulate social media is that they can’t take the heat,” Carlo Ople, founder of Creators Against Corruption, posted on social media.

“They want the people who are talking about their alleged corruption and alleged illegal activities to be silenced. This is a question about free speech, more than anything else.”

While the intention of the Discord ban might not have been to stifle free expression, Javier said it ran counter to previous court rulings.

“It runs over due process, and whether they intended it or not, if allowed to stand it would’ve set a dangerous precedent,” Javier said. “At present, the DICT and CICC continue to invoke ‘protecting children’ as their motivation. But they need to balance that with defending our rights as well.”

Diloy said authorities could earn the public’s trust by carrying out reforms, not by how quickly they acted after an incident.

“It is whether we see a sustained, technically informed and evidence-based approach – one that invests in prevention, investigation, child protection services, regulatory capacity and meaningful engagement with technology companies,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Taiwan’s coastguard vessel transfer to the Philippines has sparked a double outcry
item.description:
Taiwan’s transfer of a former coastguard vessel to the Philippines has triggered a dual controversy – raising concerns over the interests of Taiwanese fishermen and prompting strong criticism from Beijing.

The matter centres on a 61-metre (200-foot) retired cutter handed over to the Philippine Coast Guard through a non-governmental organisation on Monday, as Taipei and Manila expand practical maritime cooperation despite the absence of formal diplomatic ties.

Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) has condemned the move, accusing the island’s ruling party of ignoring infringements by Japan and the Philippines as they pursue maritime delimitation talks.
item.content:encoded:
Taiwan’s transfer of a former coastguard vessel to the Philippines has triggered a dual controversy – raising concerns over the interests of Taiwanese fishermen and prompting strong criticism from Beijing.

The matter centres on a 61-metre (200-foot) retired cutter handed over to the Philippine Coast Guard through a non-governmental organisation on Monday, as Taipei and Manila expand practical maritime cooperation despite the absence of formal diplomatic ties.

Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) has condemned the move, accusing the island’s ruling party of ignoring infringements by Japan and the Philippines as they pursue maritime delimitation talks.

The Democratic Progressive Party had failed to protect the interests of the people of Taiwan and was instead “helping an evildoer do evil”, TAO spokeswoman Zhu Fenglian said on Wednesday.

The authorities’ conduct had increased the risk of harm to the interests of Taiwanese fishermen, she warned, describing the DPP’s action as “despicable”.

On Thursday, Taiwan’s cabinet-level Ocean Affairs Council defended the donation, with minister Kuan Bi-ling saying it was intended to strengthen regional maritime safety.

“The donation agreement contains comprehensive safeguards, explicitly stipulating that the donated vessel must not be used for law enforcement against Taiwanese fishing boats,” she said.

Kuan also rejected Beijing’s criticism on the matter, arguing that Taiwanese fishermen faced more immediate risks from mainland China and citing the boarding and detention of Taiwanese vessels.

Taipei says such incidents have taken place at least three times since 2024.

The We Protect Our Seas (WPS) Foundation, a Philippine non-profit organisation focused on maritime issues, said on Monday that it had formally donated the Taiwanese cutter, renamed Training Ship WPS, to the country’s coastguard.

The ship would be deployed to Mindanao for search and rescue, humanitarian assistance and disaster response, and marine environmental protection, WPS cited Philippine coastguard commandant Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan as saying.

The foundation did not disclose the vessel’s origin or explain how it had acquired it.

However, a Philippine source confirmed to Taiwan’s official Central News Agency on Tuesday that the vessel was the decommissioned Taiwanese coastguard patrol ship Kinmen.

That corroborated earlier information obtained by the South China Morning Post that the retired cutter had been transferred to Manila from Taiwan.

The concerns over the donation reflect a long history of fisheries disputes between Taiwan and the Philippines.

In 2013, personnel aboard a Philippine coastguard vessel opened fire on the Taiwanese fishing boat Guang Da Xing No 28 in overlapping waters, killing one fisherman.

The shooting prompted Taipei to impose sanctions and step up fisheries-protection patrols, which subsequently led to a 2015 agreement to avoid the use of violence or unnecessary force in fisheries law enforcement.

Despite those efforts, tensions linger. Just last year, the Taiwanese fishing boat Sheng Yu Feng was boarded by Philippine personnel and taken to port.

The vessel and its crew were released without penalties the same day after a formal protest from Taipei, which said the boat had been fishing in waters where the two sides’ exclusive economic zones overlap.

Lawmakers from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang have also raised concerns about the Japan-Philippines maritime boundary talks, warning that the waters in question overlap directly with Taiwan’s claimed exclusive economic zone off its east coast.

KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun described the ship transfer as “rubbing salt into the wounds” of Taiwanese fishermen, while party legislator Hsu Yu-chen asked whether the vessel might ultimately be deployed in overlapping waters to board, pursue or expel Taiwanese fishing boats.

The DPP, however, has portrayed closer ties with Manila in a broader regional context.

Lawmaker Wang Ting-yu hailed the recent coastguard cooperation as a “historic breakthrough”, highlighting its strategic significance as both sides face growing grey-zone pressure from Beijing.

Zivon Wang, a military analyst at the Chinese Council of Advanced Policy Studies, a Taipei-based think tank, said geopolitics was the main reason Taipei was willing to proceed despite its history of fisheries disputes with Manila.

“The Philippines is part of the first island chain and an important link in constraining Beijing’s military expansion in the South China Sea,” Wang said, adding that the US had encouraged regional partners, including Japan and South Korea, to help strengthen Philippine capabilities.

“The United States is a major factor behind this,” Wang argued.

The transfer is unusual because previous recipients – including the Marshall Islands, Palau and Tuvalu – maintain diplomatic ties with Taipei, while the Philippines recognises Beijing and has no formal relations with Taiwan.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and never ruled out the use of force to achieve reunification. Most countries, including the United States, Taiwan’s No 1 international backer, do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Taiwanese authorities have offered few details about the vessel transfer.

Marvin H. Bernardo, a Taiwan affairs researcher from the Philippines and PhD candidate at National Chengchi University, noted that the absence of formal diplomatic relations meant an intermediary was needed to facilitate the transfer.

“Given the sensitivity of Beijing to any form of engagement with Taiwan, which they interpret as a violation of the one-China policy, it was more politically expedient to go through an NGO,” he said.

The vessel transfer comes alongside other efforts by Taipei to expand contact with Manila.

Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung has confirmed plans to open a second representative office in Cebu – after Manila – to facilitate economic cooperation. Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration has also pledged to send 100 personnel to the Philippines for a goodwill port visit in October next year.

Max Lo, executive director of the Taipei-based Taiwan International Strategic Study Society, cautioned against interpreting the donation as evidence that relations had entered a fundamentally new phase.

“This is driven by geopolitical factors. It cannot really be described as Taiwan-Philippines friendship moving to a new stage,” Lo said.

He said Taipei was also seeking to show Washington that it was willing to contribute to broader regional security efforts.

At the same time, Lo said, Manila remained cautious about antagonising Beijing, making it unclear how far the Philippines would be prepared to cooperate with Taiwan in responding to pressure from mainland China.

Bernardo said the arrangement nevertheless indicated a willingness on the Philippine side to be more flexible in its engagement with Taiwan.

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesian coal deal fuels doubts over production quota approvals
item.description:
A major coal deal in Indonesia is set to secure a powerful new partner for one of the country’s biggest miners, even as the industry worries a delay in the government’s approval of production quotas could have a severe impact on the business outlook.

Low Tuck Kwong and his daughter Elaine Low, the biggest shareholders of Bayan Resources, agreed on September 16 to sell a 30 per cent stake in Indonesia’s third-largest coal producer to fellow tycoon Andi Syamsuddin Arsyad, better known as Haji Isam.

The deal comes at a sensitive moment for Bayan after the government delayed approval of additional coal quotas for three of its subsidiaries. The uncertainty sent Bayan’s shares sharply lower in the days before the deal announcement. It rose by about 20 per cent as soon as news broke about the stake deal, hitting the upper auto-reject limit.
item.content:encoded:
A major coal deal in Indonesia is set to secure a powerful new partner for one of the country’s biggest miners, even as the industry worries a delay in the government’s approval of production quotas could have a severe impact on the business outlook.

Low Tuck Kwong and his daughter Elaine Low, the biggest shareholders of Bayan Resources, agreed on September 16 to sell a 30 per cent stake in Indonesia’s third-largest coal producer to fellow tycoon Andi Syamsuddin Arsyad, better known as Haji Isam.

The deal comes at a sensitive moment for Bayan after the government delayed approval of additional coal quotas for three of its subsidiaries. The uncertainty sent Bayan’s shares sharply lower in the days before the deal announcement. It rose by about 20 per cent as soon as news broke about the stake deal, hitting the upper auto-reject limit.

The timing has fuelled speculation that the quota hurdle might be linked to the deal, a suggestion that the government has rejected.

Under the conditional agreement, the Lows would sell 10 billion Bayan shares to Jhonlin Baratama, a subsidiary of Haji Isam’s Jhonlin Group, a commodities and logistics conglomerate.

The deal would give Jhonlin a substantial stake in a major Indonesian coal producer. Bayan produced 68 million tonnes of coal last year, compared with Jhonlin’s output of 24 million tonnes.

“Acquiring a major stake in a top-three coal producer like Bayan fundamentally rewires our energy landscape. The state must ensure this consolidation doesn’t birth a mega-cartel,” said Dipo Satria Ramli, an economist at the Centre of Reform on Economics.

Indonesian media have described Haji Isam as an ally of the president. In 2025, Prabowo awarded him the Bintang Mahaputera Utama, one of Indonesia’s highest state honours.

Haji Isam has set his sights on expanding Jhonlin’s coal output after having applied for a 60-million-tonne production quota, known as Rencana Kerja dan Anggaran Biaya (RKAB) in Indonesia, for the rest of this year.

Ahmad Zuhdi Dwi Kusuma, principal at Energy Shift Institute, an independent energy finance think tank, said Jhonlin’s 30 per cent stake in Bayan would strengthen its market position.

“Haji Isam can connect the existing ecosystem he has under his group to Bayan,” he said.

Assuming Jhonlin was successful in acquiring its new 60-million-tonne quota, which was separate from the Bayan quota, its output combined with Bayan’s could account for about one-eighth of Indonesia’s coal market, Zuhdi said.

Details about the deal remain scant, pending further announcements from Bayan.

The Lows currently hold 62 per cent of Bayan’s shares. If the 30 per cent stake sold to Jhonlin comes entirely from their holdings, they would be left with about 32 per cent, potentially leaving control of the company uncertain.

But Ricky Ho, chief investment officer and portfolio manager at Jakarta-based Four Capital, a family office investment firm, said control of Bayan would likely remain with the Lows after the sale.

“Like most Indonesian conglomerate families, they have a lot of nominees in the rest of the 38 per cent stock.”

Under Indonesia’s RKAB system, mining companies must obtain government approval for their production volume. Without an approved quota, miners cannot legally produce beyond an amount authorised by the government.

On September 11, the three Bayan subsidiaries notified customers and invoked force majeure, citing the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources’ failure to issue additional production quota permits for the rest of 2026.

“The approval has not been issued to the company’s subsidiaries, although applications for approval to amend the RKAB have been submitted in accordance with applicable laws and regulations,” Bayan director Low Yi Ngo wrote in a statement.

Without the permits, Bayan’s production in 2026 is expected to total 39 million tonnes, 43 per cent lower than last year.

When Bayan announced the force majeure status to the Indonesian Stock Exchange on September 14, its shares fell by as much as 9.2 per cent that day.

The company eventually received approval for the subsidiaries’ quotas on Wednesday, a week after the deal was announced.

The episode highlighted how coal mining operations could be severely curtailed because of delays in government approval of production volumes, according to analysts.

Without the RKAB, Bayan would face difficulties in planning its production and budget, Zuhdi said. With its quota cut by almost half, it had no choice but to declare force majeure on its existing obligations to clients, he added.

“This serves as a reminder that the regulatory side of the industry in Indonesia is increasingly the be-all and end-all factor for a miner.”

According to a report by The Jakarta Post, the government has faced questions over whether Bayan’s permit delays were linked to Haji Isam’s acquisition. Other Indonesian media outlets highlighted that the quotas were approved shortly after the deal was signed.

This Week in Asia has reached out to Bayan and Jhonlin for comment.

Ho urged caution over drawing a link between the two developments.

When questioned by reporters in Jakarta on September 16 on why Bayan’s permits were not issued on the same day as the deal announcement on September 16, the director general of minerals and coal at the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources, Tri Winarno, said: “It’s still being evaluated and examined in terms of technical aspects, so it will take time.”

He also pointed out that not all of Bayan’s permits were held up. “From all Bayan’s coal subsidiaries, only three are having their permits re-evaluated. So there’s no deliberate targeting here.”

Bayan Resources has 16 subsidiaries – all of which have separate permits to mine coal – covering 126,000 hectares in East and South Kalimantan.

Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia on Wednesday rejected any connection between Bayan’s quota crisis and its stake sale. “The two were separate processes with no link whatsoever,” he told reporters.

Nonetheless, the developments have left market participants worrying about uncertainty over regulatory decisions and their impact on the value of Indonesian mining assets.

Calling it an “unpalatable aftertaste” for investors, Ho said: “The optics remain remarkable because a regulatory approval becomes critical to production, the company declares force majeure, a major ownership transaction is signed, and the regulatory uncertainty clears almost immediately.”

Dipo said the developments would affect investors’ perceptions of official transparency. “Investors will be even more cautious about potential government intervention in the future,” he added.

Katherine Hasan, a researcher at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, said that beyond the deal, Bayan and others in the coal industry would have to balance between staying competitive even as the Indonesian government sought to increase the proportion of energy production from green sources.

The Prabowo administration is seeking to phase out all coal and fossil fuel power plants by 2040 and increase solar energy production to 100 GW by 2029.

While Bayan and its peers were aiming to bolster their cash flows by increasing domestic coal production, they faced the “political reality” of Jakarta seeking to curb its fuel subsidies and enhance the country’s long-term energy security.

item.title: [SCMP] Ukraine’s POW transfer reveal deals North Korea a propaganda blow
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has put North Korea in a propaganda bind, analysts say, by publicly revealing that Kyiv recently transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

The disclosure – made during Zelensky’s address to the UN General Assembly on Wednesday – directly challenges Pyongyang’s narrative that its soldiers fighting alongside Russian forces would choose death over surrender.

North Korea is unlikely to acknowledge the transfer publicly, but may strengthen ideological controls over its troops deployed to Russia to prevent further defections, observers say.
item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has put North Korea in a propaganda bind, analysts say, by publicly revealing that Kyiv recently transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

The disclosure – made during Zelensky’s address to the UN General Assembly on Wednesday – directly challenges Pyongyang’s narrative that its soldiers fighting alongside Russian forces would choose death over surrender.

North Korea is unlikely to acknowledge the transfer publicly, but may strengthen ideological controls over its troops deployed to Russia to prevent further defections, observers say.

“Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea,” Zelensky said during his UN address, using South Korea’s official name.

“These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realised he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself and he was shocked that fate didn’t let him die.”

The two soldiers were reportedly captured by Ukrainian forces in January 2025 after being deployed to Russia’s Kursk region to support Moscow’s war effort. Zelensky said they subsequently expressed a desire to travel to South Korea, as indicated in interviews and handwritten letters sent to organisations representing North Korean defectors.

South Korea’s Foreign Ministry declined to confirm any specific details regarding the POWs, citing concerns for the safety of the men and their families in the North.

But it did say in a statement that the issue should be resolved in a manner that “respects the free will of the individuals concerned and is consistent with international law and humanitarian principles”.

“In line with this position, the government has been engaged in necessary consultations with Ukraine and other relevant countries and organisations,” the ministry said, adding that this was “a sensitive matter” and it could not divulge details about bilateral consultations.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung expressed regret about the disclosure in a social media post on Thursday, calling it “a highly sensitive matter” that could have serious implications for diplomacy and security on the Korean peninsula.

“Considering the various issues that could arise from making the matter public, keeping it confidential was the reasonable course of action in every respect, and that was what we agreed upon,” Lee wrote in Korean.

“While I do not know the specific circumstances that led the Ukrainian side to break the agreement and go public, the situation is deeply regrettable.”

South Korean opposition lawmaker Yu Yong-weon said on Thursday that the two prisoners had left Ukraine last weekend, travelled via a third country and arrived in South Korea three to four days earlier, likely under the protection of South Korean intelligence agencies.

In July, Lee and Zelensky agreed on the sidelines of the Nato summit in Ankara to handle the North Korean POW issue based on humanitarian principles while respecting the prisoners’ wishes.

‘Propaganda nightmare’

Zelensky raised the POW issue while accusing Russian President Vladimir Putin of recruiting foreign fighters to prosecute his war on Ukraine.

“Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory … instead of simply stopping and running his own country,” Zelensky said, adding that Moscow had recruited citizens from 47 countries, including Ghana, Nepal and India.

Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, said Pyongyang would likely remain silent to protect the narrative of absolute loyalty and self-sacrifice among its troops.

“North Korea is likely to ignore the issue or show little interest, given the potential burden of allowing it to become a major political issue,” Yang said. “At the same time, Pyongyang is expected to strengthen ideological education and internal controls over North Korean troops in Russia to prevent similar defections.”

Oh Gyeong-seob, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification, described the situation as a “propaganda nightmare” for Pyongyang, as it had consistently eulogised its soldiers as heroes who take their own lives rather than surrender.

“For North Korean soldiers in Russia, this news opens a different option that is not death when they risk being captured,” Oh said, adding that Ukraine was likely to use the defection in psychological warfare targeting North Korean troops.

Questions of trust

Yang said that Zelensky’s decision to go public with the POW transfer could have broader geopolitical implications – potentially driving a wedge between Seoul and Kyiv.

“Bringing such a sensitive humanitarian issue directly into the international spotlight at the United Nations could undermine trust in relations between South Korea and Ukraine,” Yang said. “The Ukrainian president could also face criticism that a sensitive humanitarian issue is being politicised.”

Respecting prisoners’ free will should have included getting their consent before revealing their transfer, Yang added, given the risk of retaliation against their families remaining in North Korea.

“Announcing their defection without first securing their consent would constitute an inhumane act,” he said. “Zelensky himself should make clear whether the prisoners’ consent to the public disclosure was explicitly obtained.”

Yang dismissed speculation of a secret deal between Kyiv and Seoul, pointing to President Lee’s stated preference for diplomatic transparency.

Oh said the disclosure could also serve Ukraine’s broader strategy of highlighting the deepening military relationship between Russia and North Korea as Kyiv sought continued international support for its war effort.

While Seoul has provided humanitarian aid to Ukraine, it maintains a strict policy against supplying lethal weapons to any country at war.

Asian Games defections?

Zelensky’s disclosure coincided with an unconfirmed report that two members of North Korea’s delegation to this year’s Asian Games in Japan were seeking asylum.

South Korea’s Monthly Chosun magazine reported on Tuesday that the pair – part of an estimated 180-member North Korean delegation – had approached Japanese authorities expressing a desire to seek asylum in Japan rather than South Korea.

Citing a source linked to Japan’s Cabinet Intelligence and Research Office and the pro-Pyongyang General Association of Korean Residents in Japan, known as Chongryon, the magazine said the individuals’ identities and roles had not been disclosed.

Japanese authorities have not publicly confirmed the report and it is unclear whether any defections have occurred at the Games.

item.title: [SCMP] AI poses new national security threat, outgoing Hong Kong deputy police chief warns
item.description:
Retiring deputy police commissioner Andrew Kan Kai-yan has said artificial intelligence (AI) poses a new threat to national security in Hong Kong, with the force turning to the emerging technology to help combat the issue.

Kan raised the alarm after state security minister Chen Yixin warned last week of rising national security risks posed by AI. The senior mainland Chinese official also called for robust risk prevention frameworks and stronger global governance of the technology.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu outlined plans in his annual policy address last week to adopt an AI risk‑governance strategy, focusing on combating the use of such technologies in criminal activities and formulating safety‑management guidelines for AI agents.
item.content:encoded:
Retiring deputy police commissioner Andrew Kan Kai-yan has said artificial intelligence (AI) poses a new threat to national security in Hong Kong, with the force turning to the emerging technology to help combat the issue.

Kan raised the alarm after state security minister Chen Yixin warned last week of rising national security risks posed by AI. The senior mainland Chinese official also called for robust risk prevention frameworks and stronger global governance of the technology.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu outlined plans in his annual policy address last week to adopt an AI risk‑governance strategy, focusing on combating the use of such technologies in criminal activities and formulating safety‑management guidelines for AI agents.

Kan, 57, who headed the National Security Department, began his pre-retirement leave on Tuesday after 35 years on the force.

Discussing the new threat, the outgoing police official said he had seen overseas examples of AI agents launching attacks on critical infrastructure and other companies’ computer systems, as well as generating misinformation.

Anti-government forces could also use AI to commit crimes related to national security, he said.

“I totally agree … that AI poses a new security threat to national security,” he said. “We have been working to improve our capability in AI in this aspect. I can also tell you one of the tactics to combat AI crime is using AI.”

Kan pointed to AI tools used to help screen social media posts to identify potential “soft resistance” against the government as an example.

“As computers and AI become more powerful, the chances of successfully hiding your criminal intent or criminal acts are actually getting slimmer. So, it’s better not to test the law,” he warned.

The police official also said that anyone who used AI to commit crimes should be held responsible.

Kan said the current legislation was adequate for now to tackle such threats, but he did not rule out the need for new legislation in the future.

“Maybe in the future we need new laws,” he said. “Of course, technology grows very fast. We do not know next year or five years later, what the world will be.”

Discussing the relevant legislation, he cited Section 50 of the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance, which governs acts of endangering national security in relation to computers or electronic systems, saying that authorities had anticipated AI-related threats while drafting the law.

He also pointed to the Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance, which safeguards critical infrastructure and banking systems from attacks.

In his announcement of Hong Kong’s first five-year blueprint last week, Lee touched on plans to enhance the legal system and enforcement mechanisms to safeguard national security.

Kan said the four main national security threats that would require vigilance over the next five years were soft resistance, home-grown terrorism, foreign influence and espionage.

Earlier this year, national security police raided three independent bookstores over allegations that they had displayed or sold titles with seditious intent.

The deputy police chief said his officers had actually read the books and sought legal advice from the Department of Justice before taking enforcement action. “There is no such thing as blind enforcement or making arbitrary arrests,” he said.

Kan also rejected the idea of publishing a banned books list with book titles or ISBNs, arguing booksellers were responsible for ensuring the books they were selling complied with local national security legislation and comparing the situation to how restaurant owners needed to ensure food safety.

“If we issue a banned books list today, and tomorrow you publish another book that turns out to be illegal after our investigation, you’ll say, ‘hey, why are you arresting us if it wasn’t on the list?’ This simply cannot resolve the problem,” he said.

He suggested that sellers read the books before offering them and seek legal advice if in doubt. “If you say it is not easy to get legal advice … then don’t sell it,” he said.

“If you say, ‘you will not publish the book list, and I don’t know where the red line is’ – I feel this is a bit of … soft resistance,” he said, adding that there was a clear definition of sedition under the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance.

Kan said more people were engaging in soft resistance, which had become even more discreet and underground after the enactment of national security laws.

He added that people used different platforms, including cultural, arts and online media, to spread misinformation, incite hatred and instigate public resentment towards the local and central governments.

On the distinction between soft resistance and freedom of speech, he said that the key determining factors were whether the expression was intended to incite others and whether the criticism was based on concrete facts.

On September 11, three former leaders of the now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil were sentenced to up to seven years and three months in jail for inciting subversion.

Kan said that whether it was legal to commemorate the anniversary of the Tiananmen Square crackdown on June 4 in the future should be judged on a case-by-case basis.

He said that when evaluating applications for protests, police assessed threats to national security, public order and safety, as well as the potential impacts on the freedoms of others.

“Of course, if the rally or protest you join is explicitly taking up the mantle of the alliance’s ideology, or ideas aimed at opposing China and destabilising Hong Kong, then you really need to think twice about whether you’ll end up breaking the law,” he said.

Commenting on the effectiveness of putting bounties on wanted persons who had breached national security laws, Kan said: “Justice may be delayed, but it will not be denied.

“Just because they haven’t returned now does not mean they never will … world politics can change drastically.

“Will those sheltering you today betray you tomorrow? I wouldn’t rule it out. It’s certainly not impossible. When you beg others for protection and shelter, what happens to you once your usefulness runs out? We shall wait and see.”

Kan also noted that national security police had arrested people suspected of handling funds or donations on behalf of absconders, largely cutting off their means of survival.

Asked whether he would join the Committee for Safeguarding National Security after retiring, he said he wanted to take a good rest and spend time with his family first, adding that he did not have any current plans for the future.

item.title: [SCMP] Ode to the horse: 5,000 years of human-equine connection on display in new Kazakh museum
item.description:
On the scenic drive east from Almaty, in Kazakhstan, along the old corridor of the A351 highway, towards the Charyn Canyon National Park, and the Xinjiang border beyond that, sits an unassuming museum run by an unlikely duo.

Nurbol Baimukhanov, 50, is an independent, published researcher of shezhire – traditional Kazakh genealogies, historically memorised and passed down through generations – and an award-winning documentary producer who speaks in equal parts archaeology and mysticism. His son Ilyas, 23, with a MacBook tucked under his arm and an eye for systems, is pursuing a master’s in management at Satbayev University, the nation’s oldest technical institute.

On a quiet stretch of the A351, father and son have built a showcase dedicated to the ancient Botai, the multi-hyphenate people of the Eurasian steppes – hunter-gatherer-herder-settlers – who some archaeologists believe were among the first to domesticate the horse more than 5,000 years ago.
item.content:encoded:
On the scenic drive east from Almaty, in Kazakhstan, along the old corridor of the A351 highway, towards the Charyn Canyon National Park, and the Xinjiang border beyond that, sits an unassuming museum run by an unlikely duo.

Nurbol Baimukhanov, 50, is an independent, published researcher of shezhire – traditional Kazakh genealogies, historically memorised and passed down through generations – and an award-winning documentary producer who speaks in equal parts archaeology and mysticism. His son Ilyas, 23, with a MacBook tucked under his arm and an eye for systems, is pursuing a master’s in management at Satbayev University, the nation’s oldest technical institute.

On a quiet stretch of the A351, father and son have built a showcase dedicated to the ancient Botai, the multi-hyphenate people of the Eurasian steppes – hunter-gatherer-herder-settlers – who some archaeologists believe were among the first to domesticate the horse more than 5,000 years ago.

Located around 70km from Almaty, the Ush Qiyan Open-Air Museum sits near the village of Akshiy, in the Enbekshikazakh district – the kind of place most travellers pass without noticing.

Opened this summer, it rises from the flat landscape as three circular log dwellings with sloping roofs – constructed from more than 1,000 logs, the exhibition brochure proudly proclaims – and is designed to evoke what some researchers believe are among the oldest known permanent settlements of the steppes.

Ush Qiyan receives no government funds, has launched no grand marketing campaign – it is just a father, his son and their semi-domesticated horse named Ayan grazing outside.

“Kazakh culture is, first and foremost, the culture of the horse,” says Nurbol. “In gratitude to these beautiful animals, we built this museum as a temple of knowledge to enlighten people.”

Before there were empires and criss-crossing trade routes, before valiant steeds carried armies across continents and monks towards enlightenment, there was a culture that first looked at a wild horse and saw something more than prey.

It is believed that the Botai people lived in what is now northern Kazakhstan, in the 4th and 3rd millennia BC. Mighty they were not.

As far as archaeologists could detect, the Botai built no cities, wrote no epics and erected no monuments that would survive the centuries and catch the eye. Instead, what they left behind were traces of dwellings, scattered pottery and the bones of horses – thousands upon thousands of them, now housed at the North Kazakhstan Regional Museum of History and Local Lore, in Petropavl.

Archaeologists around the world now widely believe that the Botai were the first to domesticate the horse, though the claim is debated each time new evidence comes to light. Experts argue that the proof is in the bones, which show signs of bit wear on the teeth, from the bridle gear used to control them, and in the residue of mare’s milk found in their pottery, leading them to theorise that the Botai were not just hunting horses, but riding them, milking them and living alongside them. If true, it would be one of the most consequential partnerships in human history. Migration, trade, warfare, the spread of ideas and empires – all of it would eventually travel on horseback.

And yet, there is a twist. Genetic research suggests that the animal the Botai domesticated is actually the ancestor of the Przewalski’s horse – the stocky, pot-bellied wild horse that still roams parts of Central Asia. In other words, the first horse believed to be part of human culture eventually returned to the wild, rather than develop into the modern steeds we see today.

Ush Qiyan attempts to capture this paradox – the last wild-horse species being descended from domesticated ancestors, raising questions around whether the breed is truly wild or simply feral – telling a complicated story about a partnership that was formed, dissolved and formed again, as the modern horse, tamed later in the Early Bronze Age, became the engine of human history.

It all started with Ayan, a stallion who seems to straddle both worlds. In the spring of 2021, Nurbol went looking for a light-hued horse in the Altai mountain range, in eastern Kazakhstan. He had no particular reason for doing so; he says he simply, suddenly, felt like having one.

A friend had told him about a remote village with no internet and a horse bearing a rare isabelline colour. Having negotiated a price, it took Nurbol three nights by truck to take Ayan back to Almaty.

“He was born wild, near Lake Zaysan,” says Nurbol.

Ayan is, according to Nurbol, a Zhabe – one of Kazakhstan’s oldest horse breeds, distinguished by its stout frame, thick neck, muscular croup and substantial body weight. But with a pale, almost metallic coat that glows golden in sunlight, Ayan is no ordinary Zhabe.

Whether the isabelline colouring is genetically possible for this breed is another matter, but Nurbol is not a man to let science get in the way of a good story.

“It was a sign from above,” he says, referencing the heavens. “Our horse bears all the hallmarks of an ancient celestial horse. It has a powerful mind and transmits information telepathically.”

Separating fact from fiction is a secondary concern for Nurbol.

He is a researcher whose published works focus on history, archaeology and ancestry. At the same time, he is a believer who sees little boundary between myth and reality. In his telling, Ayan the horse is both a living animal and the latest chapter in a legend that began with the Botai people and culture five millennia ago.

“In the Chinese epic Journey to the West, the White Dragon Horse came from the West,” says Nurbol, noting that, in the text, “the tale of the monk [Tang Sanzang] who met a White Dragon Horse happened somewhere in our area. [Kazakhstan] is a land of legends where myth and reality intertwine”.

Ayan eventually inspired the construction of Ush Qiyan, which began in the summer of 2024. It took about two years to finish, building only in the warmer months, with a small crew, and involved no architects or contractors in the conventional sense – just workers stripping bark from logs under a punishing sun.

“Construction was not easy,” Nurbol recalls. “It was very hot. People were breaking down like matchsticks.”

All the logs had to be processed and cut by hand, following what Nurbol dubs “experimental archaeology” – a scientific approach to understanding how ancient nomads built their dwellings, and the physical labour involved. It was, in his words, an attempt to recreate not just the look of the Botai world, but the toll it took.

Money for the project came entirely from the Baimukhanovs, and though that choice was deliberate, it had consequences. Nurbol remembers days when, due to a lack of funds, “we were idle and wondering how to raise money to continue construction. [But] this was our conscious choice, and we are pleased with the result”.

Ilyas was born in Almaty and grew up tagging along on his father’s scientific expeditions across Kazakhstan. Ush Qiyan, in some ways, is the culmination of a childhood spent among artefacts and open landscapes. Now in his early adulthood, Ilyas speaks with the composure of someone a decade older.

“My father and I are like-minded people,” he says. “I represent the younger generation, a new perspective.” While Nurbol supplies the vision, the younger Baimukhanov thinks about sustainability, management systems and visitor services.

His own “eureka!” moment came years earlier, in the Botai region of northern Kazakhstan, where he met the influential archaeologist Viktor Fedorovich Zaibert, who discovered, excavated and opened the Botai settlement site in 1980, in the Aiyrtau district. In doing so, Zaibert gave the world some of the earliest evidence for horse husbandry and domestication. “He [was] an amazing person,” Ilyas recalls. “He told fascinating stories about history.”

What struck him were the traces of ancient circles still visible in the earth – the outlines of dwellings long gone – and the bones and pottery scattered across the ground, some more than 5,000 years old.

“I am happy to have interacted with such a great archaeologist and seen the artefacts in person. It’s unforgettable,” says Ilyas. Zaibert died in 2022, but his influence, legacy and memory live on in the log walls of the museum.

A visitor to Ush Qiyan moves through the three log structures, each roof shaped like an inverted basket, echoing the ancient yurts of the early nomads. Inside, scientific replicas of nomadic dress from various periods, made from materials such as hide, bone and leather, created for the 2018 documentary Equus: Story of the Horse, which Nurbol co-produced, hang alongside other props. Installations showing reconstructions of historical dwellings and horse sculptures fill the spaces between, and films are screened for guests who want to linger.

In another room, Daniyar Sarbassov, a 36-year-old artist from the Bayanaul district, showcases his work: castings of horses, mostly.

“Daniyar is our friend,” says Nurbol. “He’s a talented sculptor with great potential.” But the connection to the museum runs deeper than friendship. Sarbassov’s horses are not decorative – they carry, as Nurbol puts it, “the code of the Great Steppe”.

One of his pieces, an aluminium-and-bronze statue titled Zhuyrik (2022), was sculpted earlier, in his studio, when Sarbassov had no knowledge of Ayan, or the world Nurbol was building. But when he spotted the ivory-coloured horse, something shifted. “After seeing Ayan, I decided that this work would be better placed at the entrance of the museum,” he says.

In Sarbassov’s description, Zhuyrik is not simply a horse running.

It is “a creature that merges with the wind and moves together with the air”. Its smooth surface catches the natural light from the structure’s oculus as it shifts throughout the day, seemingly dissolving the boundary between the horse’s body and the surrounding space.

“A truly swift horse is difficult to perceive in its entirety,” he says. “Its speed is often experienced through the impression, trace and sensation of movement left in our memory.”

As its metallic shine echoes Ayan’s coat, Sarbassov calls it “a spiritual symbol of the museum”. He hopes it will remain there permanently, and that visitors will find their own meaning in the work: “One viewer may see freedom in the image of a horse, another may be reminded of their ancestors, while a third may discover an entirely different meaning. My hope is that they will pause for a moment to reflect on their own history, their homeland and their place as human beings within this vast expanse of time.”

Outside, Ayan grazes, unaware of the symbolism attached to him. Nurbol considers him the living echo of the story Ush Qiyan exists to tell: the wild horse that came to humans, changed their world and still carries that independence in its blood. Whether that story belongs to history or to myth is, by now, beside the point.

Between them, a father and son have built a temple to the horse, raised by hand, off the beaten track. “We live in a complex era of digital technology; it’s difficult to be surprised by anything,” says Nurbol. “But at the same time, we look to the future without forgetting the past. Our museum is like a time machine.”

But a time machine moves forwards, too. More visitors will be drawn by the same road that connected cultures. Ush Qiyan sits beside it, ready to welcome those who pause on their way to somewhere else. “The Great Steppe has always been a place of meeting,” says Nurbol. “We are open to dialogue with the world.”

item.title: [SCMP] Xi-Trump atmospherics welcomed but mask structural rifts: analysts
item.description:
During their three-day summit that ended on Friday, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping worked overtime to underscore their increasingly close relationship even as the meeting produced few concrete deliverables.

But the fact that the two economic and military giants are talking – and pledging to talk some more – suggests some period of relative stability ahead, certainly relative to last year’s all-out trade war, chest-thumping and market turmoil, said analysts, companies and former US officials.

“Both countries are demonstrating some degree of restraint,” said Sara Schuman, managing director at consultancy Beacon Global Strategies and a former US diplomat in Beijing. “The optics that President Xi is travelling to Washington and he’s receiving a full state visit with a state dinner, this is in itself the core deliverable.”
item.content:encoded:
During their three-day summit that ended on Friday, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping worked overtime to underscore their increasingly close relationship even as the meeting produced few concrete deliverables.

But the fact that the two economic and military giants are talking – and pledging to talk some more – suggests some period of relative stability ahead, certainly relative to last year’s all-out trade war, chest-thumping and market turmoil, said analysts, companies and former US officials.

“Both countries are demonstrating some degree of restraint,” said Sara Schuman, managing director at consultancy Beacon Global Strategies and a former US diplomat in Beijing. “The optics that President Xi is travelling to Washington and he’s receiving a full state visit with a state dinner, this is in itself the core deliverable.”

By that definition, the visit was chock full.

Xi said the two leaders were “making history” with two summits in four months and two more meet-ups planned, one in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen and another the following month at the G20 Trump is hosting in Miami.

And Xi spent the Mid-Autumn Festival outside China, only the second time during his near 14-year administration he has done so.

Trump, for his part, greeted Xi in person when he arrived at the airport, a role usually reserved for lower-level officials and a courtesy that the Chinese president did not extend to Trump when he landed in Beijing in May.

Both leaders also spent the 42-hour visit implicitly or explicitly framing China as an equal or near-equal global power, outlining the “great promise” of the bilateral relationship built on “mutual trust”, foreshadowing “a truly great friendship” like a “river that never stops flowing” as they “steer the giant ship of China-US relations steadily forward towards the future”.

No mention of rare earth minerals stand-off

Unspoken was the hugely consequential cudgel China has unsheathed: its global grip on rare earth minerals, which has fundamentally shifted the power balance after Trump pushed Beijing to the wall, threatening tariffs in excess of 125 per cent during last year’s “Liberation Day”.

Add China’s accelerated bid to diversify its trade dependence on US markets, its increasingly competitive artificial intelligence industry and its dominant position in electric vehicles, lithium batteries and renewable technologies, and it is not difficult to understand Beijing’s growing confidence.

Since then, Beijing has negotiated a trade truce with the US, which was extended this week until January 10; seen the transactional US president reframe Taiwan and high-end semiconductors as negotiable; forestalled a planned US$14 billion arms package to Taipei; pushed away US threats to sanction Chinese banks and refineries for bypassing Washington’s Iran sanctions and watched as greater distance opened between Washington and such long-time allies as Japan and South Korea.

“This is Xi Jinping’s world, and we’re all living in it,” said Scott Kennedy, senior adviser at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). “The administration’s China strategy was poorly designed from the beginning. They thought they could use massive unilateral pressure to force China to make concessions, and that did not occur. In fact, the opposite did.”

Time and relative stability afford China more time to develop its increasingly successful trade strategy, allow Beijing to focus on its domestic economy rather than respond to erratic tariff gyrations, and see Washington increasingly distracted by Trump’s war of choice in Iran, the trade war with Canada, and his record-low popularity leading into the November midterm election.

Missing Chinese holidays, travelling repeatedly to the US by a president whose trips are carefully calibrated, displaying keen interest in Trump’s new helipad and supporting his bid to rebrand AI as “Super Intelligence”, expressing warmth hardly instinctual in China’s more austere political culture and making favourable references to Trump’s “make America great again” mantra may be a small price to pay.

“China has flexed its muscle, established its ability to counterstrike and the credibility of its retaliation,” said Yun Sun, China director at the Simson Centre. “Xi Jinping will visit Washington any day to be the peer of his US counterpart.”

In addition to the two-month trade truce extension, the week’s modest, more conventional deliverables included a likely Board of Trade deal involving reciprocal trade carve-outs subject to reduced tariffs that is likely to include some combination of “non-strategic” farm products, apparel, consumer electronics and other manufactured goods. Details are due out on Monday.

But analysts also said the increasingly frequent meetings between Xi and Trump, who favours in-person negotiations unencumbered by extensive planning or expert input, make it difficult to expect the sort of big-dollar deals and structural reforms that often took years of intensive negotiation under past US administrations.

Warm “friendship” at the very top also masks underlying seams, analysts said. Hawks on both sides quietly resist ostensibly closer ties. Important lower-level channels across the Pacific have winnowed as both presidents pared down officials in the military and broader bureaucracy. And growing competition and rivalry leave deep reservoirs of distrust. The lack of written agreements also lays the groundwork for misunderstanding.

“There’s been so much miscommunication or differing perceptions from both sides coming out of these summits,” said Emily Kilcrease, senior fellow at the Centre for a New American Security and a former senior US Trade Representative negotiator.

“Given how low the trust is between these two countries, it’s really important that people know who their counterparts are and can call them when there’s a crisis.”

US visit helps Xi-Trump bromance to blossom

Framing the budding Trump-Xi bromance are more than a few similarities, analysts said. Both believe they are battling “deep state” bureaucratic resistance. Both enjoy the pomp and pageantry of their power.

Both believe their economic model is superior, that their AI and technology will win out. And both face domestic economic challenges.

“When you see Xi Jinping and Donald Trump together, each of them believes that time is on their side,” said Edgard Kagen, a CSIS senior adviser and former political chief with the US Embassy in Beijing. “The US [believes it] will develop alternative sources of critical minerals and rare earths, and so time is on the US side. When Xi Jinping sits down with Donald Trump, he very much believes the US is in a hurtling decline and the time is on China’s side.”

“Neither of them has an interest, at least at this point, in an escalation on trade issues.”

Two more presidential meetings this year are likely to help maintain bilateral stability. They are also likely to push off any Taiwan arms package.

But the prospect of Trump alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin at both – Moscow’s representative attended the two-day G20 Finance Ministers meeting in North Carolina starting August 31, and Putin is expected in Shenzhen – could further weaken traditional US alliances, some said.

“Trump continues to berate many of our closest allies, from Canada to Europe to Korea to Japan. At the same time, when he meets with US adversaries, usually he says relatively nice things,” said Zack Cooper, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and a former National Security Council official.

“That message would be heard loud and clear, and it will just further accelerate the drive from a lot of US allies to decrease their reliance on the United States. And it may embolden Russia and China to test those alliances even more.”

With so much at stake, experts say, the test will be whether this week’s atmospherics lead to longer-term equilibrium or a return to instability.

“You can have a state visit, respectful rhetoric, a very good dinner, while both governments continue to build tools to compete with each other the next day,” said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the Federation for the Defence of Democracies and a former US diplomat.

“I don’t expect a reset in US-China relations. I do not expect a grand bargain on trade. I don’t expect Washington and Beijing to resolve their technology competition, economic security disputes, or any fundamental disagreement over Taiwan.”

“It’s a summit about managing stalemate, not resolving it.”

item.title: [SCMP] China set to decide if Costa Rican or Guyanese diplomat becomes first woman UN chief
item.description:
China is poised to decide which of two Latin American women becomes the first to lead the United Nations, after three rounds of informal voting in the Security Council failed to produce a favourite.

Several UN delegations that spoke to the South China Morning Post over the past three days said Beijing was weighing Rebeca Grynspan, the Costa Rican economist who heads UN Trade and Development, and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, Guyana’s ambassador to the UN.

The same delegations said China had ruled out Rafael Grossi, the Argentine director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency. Grossi is widely seen as Washington’s preferred candidate and was nominated last year by Argentine President Javier Milei.
item.content:encoded:
China is poised to decide which of two Latin American women becomes the first to lead the United Nations, after three rounds of informal voting in the Security Council failed to produce a favourite.

Several UN delegations that spoke to the South China Morning Post over the past three days said Beijing was weighing Rebeca Grynspan, the Costa Rican economist who heads UN Trade and Development, and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, Guyana’s ambassador to the UN.

The same delegations said China had ruled out Rafael Grossi, the Argentine director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency. Grossi is widely seen as Washington’s preferred candidate and was nominated last year by Argentine President Javier Milei.

China has kept cordial but cooler relations with Milei since his 2023 presidential campaign, when he called the Chinese government “assassins” and promised to cut ties in favour of the “civilised side of life”.

Under UN rules, the 193-member General Assembly appoints the secretary general on the recommendation of the 15-member Security Council. The winner will succeed current UN chief Antonio Guterres, whose second term ends on December 31. The assembly has never rejected a name put forward by the council.

A candidate needs at least nine votes in the council and no veto from any of the five permanent members, which are China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Before a formal vote, the council holds secret straw polls in which members mark each candidate “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion”. Colour-coded ballots, used in later rounds, show whether a discourage vote came from a permanent member, though not which one.

Both Grynspan and Rodrigues-Birkett travelled to Beijing this year to meet Foreign Minister Wang Yi, but China has not publicly endorsed either of them.

Grynspan led the first straw poll in July with 10 encourage votes, and Rodrigues-Birkett came first in the second round in August.

In the third poll a week ago, Grynspan received nine encourage votes, five discourage votes and one no opinion, according to diplomats with knowledge of the tally sheets. Rodrigues-Birkett received eight encourage votes, and her discourage votes rose from three to six.

Grossi, Ugandan diplomat and former UN under-secretary-general Olara Otunnu and Senegal’s former president Macky Sall received five encourage votes each. Former Ecuadorian foreign minister Maria Fernanda Espinosa received three, and Ecuador’s Ivonne A-Baki received none.

The results do not show whether any of Grynspan’s five discourage votes came from a permanent member. In the 2016 race, which took six straw polls, Guterres did not fall below 11 encourage votes.

China has not said publicly which candidate it prefers, but the Brics summit in New Delhi earlier this month could serve as a hint of what Beijing thinks of the contest.

During the summit, the Brics leaders adopted a joint declaration noting that “no woman has ever been elected for the role of Secretary-General” and that only one national from Latin America and the Caribbean had held the post.

Also, China’s ambassador to the UN, Fu Cong, reportedly said in May that Beijing supported regional rotation for the organisation’s top job and would be “pleased to see a woman in the post”, according to Costa Rican news site El Observador. Grynspan thanked him for the remarks at the time.

Bachelet’s withdrawal

While the choice between the leading female candidates appears wide open, another contender has categorically failed to win China’s favour.

While there is no confirmation on its position on Grynspan and Rodrigues-Birkett, three sources familiar with the matter told the SCMP that the Chinese delegation “decisively voted against” Michelle Bachelet, the former Chilean president.

Bachelet withdrew from the race last Saturday, a day after she received one encourage vote and 11 discourage votes in the third poll. Her withdrawal left seven officially nominated candidates in the race.

Chile’s government under President Jose Antonio Kast withdrew her nomination earlier in the year, and her candidacy continued with the backing of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Mexico. Conservative US lawmakers had also urged Washington to veto her over her support for abortion rights, Reuters reported.

Bachelet’s relationship with Beijing deteriorated during her term as UN high commissioner for human rights. She visited Xinjiang in May 2022 and Western governments criticised the trip as too soft on China.

Then, minutes before her UN term ended in August that year, her office published an assessment of Xinjiang. It said abuses against Uygurs and other mostly Muslim minorities in the region “may amount to crimes against humanity”.

China’s mission in Geneva rejected the report as disinformation serving the US and other Western countries.

Meetings with Wang Yi

Grynspan met Wang in Beijing in June and, according to the Chinese foreign ministry, reaffirmed her commitment to the one-China principle. She also praised China’s support for multilateralism and the UN Charter.

Wang told her that her remarks showed an understanding of the concerns of Global South countries.

He said the next secretary general should uphold the UN Charter and be capable, fair and responsible, and that China would take part in the selection with a “constructive attitude”.

Grynspan has led UN Trade and Development since 2021. In 2022 she helped broker the Istanbul agreements, which reopened Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea and eased Russian food and fertiliser shipments.

Rodrigues-Birkett also met Wang in Beijing, although a month later. The ministry said she “expressed support for UN General Assembly Resolution 2758”, which Beijing cites as the basis of its claim to represent China at the UN, and “reaffirmed the one-China principle”.

She also praised Chinese President Xi Jinping’s four global initiatives and China’s proposal for a World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. The Chinese-language readout quoted her as calling China “a leader on development issues”.

After the meeting, Guyana’s Department of Public Information reported that China supported her candidacy. It later apologised and said the report had “mischaracterised Beijing’s position”.

In February 2021, Guyana cancelled an agreement for a Taiwan office less than 24 hours after it was announced, following a public objection from the Chinese foreign ministry.

Yet, two sources from countries represented at the Security Council told the SCMP that Grynspan had a slight advantage with Beijing. But they said the Chinese delegation was wary of her because of her ties to Israel and her perceived closeness to Washington.

Chinese commentators have also pointed to Grynspan’s Jewish background and relatives in Israel. She would be the UN’s first Jewish secretary general.

Meanwhile, the New York Times reported this week that the US had indicated it would block Rodrigues-Birkett. The newspaper said the objection related to her statement to the Security Council in 2024 that “a veritable genocide” was taking place in Gaza.

A State Department official told the newspaper that the US wanted a candidate who would pursue substantial reform and streamline the organisation. The Guyanese government has not commented publicly on the report.

China’s mission to the UN and the US State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

On Tuesday, Rodrigues-Birkett joined Guyanese President Irfaan Ali in New York as he signed the Shield of the Americas security communique with US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, on the sidelines of the General Assembly.

Next steps

The sources heard by SCMP said they expected the race to be discussed during Xi’s visit to Washington this week. They said it was not clear whether Xi would raise it with Trump or leave it to a meeting between Wang and Rubio.

Xi met Trump at the White House on Thursday but did not travel to New York for the General Assembly’s high-level week.

The race remains open, and diplomats said new compromise candidates who are acceptable to all five permanent members could still emerge if the deadlock persists. Some rumoured names could include Emirati diplomat and former UAE permanent representative to the UN Lana Nusseibeh , former Dutch minister Sigrid Kaag, and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. None of them has said they would run.

The split among the permanent members has no precedent in recent UN selections, and it risks disrupting the organisation’s leadership if no successor is chosen by the end of the year.

Guterres has made clear he does not intend to stay on in an interim capacity while the council searches for a successor. He has already begun arranging his permanent return to Portugal, according to a UN source.

A fourth straw poll could be held after the high-level week ends on Monday. In 2006 and 2016, the council held its final straw polls in early October.

item.title: [SCMP] Trump hails WWII ‘ally’ China as Xi tells of bonds ‘forged in blood and fire’
item.description:
In a surprise nod to shared history, US President Donald Trump called China a World War II ally as he welcomed Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday ahead of summit talks.

But the historical reference was far from one-sided, with both leaders repeatedly referring to the joint fight against Japanese aggression as they sought to emphasise the long history of US-China friendship and the need to seek common ground.

“If we focus on our common interests, I’m confident there is much we can achieve,” Trump said in the White House foyer during the state welcome ceremony ahead of formal talks with the Chinese president.
item.content:encoded:
In a surprise nod to shared history, US President Donald Trump called China a World War II ally as he welcomed Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday ahead of summit talks.

But the historical reference was far from one-sided, with both leaders repeatedly referring to the joint fight against Japanese aggression as they sought to emphasise the long history of US-China friendship and the need to seek common ground.

“If we focus on our common interests, I’m confident there is much we can achieve,” Trump said in the White House foyer during the state welcome ceremony ahead of formal talks with the Chinese president.

“The pursuit of those common interests has connected our people across the vast oceans, across big tremendous distances, and many differences, and even made us allies in World War II,” he noted.

Trump went on to praise the “brave American pilots” of the Flying Tigers who had volunteered to “fight for China’s survival”, and said that he was happy to work with Xi in the same way.

“Just as our people worked together to win that war, President Xi and I will continue working together to forge a better future for both of our nations,” he said.

The Flying Tigers were American volunteer pilots who came to China in 1941 to fight Japanese forces alongside Chinese troops, before the US formally entered the second world war. They flew fighter missions against Japanese aircraft and helped to defend Chinese cities and supply routes during the conflict.

“They were just unbelievable,” Trump said.

His remarks came days after Japan – now a US treaty ally – renewed its call to remove the “former enemy state” clause from the UN Charter, and after Trump’s talks in New York with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

The clause “must be deleted”, Takaichi told the UN General Assembly in New York on September 22, pointing to a 2005 consensus resolution where world leaders had “resolved” to remove it.

The clause allowed allied states to act against defeated World War II enemy states without UN Security Council approval, but has been declared obsolete by the world body twice - in 1995 and 2005.

While Trump made no direct reference to Japan, Xi was more forthcoming – explicitly naming the country as he underlined China-US friendship forged in “blood and fire” during the war.

“During the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression, Chinese soldiers and civilians rescued hundreds of American pilots at the cost of hundreds of thousands of Chinese lives,” he said during Thursday’s state dinner.

“Such a friendship, forged in blood and fire, will surely live on through the generations.”

Xi also recalled the wartime “Hump” aerial resupply route over the Himalayas, citing the perilous joint operation as a testament to how the two countries united to sustain Chinese resistance against Japan.

The Hump became a vital lifeline for China after Japanese forces severed the Burma Road in 1942, cutting off military and humanitarian supplies, while Chinese soldiers and civilians helped to rescue hundreds of American pilots forced down along the route.

That cooperation came at a heavy cost for China, which suffered enormous civilian losses during the war, Xi noted.

It was the second time Xi had drawn on their shared history within hours. During the state welcome ceremony in the morning, he noted how soldiers on both sides had “fought shoulder to shoulder against fascist aggression”

“[The] Chinese people have never forgotten that part of history, nor have the American people,” he asserted.

The timing of the remark was particularly sensitive, given Japan’s stepped-up calls to remove the UN “enemy state” clause following its recent invocation by Chinese and Russian officials as tensions with Tokyo escalate.

Reacting to Takaichi’s speech at the General Assembly, the Chinese foreign ministry said on Wednesday that the clauses were “a legal mechanism in the UN Charter. For 81 years, these clauses have served to prevent the resurgence of fascism and militarism and defend the post-war international order. They are still relevant today.”

Trump’s use of the word “allies” in describing past US-China cooperation against Japan caused unease among Japanese media.

The Japan Times, for example, said the remarks were “likely to raise eyebrows in Tokyo, a US ally currently embroiled in a festering dispute with Beijing and facing pressure from Trump on both trade and defence issues”.

China-Japan ties have been marked by recurring tensions over Japan’s wartime occupation and atrocities in China, as well as disputes over Tokyo’s handling of that history.

Relations sharply deteriorated last year after Takaichi said that a Taiwan contingency could be a survival-threatening situation for Japan, justifying a military response. Beijing demanded an apology and imposed a slew of retaliatory measures, including curbs on rare earth exports.

Takaichi met Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on September 22, just ahead of Xi’s arrival in Washington. According to NHK News, she told Trump that she wanted to “seize the opportunity to demonstrate to the world” the strength of the US-Japan alliance.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States – Taiwan’s main international backer – do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

In Washington, Xi also highlighted the shared economic and cultural history of the two nations, tracing the relationship to America’s earliest years.

After the US gained independence, it “turned its eyes to China”, Xi said in his dinner address. The two countries began trading, he said, “exchanging goods to meet each other’s needs and draw on our complementary strengths”.

George Washington, he noted, had personally acquired a large collection of Chinese porcelain.

Xi then fast-forwarded to 1971, when “ping pong diplomacy” and the “political wisdom embodied in a small ball moving the globe” helped Mao Zedong, founder of the People’s Republic of China, and then-US president Richard Nixon open the door to rapprochement.

The redwoods Nixon later sent as a state gift “took root in Zhejiang province, where I worked for several years”, Xi added.

Trump’s speech was similarly filled with historical references to US-China friendship, as the gala dinner capped a day of pageantry, politics and protocol.

“President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” he said.

“Together, we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations.”

Trump invoked figures and events ranging from Sun Yat-sen, the founding father of modern China, to America’s declaration of freedom 250 years ago.

“Long ago, European explorers first discovered the American continent as they searched for a new way to reach China in the East,” Trump said, as he spoke about the first formal Chinese delegation to travel to the US and China’s first state dinner in Washington.

Despite the early historical reflections, including one about the first trade ships arriving on the banks of the Pearl River from New York, Trump took a midpoint detour to focus on the White House ballroom renovations – a frequent talking point for the president.

Going admittedly “off script”, Trump invited guests in the East Room to take a look at the new White House ballroom “in honour of President Xi and Madame Peng”, despite the project still being under construction.

The new ballroom would host more than 1,000 people, substantially more than the East Room, Trump said, claiming US presidents had wanted this for more than 150 years.

Trump then returned to the symbolism, gifting Xi a sculpture of a bald eagle that he said was made by an American artist and designed by him and the first lady, Melania Trump.

“The bald eagle is a national symbol of the United States and an embodiment of the free and soaring spirit of America, and we hope it will find a nice place, a wonderful place in Beijing,” Trump added.

The bald eagle has been featured on the Great Seal of the United States since 1782. It was officially designated the national bird of the US when Trump’s predecessor Joe Biden signed an act of Congress into law in December 2024.

In his closing remarks, Trump returned to history, referencing America’s 250th anniversary, marked on July 4 this year.

He raised a toast to his Chinese counterpart and his wife, as well as the long relationship between China and America that had bridged “thousands of miles and spanned hundreds of years”.

“May all of our people know a future of harmony, peace, and success,” Trump said.

The speeches were made to a packed room of invitees, including Chinese and US government officials, American business leaders and some Supreme Court justices.

Several prominent American CEOs made the guest list, including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Tesla’s Elon Musk, but no Chinese business leaders were present.

This stood in stark contrast to the Beijing summit in May, when Trump brought a delegation of nearly 20 top executives, many of whom were spotted at the state banquet hosted by Xi.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore minister Chan Chun Sing’s Mandarin diplomacy strikes China chord
item.description:
Singapore Defence Minister Chan Chun Sing’s use of Mandarin and Chinese philosophy in his speech at a major security forum in Beijing has won him praise on Chinese social media, while shedding light on how cultural familiarity and language can be diplomatic tools for the city state.

Videos of Chan at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum quoting ancient philosopher Mencius, or Mengzi in Mandarin, have gone viral on platforms such as Weixin and Baidu, with users hailing his command of the language and knowledge of Chinese thought.

Observers say that through resonating with the hosts, Chan managed to convey Singapore’s sterner message of a call for major powers to build trust instead of coercion, though there is a risk that linguistic bonds may raise the expectation for Singapore to sympathise with Beijing’s interests.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore Defence Minister Chan Chun Sing’s use of Mandarin and Chinese philosophy in his speech at a major security forum in Beijing has won him praise on Chinese social media, while shedding light on how cultural familiarity and language can be diplomatic tools for the city state.

Videos of Chan at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum quoting ancient philosopher Mencius, or Mengzi in Mandarin, have gone viral on platforms such as Weixin and Baidu, with users hailing his command of the language and knowledge of Chinese thought.

Observers say that through resonating with the hosts, Chan managed to convey Singapore’s sterner message of a call for major powers to build trust instead of coercion, though there is a risk that linguistic bonds may raise the expectation for Singapore to sympathise with Beijing’s interests.

At the summit on Wednesday, attended by delegates from nearly 100 countries and helmed by Chinese defence chief Dong Jun, Chan spoke mostly in English but switched to Mandarin occasionally and cited Mencius, saying: “Power may compel others to comply. But in the end, it is trust that truly wins others over.”

Social media users also drew comparisons between Chan and US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth, praising the former for displaying wisdom which exceeded that of a counterpart helming the military of a much larger country.

On Chan’s use of Mandarin, a Weixin user commented: “This minister is not an ordinary person; he knows Chinese culture like the back of his hand.”

Many also said Chan’s Mandarin was proof that the language and Chinese culture were gaining traction on the global stage.

The Singapore minister also urged superpowers to shoulder higher expectations from smaller states, stressing that countries should strengthen their own security but not at the expense of others.

“The more responsible major powers are, the less concerned small countries will be,” he said in Mandarin.

Singapore welcomed China’s aspiration to be a “responsible major country”, Chan said, adding that Beijing’s “reform and opening up” policy had contributed greatly to regional and global prosperity.

“As the People’s Liberation Army approaches its centenary, there is much potential for it to make a positive contribution to global stability and security,” he said.

Diplomatic move?

Observers hail Chan’s use of Mandarin and historical references as a clever diplomatic move, showcasing an appreciation and understanding of China and its culture.

Stefanie Kam, an assistant professor at S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS), described Chan’s switch to Mandarin as deliberate and a “clear effort to show cultural awareness and diplomatic tact”.

“For a defence minister to quote an old Chinese classic like this is quite strategic; it makes it hard for the Chinese audience to disagree because they would be disagreeing with their own classic,” she said.

Adam Liu, a political scientist and assistant professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, pointed out that Chinese leader Xi Jinping often quoted ancient Chinese teachings.

“Speaking in Mandarin and drawing on Mencius is a way of saying: I am addressing you in your own idiom, on your own terms. That tends to land well,” he said.
