Densely layered with winding copper traces that resemble an illuminated cityscape from above, these boards must survive extreme heat and power loads while shuttling vastly more data at far higher speeds, providing the physical foundations for the AI chips crunching numbers across the region’s data centres.

Thailand has attracted billions of US dollars of data-centre investment in recent years on the promise of booming AI demand – so much, so fast that the capital is arriving well ahead of the physical buildout of centres themselves.

But data centres are voracious consumers of water and electricity while creating comparatively few jobs, and domestic critics argue that beyond a handful of landlords, Thailand risks getting the environmental costs without the economic rewards.

Delta Electronics Thailand, the local arm of the Taipei-headquartered “grid to chip” manufacturer that became the first company on the Thai stock exchange to be valued above US$100 billion in February, is now eyeing a bigger prize – the power and cooling systems that keep those centres humming.

In the Thai electronics world, Delta is the gatekeeper to the big data-centre contracts – and as it grows, Thailand and its PCB makers are desperate to keep it on side.

“Thailand is moving beyond cost competitiveness towards higher-value industries,” Delta said in a statement, pointing to “advanced engineering talent, energy infrastructure readiness and supply chain depth” as the areas that, with “continued progress” and “pro-business policies”, could give the country a lasting regional edge.

Not everyone shares that confidence. Analysts the world over have grown increasingly nervous about an AI investment bubble and what its bursting might do to countries that have calibrated their industrial strategy on the boom continuing.

Even Delta admits to being “mindful” of “tariff uncertainty, engineering talent gaps, supply chain constraints, intensifying competition in AI infrastructure” and the difficulty of scaling manufacturing “while maintaining quality and profitability”.

Down on the factory floor, the constraints are more immediate. PCB manufacturing demands “a crazy amount of water each day”, according to Thailand Printed Circuit Association chief Phutana – and it needs to be “high purity”, competing directly with the needs of households and other industries.

“The next wave of investment is there. Everyone in AI servers and data centres is looking for new land to expand their facility.” he said. “The customers cannot wait.”

Layered on top of water constraints is a supply squeeze on laminates – the non-conductive, rigid base material that forms the physical foundation of circuit boards – and essential chemicals, a knock-on effect of the US-Israel war on Iran disrupting imports.

Thailand’s Board of Investment says it is exploring ways to free up more water and power, but critics argue the country is sprinting ahead of its own capacity to sustainably keep pace.

Somnuck Jongmeewasin, research director at environmental monitor and advocacy group EEC Watch, said automation had killed the jobs case for hosting PCB plants at all.

Relocation incentives meant most equipment was imported, he said, with little technology transfer or upskilling of local workers – turning Thailand into an “assembly line” for foreign capital rather than a genuine beneficiary.

“The factories that come here don’t use as much labour as they used to,” he said. “If they come from Chinese capital, they barely hire Thai workers at all. Blue collar [workers] are Myanmar, white collar are Chinese.”

Despite the scepticism, there is a more hopeful reading – one rooted less in job numbers than in opportunity.

Thailand’s education system produces precious few science, technology, engineering and mathematics graduates each year and PCBs may be one of its rare growth industries suited to hiring them.

“Thailand faces a severe shortfall in meeting the surging demand for PCB and electronics workers,” said Panisa Harnpathananun of the National Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation Policy Council in Thailand.

She estimated the sector would need roughly 225,000 high-skilled workers over the next five years, against the around 1,100 electronics engineers Thai universities produced in 2024.

“This deficit is driven by an ageing population and a structural educational mismatch,” Panisa said.

Plans are afoot to close that gap, including a “sandbox” scheme to fast track engineering degrees and proposals to retrain redundant car industry workers for PCBs and semiconductors.

In a country short on other engines of growth, Panisa said PCBs might offer “the most critical opportunity and the strategic careers” its graduates were likely to find.

item.title: [SCMP] Summits for all diplomatic seasons: how the US has set the stage for Xi Jinping
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US is his first to the country since 2023 and his eighth face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump. From informal walk-and-talks to a state dinner, Xi’s meetings across four American administrations show how personal rapport and official diplomacy reflect the growing complexity of US-China relations.

Xi’s first US visit as president: a shirtsleeves summit

In June 2013, just months after assuming the presidency, Xi travelled to the United States following a tour of Latin America.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US is his first to the country since 2023 and his eighth face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump. From informal walk-and-talks to a state dinner, Xi’s meetings across four American administrations show how personal rapport and official diplomacy reflect the growing complexity of US-China relations.

Xi’s first US visit as president: a shirtsleeves summit

In June 2013, just months after assuming the presidency, Xi travelled to the United States following a tour of Latin America.

According to then US president Barack Obama, “Our decision to meet so early [in Xi’s term] signifies the importance of the US-China relationship.”

Instead of heading to the diplomatic protocol-heavy capital of Washington, Xi’s historic first meeting with Obama took place at the Annenberg Retreat at Sunnylands, a 200-acre (81-hectare) estate in Rancho Mirage, California.

Originally built as a winter haven by publishers and philanthropists Walter and Leonore Annenberg – close friends of former US president Dwight Eisenhower – the estate holds a unique place in American history as a secluded sanctuary that has often hosted political heavyweights.

Its rare blend of luxury and isolation made Sunnylands an ideal setting for the summit. Without the rigid and pre-scripted constraints of traditional diplomacy, its selection was considered unusual.

But some suspicions remained. Xi and his delegation opted to stay at the nearby Hyatt Regency in Indian Wells rather than at Sunnylands, a move many in the American media attributed to concerns about possible US eavesdropping.

Over June 7 and 8, Xi and Obama engaged in more than eight hours of dialogue spanning two formal sessions, a private dinner and a morning walk, during which they took a break in the shade on a custom California redwood bench that Obama presented to Xi.

During the dinner, Xi reportedly toasted Obama with Moutai, China’s famed high-end liquor.

China said the summit established the groundwork for a “new model of major-country relations”.

White House officials later said the meetings built a stronger relationship between the two leaders, while yielding progress on important global challenges like cybersecurity, North Korea and greenhouse gas emissions.

Xi’s first US state visit: a packed ‘unforgettable journey’

In September 2015, Xi embarked on his first formal state visit to the US. His cross-country itinerary began in Seattle, where he met with senior American officials and business leaders, continued to Washington for formal diplomatic engagements with Obama, and concluded in New York to attend the 70th anniversary summit of the United Nations.

Upon their arrival in Washington on September 24, Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan were greeted on the tarmac by then US vice-president Joe Biden and his wife Jill Biden. That evening, Obama hosted Xi for a private dinner at Blair House.

Located across Pennsylvania Avenue from the White House, Blair House serves as the US president’s guest house for visiting diplomats and dignitaries. It is also where the US president-elect and first family live before taking the oath of office.

The next morning, official protocol commenced on the White House South Lawn with a full military arrival ceremony, featuring a traditional 21-gun salute. Following a joint press conference, Xi attended a diplomatic lunch hosted in the US State Department’s Benjamin Franklin State Dining Room.

The diplomatic high point came that evening with a lavish state dinner in the White House East Room. The guest list gathered about 200 prominent figures from Hollywood, Silicon Valley, international diplomacy and corporate leadership.

The menu, created by Chinese-American Anita Lo, highlighted American cuisine accented with Chinese nuances. Guests were served wild mushroom soup, poached Maine lobster, grilled cannon of Colorado lamb and a poppy seed bread-and-butter pudding.

During the toasts, Obama acknowledged lingering strategic differences while expressing hope that the two countries’ peoples would “work together like fingers on the same hand in friendship and in peace”.

Xi described the visit as an “unforgettable journey”, noting the warmth he encountered from the west coast to the east.

Following the state dinner, American R&B artist Ne-Yo delivered a performance of his hit “Because of You”, drawing applause across the room.

Mar-a-Lago summit: ‘family-style’ diplomacy

In April 2017, Xi met with Donald Trump, early in his first presidential term, at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, as both countries sought to steady a relationship frayed by months of friction.

Trump had spent his presidential campaign repeatedly hammering Beijing over trade practices and had further unsettled mainland Chinese leadership by accepting a congratulatory phone call from then Taiwanese leader Tsai Ing-wen, marking a sharp departure from decades of diplomatic precedent set in 1979.

The choice of Mar-a-Lago over a rigid White House visit was designed to create an informal backdrop for the two leaders to build personal rapport, echoing Xi’s 2013 Sunnylands summit with Obama.

As with the 2013 visit, Xi and the Chinese delegation did not stay on the grounds of the meeting venue. Instead, they checked in at the nearby Eau Palm Beach Resort & Spa.

The summit emphasised personal, family-centric diplomacy. Trump and his wife Melania Trump hosted Xi and Peng for a welcome dinner featuring pan-seared Dover sole, New York strip steak and Sonoma Chardonnay.

A stand-out moment of soft diplomacy came when Trump’s granddaughter, Arabella Kushner, who learned Mandarin from a Chinese nanny, sang the traditional folk song “Jasmine Flower” and recited classical Chinese poetry for the visiting couple.

However, the relaxed atmosphere was soon eclipsed by hard-power dynamics.

Over chocolate cake for dessert, Trump informed Xi that the US had just launched missiles against a Syrian airbase in retaliation for a chemical weapons attack. Trump later claimed Xi understood the move, but analysts said that Beijing rarely welcomed such unscripted surprises.

Filoli Estate summit: nostalgia to thaw a deep freeze?

In November 2023, Xi travelled to San Francisco to attend the 30th Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) economic leaders’ meeting and hold a summit with then US president Joe Biden. While Xi stayed at the St Regis Hotel near downtown San Francisco, the retreat itself was staged 48km (30 miles) south at the historic Filoli Estate, a secluded country house.

The summit came at a critical inflection point. Relations had plummeted to their lowest point in decades after Beijing severed high-level military contacts following then-US House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan in August 2022.

Tensions spiralled further in February 2023 when the US shot down a suspected Chinese surveillance balloon off the US east coast.

Against this backdrop, carefully choreographed personal optics were deployed to lower the temperature.

As Xi arrived at Filoli, Biden greeted him. Later, Biden pulled out a phone to show the Chinese leader a photograph of a young Xi posing in front of the Golden Gate Bridge during a 1985 trip as a county-level official.

“Do you know this young man?” Biden asked.

“I know,” Xi replied with a smile. “It’s me 38 years ago.”

“You haven’t changed a bit,” Biden quipped, drawing laughter from the crowd of staff and fellow officials.

Following a four-hour working session and lunch, the two leaders took a short walk together through the garden grounds.

Yet, tensions resurfaced shortly after the retreat concluded.

At a solo press conference, Biden repeated his view that Xi was effectively a dictator in the sense that “he’s a guy who runs a country that is a communist country that’s based on a form of government totally different than ours”.

The comment was captured alongside video of then-US secretary of state Antony Blinken visibly wincing in the audience, a moment that went viral worldwide.

item.title: [SCMP] Big picture or big deals? What the Xi-Trump summit holds for China and the US
item.description:
With the balance of power shifting between the US and China, the success of this week’s summit hinges not on headline-grabbing deals, but on practical, cautious consensus under a new strategic stability framework, according to Chinese researchers.

Media outlets in China have given heavy coverage to President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the United States, highlighting its “historic, milestone significance”. It follows US President Donald Trump’s Beijing visit in May.

Xi’s arrival in Washington on Wednesday dominated state media headlines, with images and footage of Trump greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac in a red-carpet welcome that included honour guards, a military band that played both national anthems, a 21-gun salute and a jet flyover.
item.content:encoded:
With the balance of power shifting between the US and China, the success of this week’s summit hinges not on headline-grabbing deals, but on practical, cautious consensus under a new strategic stability framework, according to Chinese researchers.

Media outlets in China have given heavy coverage to President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the United States, highlighting its “historic, milestone significance”. It follows US President Donald Trump’s Beijing visit in May.

Xi’s arrival in Washington on Wednesday dominated state media headlines, with images and footage of Trump greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac in a red-carpet welcome that included honour guards, a military band that played both national anthems, a 21-gun salute and a jet flyover.

In contrast, American media coverage of Xi’s arrival was more muted, as the major television networks continue a stand-off with the White House. Those in the White House pool – including ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC – have boycotted coverage of Trump’s public events in protest against his administration’s ban on several media outlets including CNN.

Camera crews had set up at Joint Base Andrews in anticipation of a court ruling to lift the ban but dismantled their equipment after a federal judge deferred his decision. As a result, the arrival of China’s top leader was captured by a handful of smaller digital outlets, The New York Times reported on Wednesday.

The media chaos underscores the deep partisan strife and divisions in the United States – turbulence that will make it harder for the visiting Chinese officials to set the tone for stable ties during Xi’s visit.

Trump has met several foreign heads of state since taking office in January last year, but the high-level airport reception for Xi is particularly unusual. Trump has never greeted a visiting leader at Joint Base Andrews, typically waiting to greet them at the White House instead.

When Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made her first visit to Washington in March, she was greeted at Joint Base Andrews by US Air Force Colonel Gary Charland, before going to the White House for talks with Trump.

This week, Takaichi met with Trump again during the UN General Assembly in New York, a day before Xi’s arrival in Washington.

Chinese media gave wide coverage of her landing at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport, highlighting that she was met by Japanese officials – with no red carpet, protocol delegation or US officials in attendance.

Sun Chenghao, a fellow with the Centre for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University, said Xi’s airport welcome “sends a clear political signal”.

“It shows Trump’s high regard for the Chinese leader and US-China relations, as well as his intent to advance further improvements in relations through head-of-state diplomacy,” Sun said.

Several major US think tanks noted in reports this week that the summit would be more of an exercise in diplomatic optics and unlikely to produce substantial progress beyond a temporary extension of the Busan truce. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday local time that the agreement would be extended past its November deadline to January 10.

But it is widely acknowledged that the summit is too important to fail – for both sides.

Trump’s sinking approval ratings at home are threatening to drag down Republicans in November’s midterm elections, with voters blaming his administration for high prices and a shaky economy.

Beijing is also facing domestic pressures. Beyond a sluggish economic recovery, the ruling Communist Party is preparing for its fifth plenum in October – a key gathering to discuss a new line-up of party leaders.

“Trump faces midterms in under six weeks. Xi returns home to begin a year-long run-up to next fall’s party congress, where he is expected to secure another five-year term,” Rush Doshi, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote in a report on Tuesday.

Chinese researchers argued that given the turbulence of relations in recent years, securing any tangible agreements or reinforcing existing frameworks would be an achievement in itself.

The two nations have a dense, concrete agenda spanning agricultural purchases, aircraft procurement, semiconductor technology, critical minerals and the potential extension of a tariff truce.

“Considering the overarching backdrop of competition and even conflict that has defined US-China ties for quite some time, reaching actionable agreements on these specific topics is valuable,” said Wang Yong, director of the Centre for International Political Economy at Peking University.

“It is simply unrealistic to expect a single, sudden ‘megadeal’ that resolves all problems at once.”

According to Wang, the most profound shift lies in Beijing’s increasingly proactive role in shaping the direction of bilateral ties. This stemmed from a substantive, realigning shift in the power balance, which had forced Washington to recognise Beijing as a peer competitor, he said.

Echoing this perspective, Shen Yi, executive director of the Centre for National Security Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, cautioned that anyone who overlooked this shifting equilibrium risked underestimating the value of strategic consensus and ignoring the progress made through established mechanisms.

Shen also noted that the vicious cycle of retaliatory tariffs had stopped, or at least had been suspended, indicating that the bilateral economic and trade consultation mechanism was functioning.

Furthermore, Washington was gradually coming around to Beijing’s view that bilateral trade and investment offered mutual benefits and that economic ties should not be entirely driven by security.

Shen said it would be impossible to iron out all the differences in one or two meetings and that summit diplomacy served mainly to set the overall tone.

“Even if the leaders agree only on broad principles, it provides a crucial guiding framework for pushing relations forward, particularly on the Chinese side,” Shen said.

“We can maintain cautious optimism that the ‘constructive strategic stability’ framework will be enriched with more substance through incremental, prudent progress.”

Wang said Beijing’s priority was to stabilise ties by reinforcing the new strategic framework agreed on at the Beijing summit with practical deals and communication mechanisms, while maintaining normal trade in non-sensitive business sectors.

However, execution remains a major hurdle. Shen said the basic challenge was a trust deficit, given the Trump administration’s record of reneging on commitments.

The stakes are equally high regarding Taiwan, which Trump has previously referred to as a “very good negotiating chip”.

The South China Morning Post reported earlier that Washington was considering delaying arms sales to Taipei ahead of Xi’s visit.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Shen said the “Taiwan card” was historically a by-product of an asymmetric power dynamic. That leverage, however, was fading as China’s strength grew and Beijing reserved the right to counter.

“Were the US to take a positive stance on Taiwan, would China not reciprocate?” Shen said.

Ultimately, across all flashpoints – including Taiwan – the core dilemma is not whether promises can be made, but whether Washington has the will and capacity to enforce them, according to Shen.

“A defining feature of US-China relations is that Beijing’s stance and actions on core national interests remain steady and predictable,” Shen said. “The uncertainty stems from the American side.”

Additional reporting by Caroline Lin and Orange Wang

item.title: [SCMP] Can the US and China verify an AI deal? Start-ups are starting to build the tools
item.description:
There are growing calls for Washington and Beijing to agree to slow down development of artificial intelligence. But even if they wanted to do so, how could they verify that the other side would do the same?

A group of researchers and start-ups is developing technology intended to make this a possibility, without relying on trust alone. Their proposed tools would allow third parties and governments to check some claims about how AI models are being trained or used – possibly without needing access to the AI models and infrastructure themselves.

This work is drawing attention ahead of Thursday’s meeting in Washington between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, at which AI is expected to be a topic of discussion. Still, advocates of the technology, known as “AI verification”, acknowledge that much work still needs to be done before the technology could be relied upon to monitor the vast computing facilities used to develop advanced AI.
item.content:encoded:
There are growing calls for Washington and Beijing to agree to slow down development of artificial intelligence. But even if they wanted to do so, how could they verify that the other side would do the same?

A group of researchers and start-ups is developing technology intended to make this a possibility, without relying on trust alone. Their proposed tools would allow third parties and governments to check some claims about how AI models are being trained or used – possibly without needing access to the AI models and infrastructure themselves.

This work is drawing attention ahead of Thursday’s meeting in Washington between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, at which AI is expected to be a topic of discussion. Still, advocates of the technology, known as “AI verification”, acknowledge that much work still needs to be done before the technology could be relied upon to monitor the vast computing facilities used to develop advanced AI.

Nonetheless, they argue that a recent surge in interest from both policymakers and industry is likely to rapidly accelerate progress in the field.

“The level of interest has just kind of exploded in the last few weeks and months,” said Connor Dunlop, head of policy and strategy at San Francisco-based Lucid Computing, a leading AI verification start-up.

On Monday, leaders and representatives from 20 countries including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong issued a public letter that called for greater controls on frontier AI systems. The letter cited recent incidents in which cutting-edge AI systems from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic circumvented safeguards and conducted cyberattacks.

The call to action proposed the creation of an international governance institution that could perform AI verification, without specifying how this should be done.

According to Tom Milton, co-founder of UK-based AI verification consultancy Amodo Design, there are two main claims that Washington and Beijing would likely want to be able to verify as part of any future international AI treaty: whether a data centre in the other country is training a new AI model or merely serving an existing one, and whether an AI model being served is the one it is purported to be.

The reason is that data centres only serving existing AI models – a process called inference – rather than training new ones would mean that the country is not advancing AI capabilities. Meanwhile, the governments might also want to verify that a data centre in the other country is running a model known to be safe instead of an unsafe one.

One proposed verification mechanism is called “recomputation”, in which an AI system’s outputs are checked by running the same calculation again on a different system, with the same inputs and settings, to see if the same result is achieved.

According to a report from the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, equipping data centres with such verification technology could only cost a small percentage of the facility’s upfront costs, given that the recomputation process would rely on commodity hardware. Compute costs arising from the verification process could also be kept low by only testing a small random sample of all AI activity in the facility.

Both Amodo and Lucid Computing have begun testing such solutions in real-world settings. Earlier this month, Lucid began 18 months of “adversarial” testing of its recomputation solution on a cluster of 16 Nvidia H100 semiconductor chips in Sweden, provided by the government-funded research institute RISE.

Amodo is also in talks to scale up its testing to a cluster of 128 graphics processing units (GPUs), said Milton. He acknowledged, however, that the field is still in its infancy, with the need to validate such solutions at the scale of cutting-edge data centres, which have hundreds of thousands of GPUs installed.

Political and commercial barriers also present a real challenge, with both China and the US pouring trillions of dollars into advancing their AI capabilities amid their fierce tech rivalry.

Chinese state media in recent weeks have dismissed US industry giants’ calls to “pace” the development of AI as efforts to entrench their industry-leading positions and suppress China’s AI development.

Bad blood between the two countries has affected proposed technical solutions to AI governance issues before. Beijing last year rebuffed suggestions that US chipmaking giant Nvidia could install technology in its chips to verify their location as part of efforts to comply with US export controls. Chinese officials feared the technology could be used by Washington to sabotage the country’s AI infrastructure.

Still, the first step would be to let politicians know that technical solutions to verify AI development are there if they want them, rather than have them wrongly believe that verification is impossible on a technical level, said Milton.

He pointed to US-Soviet nuclear arms control agreements in the 20th century, when the two countries overcame high levels of mutual distrust by using multiple verification mechanisms, including satellites and unique identifiers.

“Obviously the technology is not perfect yet … but it doesn’t have to be to help build early confidence that an agreement is possible,” said Milton.

Amid growing signals from industry and policymakers that such technology is needed, investors are also showing signs of interest. Last month, Israeli AI verification start-up Attestable raised US$20 million in seed funding with major investors including Silicon Valley hedge fund Altimeter Capital.

The firm is applying a cryptographic technique called “zero-knowledge proof” (ZKP) to its proposed verification solution, using mathematics instead of recomputation to allow parties to verify that a response to a query was provided by the exact AI model specified.

The technique, already used in blockchain technologies, is called “zero knowledge” because it does not reveal information about the underlying model or data. This could help allay the fears of governments and companies about leakage of sensitive information, said Miro Pluckebaum, founder of the Singapore AI Safety Hub (SASH).

“The sentiment within the research community is that something workable can be built within six to 12 months,” he said. “The myth as we see it is that verification would be impossible.”

SASH, a non-profit organisation based in the Asian city state, is trying to promote international collaboration on AI verification as early as possible to ensure that the field is not viewed as the exclusive tool of any country, said Pluckebaum.

While Beijing’s stance on AI verification remains unclear, Pluckebaum said that the open-source nature of the field’s early results would allow Chinese researchers to also test the underlying cryptographic techniques and contribute to their hardening.

Amodo, Lucid and SASH have all committed to open sourcing their research findings.

Growing signals from politicians that this technology is needed will also help with one of the field’s main bottlenecks today, which is a lack of talent, said Lucid’s Dunlop. He estimates that there are only around 50 people working on AI verification technology globally.

“I think there should probably be 100 times more people working on this, given what’s at stake,” he said.

Government support could also spur greater participation among leading tech giants. To underpin a global AI treaty, AI verification would require compatibility with the wide range of chip and model configurations available in the market today, covering not just US but also Chinese chips and frontier AI models from the likes of Huawei Technologies and DeepSeek.

“Ideally we would see many teams working on verification, both inside and outside frontier AI companies, trying out their solutions on as many different ‘stacks’ as possible,” said Dunlop.

Dunlop, Milton and Pluckebaum are all in New York this week at the United Nations General Assembly to explain their work to politicians and experts.

“There’s already been a lot of progress with an extremely small number of people working on this,” said Dunlop. “Let’s ramp that up and see how much more progress we can make.”

item.title: [SCMP] Xi lands in US for high-stakes summit with Trump amid deep tensions
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping landed at Joint Base Andrews late Wednesday afternoon after a 15-hour flight where he was met on the tarmac by US President Donald Trump in an unusual move for a top American leader as the two sides extended a trade truce.

The closely watched visit – Xi’s first summit in the United States in 11 years – comes as the two nations grapple with a host of thorny issues beneath the flowery language and statements of friendship, including artificial intelligence, critical minerals, tariffs, Ukraine, the Iran war, Taiwan and military relations.

Xi, accompanied by first lady Peng Liyuan, senior Chinese official Cai Qi, Foreign Minister Wang Yi and several other Chinese dignitaries, were greeted with a modest arrival ceremony.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese President Xi Jinping landed at Joint Base Andrews late Wednesday afternoon after a 15-hour flight where he was met on the tarmac by US President Donald Trump in an unusual move for a top American leader as the two sides extended a trade truce.

The closely watched visit – Xi’s first summit in the United States in 11 years – comes as the two nations grapple with a host of thorny issues beneath the flowery language and statements of friendship, including artificial intelligence, critical minerals, tariffs, Ukraine, the Iran war, Taiwan and military relations.

Xi, accompanied by first lady Peng Liyuan, senior Chinese official Cai Qi, Foreign Minister Wang Yi and several other Chinese dignitaries, were greeted with a modest arrival ceremony.

“China and the United States are great nations, and their peoples are great peoples.,” Xi told Trump, according to Xinhua News, in a written statement conveyed to the US president. “The two peoples have enjoyed long-standing friendly exchanges, and their interests are deeply intertwined.”

After an “unscheduled” second day of negotiations on Wednesday between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, Bessent told Fox News that the two sides agreed that a trade truce set to expire on November 10 had been extended by two months. China’s embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

There was a several-minute delay after Xi’s plane landed as US personnel awkwardly steered a rolled-up 100-foot (30.4 metre) red carpet on a small trolley to a position beneath the Chinese aircraft.

The trolley almost tipped over before staff righted it as, directed by a functionary seeking to get it properly aligned, unrolled the floor covering as military personnel on their knees removed creases and protocol chief Hong Lei and Wang watched from the aircraft doorway.

Trump and first lady Melania then emerged from the “Beast” presidential limousine at 6pm and greeted Xi and his wife as they descended the jetway.

The two couples chatted for a few minutes then watched a 21-person honour guard and listened as the Chinese and American national anthems played, cannons fired a salute and two B-1 bombers thundered overhead before the two sides parted in opposite directions after roughly 15 minutes.

The concise ceremony also included a rendition of “Fanfare for the Common Man”, a short, loud, ceremonial piece featuring brass instruments and percussion traditionally played to announce someone important.

Xi’s arrival has been framed as a mirror image of Trump’s summit in Beijing four months earlier. The time on the ground will be limited to 48 hours; there will be no side visits outside the capital; and the programme will include a state dinner and military viewing. The carefully choreographed visit is in part meant to underscore respect and the equality of the two wary competitors, an issue of particular importance to Beijing.

A couple of big differences with the reciprocal May trip, however: there were no Chinese business executives accompanying Xi on his “special plane,” a modified Air China Boeing 747-8 Intercontinental, landing under grey skies on Wednesday, amid questions over whether they will appear at all.

In contrast, Trump brought along two US chief executives aboard Air Force One in May, part of a 17 CEO contingent that reportedly arrived without giving Beijing much notice.

Sources say the limited ongoing clarity over a Chinese CEO delegation is due in part to the lack of progress on a proposed Board of Investment and to bilateral communication problems.

Xi urged the two sides to find common ground.

“Both sides should move towards each other to foster a stable relationship characterized by cooperation as the mainstream, measured competition, manageable differences, and the prospect of peace,” Xi said, according to Xinhua.

A second difference relative to China’s detailed hosting has been the shortfall in planning and logistics done by a distracted US administration in recent weeks compared with China’s near-compulsive approach.

While the White House has been juggling its Iran war of choice, a Canadian trade showdown, Trump’s record-low popularity and a pending November election, summit preparation has also been frustrated by the small number of US decision-makers and an impetuous president inclined to rip up plans on short notice.

This was seen in part by the addition of a second day of “unscheduled” negotiating by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng on Wednesday just hours before Xi landed. Traditionally, intense summit planning begins up to six months in advance with deals and deliverables are largely decided weeks ahead of the date.

High on the agenda for a meeting with low deliverable expectations will be some movement on artificial intelligence, a key part of Bessent’s portfolio and a source of rising tensions in recent months as the two nations tout competing visions, promote rival companies and adhere to different regulatory environments.

Another entrenched problem almost certainly on the agenda is Iran. Trump badly wants China’s help in forcing Tehran to the bargaining table to end a war he started nearly seven months ago. But China, which was buying over 80 per cent of Iran’s exported crude before the conflict, has balked at turning the screws on its Middle Eastern partner.

Asked by reporters if Iran would be discussed, Trump said: “I’ll be talking about that and many other subjects but it’s all coming along, including that.”

Another key issue involves the 90 per cent of global rare earth mineral processing that China controls. Beijing has meted out sparingly to US companies this essential component of most tech products since Liberation Day when Trump threatened tariffs of over 80 per cent on the Asian export behemoth. This has given China enormous leverage over the US and fundamentally changed the power dynamic between the world’s two largest economies, clout that China is in no hurry to give up.

The two could also discuss further extending the one-year trade truce agreed to late last October in South Korea and now deferred until January. This could give the two leaders leeway to announce a longer truce at an Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen later in November or at a Group of 20 summit in Miami in December.

Framing the tussle is a disagreement over how long an extension is acceptable. China would like to see it last through early 2029 when Trump’s tenure ends while Washington believes shorter, more frequent pacts give it greater leverage to ensure China follows through.

Another dynamic in the background of this week’s talks is the divergence often seen between an increasingly pro-China Trump and China hawks in his administration and in Congress.

Asked by reporters on Wednesday evening whether he agreed with Joseph Weirsky, his counterterrorism acting director, that fentanyl coming from China amounted to war by other means, Trump suggested the issue was largely settled.

“That’s not good,” he said. “But they’ve been tariffed and really penalized very strongly.”

Trump’s tarmac greeting on Wednesday marked the first time a US president welcomed a foreign leader at an airport in 11 ‌years, when President Barack Obama welcomed Pope Francis in 2015 at Joint Base Andrews. And before that, over a half century earlier, former US president John F. Kennedy met then British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan at Andrews Air Force Base, its former name.

item.title: [SCMP] Donald Trump built a US$5 million White House helipad. Don’t expect Xi Jinping to use it
item.description:
US President Donald Trump has been very eager to show off to Chinese leader Xi Jinping his new US$5 million White House helipad, his latest bid to stamp his image on Washington.

While Xi might act impressed and compliment the US president on his latest building project – part of Trump’s bid to match Xi’s splendour-filled hosting four months ago in Beijing and show the Chinese that Americans can build infrastructure too – do not count on Xi actually trying it out with a chopper ride this week during his first state visit to the US in 11 years.

“I’m sure Xi will appear impressed, like, oh, this is really remarkable. I’m never getting on,” said Yun Sun, senior fellow with the Stimson Centre. “I don’t think the Chinese security protocol will allow for a helicopter take-off or landing or for Xi Jinping to take a ride.”
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump has been very eager to show off to Chinese leader Xi Jinping his new US$5 million White House helipad, his latest bid to stamp his image on Washington.

While Xi might act impressed and compliment the US president on his latest building project – part of Trump’s bid to match Xi’s splendour-filled hosting four months ago in Beijing and show the Chinese that Americans can build infrastructure too – do not count on Xi actually trying it out with a chopper ride this week during his first state visit to the US in 11 years.

“I’m sure Xi will appear impressed, like, oh, this is really remarkable. I’m never getting on,” said Yun Sun, senior fellow with the Stimson Centre. “I don’t think the Chinese security protocol will allow for a helicopter take-off or landing or for Xi Jinping to take a ride.”

“They know how dangerous that thing is. It’s a flying coffin.”

There is no formal published statute or civil aviation law in China explicitly barring top leaders from flying in helicopters, experts said.

But a de facto ban is enforced as part of strict internal protocol maintained by the Central Guard Bureau, which oversees security for the nation’s top leaders.

Last month, Trump gushed for several minutes during a media show-and-tell about the helipad’s “flawless” black California granite, compressive strength and “million-year life”.

From Trump’s perspective, the helipad is easy to show off. Its swift completion stands in sharp contrast to his other legally embroiled projects: the estimated US$800 million White House ballroom expansion, the US$100 million 250-foot (76.2-metre) “Arc de Trump” and the troubled US$15 million reflecting pool renovation.

The US president appears to fully expect that his Chinese counterpart will be wowed.

“We’re building a helipad, a beautiful helipad … It could be ready by the 21st [of September],” he told reporters last week, noting Xi’s coming visit. “The planned White House ballroom will not be completed in time, but the helipad will be.”

Trump has expressed his belief that Xi – a leader the US president has variously described as his “friend for life,” “central casting, brilliant guy” and “tough, smart and a great leader” – would be particularly impressed by the 100-foot-diameter “Seal of the President of the United States” insignia affixed to the helipad surface.

“It’s got the seal of the White House on it in granite, in carved granite. It’s really a beautiful thing,” he said.

During his presidency, Xi has overseen some 25,000 miles (40,000km) of high-speed railway in China; about US$1 trillion in Belt and Road Initiative projects spanning 150 countries; building of the ongoing US$580 billion Xiongan New Area smart city; and the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, a new Beijing airport and the world’s longest bridge and tunnel sea crossing, to name a few.

Some have suggested that an added benefit of the helipad from Trump’s perspective is that it would allow foreign dignitaries to avoid street demonstrations.

“Trump had the heliport built over the Rose Garden for Xi, so he didn’t have to look at protesters en route in the motorcade from Andrews,” said Kevin Nealer, a principal with the Scowcroft Group consultancy and a former member of the President’s Intelligence Advisory Board. “Xi hates copters and avoids using them at home.”

Nealer was referring to Washington’s Joint Base Andrews, where in a highly unusual, high-honour move, the president announced that he would greet Xi in person on the tarmac, a role usually reserved for lower-level officials.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has reportedly told overseas diplomats when arranging presidential trips that its top leaders travel almost exclusively by fixed-wing aircraft for long distances and in armoured motorcades for shorter distances.

The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Helicopters are statistically at greater risk of mechanical failure and rotor-related accidents. And China believes they are more difficult to defend against missiles or other attacks than vehicles or planes equipped with heavy armour, missile defences and secure jammer capability, according to a former US military official.

During their 2019 summit in India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi travelled to the meeting site by helicopter, while Xi drove some 35 miles in his custom Hongqi limousine, adhering to Chinese rules disallowing leaders from using helicopters, Beijing’s foreign ministry said at the time.

For the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea in 2018, other leaders travelled by helicopter or boat owing to local crime rates and infrastructure.

In its lead-up, however, China funded and built a dedicated multi-lane highway called “Independence Boulevard” leading to the local parliament, allowing Xi to travel in a bulletproof Hongqi limousine along the pre-cleared roadway.

At the 2015 Apec summit in Manila, Xi declined a helicopter lift availed by other heads of state from Ninoy Aquino International Airport directly to coastal hotels and the summit convention centre meant to circumvent the city’s infamous traffic.

Lower-level officials and People’s Liberation Army officers use choppers. And senior officials have deployed them during inspections and disaster responses, including several flights by then-Chinese premier Wen Jiabao during the 2008 Sichuan earthquake.

But by most accounts, the unofficial ban was cemented when Xi took power in 2012.

Chinese helicopters have had a mixed record.

In their infancy, they relied heavily on Soviet technology. In the 1950s, Moscow provided blueprints of its Mil Mi-4 “Hound” transport chopper that formed the basis of the Harbin Z-5, China’s first serial production model.

Efforts to ramp up production coincided with the Great Leap Forward and the Sino-Soviet split, however, and early models saw severe manufacturing defects, including rotor-blade metal fatigue, structural vibrations and substandard metallurgical quality in engine and transmission parts.

“China’s record of engine maintenance is not great,” said Dennis Wilder, a senior fellow at Georgetown University and former CIA officer. “I did once fly to the Great Wall on an old Soviet helicopter. Never again.”

But quality has improved significantly, and its Z-20 multi-role platform, seen as resembling the Sikorsky Black Hawk, and Z-10 and Z-19 attack helicopters are credited with significantly upgrading the PLA Army’s air assault capabilities.

Along with greater reliability, China has built an export market. Its selling points include a lower price tag and deals largely free of human rights or other political stipulations relative to Western suppliers, although some countries including Cameroon and Pakistan have reported operational and maintenance issues.

In the nearly unimaginable eventuality that Xi did agree to fly on a US helicopter in Washington, he might well insist that another very special passenger tag along, analysts said.

“If Xi Jinping really takes a ride, Trump will have to be on the plane with him. But I think the Chinese default answer is going to be no,” Sun said. “He’s only here for one day. It’s a very short trip.”

item.title: [SCMP] Boeing’s 200-jet China deal could hinge on Trump-Xi talks: industry insiders
item.description:
When President Xi Jinping travels to Washington later this month, he is likely to hop over the Pacific on a Boeing 747 jumbo jet. He will also hold the fate of the American planemaker’s much-touted China deal in his hands.

Beijing agreed to purchase 200 Boeing aircraft during US President Donald Trump’s visit to China in May. But the deal has yet to materialise – and the negotiations could depend on the outcome of Xi’s coming meeting with Trump in the Oval Office, according to industry insiders.

With key details still needing to be agreed – especially the time frame for any purchases – the final deal was likely to be shaped by the broader economic and political bargaining between the two presidents, they said.
item.content:encoded:
When President Xi Jinping travels to Washington later this month, he is likely to hop over the Pacific on a Boeing 747 jumbo jet. He will also hold the fate of the American planemaker’s much-touted China deal in his hands.

Beijing agreed to purchase 200 Boeing aircraft during US President Donald Trump’s visit to China in May. But the deal has yet to materialise – and the negotiations could depend on the outcome of Xi’s coming meeting with Trump in the Oval Office, according to industry insiders.

With key details still needing to be agreed – especially the time frame for any purchases – the final deal was likely to be shaped by the broader economic and political bargaining between the two presidents, they said.

“It’s all about the three Ws: whether, when and what,” said a retired aviation executive, who previously oversaw fleet management and engineering at one of China’s largest state-owned airlines.

“With Trump’s Beijing trip in May and the 200-jet deal announcement, the ‘whether’ part is now agreed upon … But a call on when to place actual orders needs to be determined by Chinese trade officials, a vice-premier or even needs a nod from the top leader.”

In May, China agreed to purchase at least 200 Boeing planes as a key deliverable from Trump’s state visit – the country’s first deal with the US aviation giant for nearly a decade.

At the time, China’s Ministry of Commerce said aviation was an area where both nations could deepen “mutually beneficial, win-win” cooperation, adding that the two presidents had reached an “important consensus”, without elaborating.

The White House, meanwhile, called the 200-jet deal an “initial purchase”, with Trump claiming that China could commit to buy up to 750 aircraft if certain conditions were met.

The deal has appeared to stall in the months since. No details have been released regarding the number or models of Boeing aircraft involved, nor which Chinese airlines will be placing orders.

No Chinese government agencies have provided updates on the deal’s status. There have not been any related announcements from Chinese airlines, either.

But the silence does not mean the deal is off. Xin Qiang, a professor with Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, said Beijing had been facing growing domestic calls to buy from Boeing in recent months – and that Xi’s US trip could present an opportunity to advance the deal.

“Many US-focused analysts and government departments have since this year made stronger recommendations to the top leadership [to place orders with Boeing],” Xin said.

“With Xi’s coming visit to Washington – which in itself is a sign of continued easing of tensions – the decision to advance the purchase makes perfect sense,” he added. “The reality is that there are very few high-end industrial products – Boeing aircraft being a prime example – that China has the need to buy and the US is able to sell.”

In May, Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg cautioned that “official orders” from China “will come later in the year”, as the company was still working to iron out specifics with Chinese clients.

“My primary objective was to reopen that [Chinese] market … and we accomplished that,” said Ortberg, who was part of the US business delegation that accompanied Trump on his trip to Beijing.

“I think people focused a bit too much on the initial quantity,” he continued. “The order is a good start.”

In July, Ortberg told CNBC that Boeing was in the process of finalising the contracts. “China will allocate the total quantity to individual airlines, then we negotiate the contracts with individual airlines,” he said. “We are in the process right now. We will have contracts here shortly.”

A source with flag carrier Air China confirmed the airline was involved in discussions over a potential Boeing order.

“We are involved in this, but it is not something on which individual airlines can make a final decision – it requires coordination and advancement by the National Development and Reform Commission,” the source said, referring to China’s top economic planning body.

Beijing was currently maintaining a “silent period” regarding the deal status, the person added. “Our approach is to proceed and be ready, without making public comments.”

The last time China bought from Boeing was in 2017, when a US$37 billion, 300-plane contract was announced during Trump’s first state visit to Beijing.

But the US firm was later frozen out of the world’s second-largest economy, as US-China tensions rose and Boeing experienced a string of safety issues. In the meantime, China has directed huge orders to the company’s European rival, Airbus.

Airbus has landed a series of fresh contracts in China in recent months, with Chinese airlines including China Eastern, China Southern, Air China, Xiamen Air and Spring Airlines signing formal agreements for hundreds of European-made aircraft.

Switching wholesale to Airbus, however, would not be easy for China. Several Chinese airlines – including China Eastern-owned carrier Shanghai Airlines and Air China subsidiary Shandong Airlines – have all-Boeing fleets. These carriers have needed new aircraft for years to renew their ageing stock, according to independent aviation analyst Li Hanming.

“China does need Boeing,” said the retired airline executive, who declined to be named as he was not authorised to speak with the media. “The art of the deal [for Beijing] is to balance commercial need with geopolitical bargaining.”

For some market observers, one of the concessions Beijing will want to extract before proceeding with any Boeing deal will be securing supplies for China’s domestically made C919 passenger jet.

While the C919 is assembled in China, many of the plane’s parts are sourced from overseas – including the Leap-1C engine, which is produced by CFM International, a consortium between America’s GE Aerospace and France’s Safran.

In May, China’s commerce ministry said the US would “provide China with adequate supplies of engines and spare parts” for its aviation firms. The Boeing deal could be tied to firming up that guarantee.

For the executive, the coming Xi-Trump meeting could provide an opportunity for “breakthroughs” in such negotiations. “What’s better than the two presidents meeting face-to-face again?”

Additional reporting by Zhu Wenqian

item.title: [SCMP] Former WTO head Pascal Lamy on the EU’s China choice: get a rebalance, or go protectionist
item.description:
Pascal Lamy served two consecutive terms as director general of the World Trade Organization from 2005 to 2013. Before that, he spent decades in various French government roles, contributing to the building of the European Union. He was chief of staff to European Commission president Jacques Delors from 1985 to 1994, and European trade commissioner from 1999 to 2004.

Here, he discusses Europe’s trade tensions with China, the continent’s growth potential problem and the WTO’s need for stronger enforcement mechanisms.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
item.content:encoded:
Pascal Lamy served two consecutive terms as director general of the World Trade Organization from 2005 to 2013. Before that, he spent decades in various French government roles, contributing to the building of the European Union. He was chief of staff to European Commission president Jacques Delors from 1985 to 1994, and European trade commissioner from 1999 to 2004.

Here, he discusses Europe’s trade tensions with China, the continent’s growth potential problem and the WTO’s need for stronger enforcement mechanisms.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

In France, many have expressed doubts about the future of free trade. Former finance minister Eric Lombard said last year that free trade is dead, killed by the US and China. Do you agree?

No, free trade is not dead. And by the way, I never ever use the expression “free trade”. I’ve been in this business for decades now, and I’ve never used this expression, which is for one simple reason: it is misleading. Trade is never free. It is either more or less open. Free trade is not dead, it was never born.

The question is whether the previous decades we’ve seen, which have consistently moved in the direction of more open trade – this being evidenced by the growth of the volume of international trade – whether this volume is still growing or not.

If you look at the numbers, which we have to do, especially if we discuss trade, trade is still growing in volume. This means that trade is more open than it used to be. But there is a catch: the growth of international trade, at least benchmarked against the growth of the economy, has slowed.

The slowdown can be attributed to many reasons. Starting with the main factor, which is the fragmentation of production systems that has led to the global supply chains that now span the world. The expansion of the supply chain, the fragmentation of production, has limits. It is efficient and productive at some stage, for some products in some conditions.

But we’ve probably reached a stage where the efficiency gains stemming from the multi-localisation of production systems are slowing, with decreasing yields, like any productivity curve. At some stage you reach a level where economies of scale are less important than at the beginning of the process.

Reason No 2 is that trade openness trends are now counterbalanced by trade-restricting attitudes among a number of international trade players, given the United States’ position and the huge growth of China’s exports and surplus. There are also growing reactions in some places to the expansion of international trade for social or environmental reasons. Its growth is slowing because of various reasons, but overall, international trade is still expanding.

So what, in your view, are the main problems facing the global trade system?

As Europeans, we have three problems in global trade today. A small one, a medium-sized one and a big one.

The small one is the US. The US has embarked on a protectionist crusade, which stems from the deep belief by US President Donald Trump that tariffs are the Swiss army knife of the 21st century economy, which is not so. The ones who pay the price for that at the end of the day are US consumers. But even if he makes a lot of noise about his attempt to de-globalise the planet, this will not happen.

Then we have the medium-sized problem, which is that the World Trade Organization, the international institutional engine for opening trade, is not working in the way it used to work.

This is mainly a problem of organisation. The fact that the US de facto left the WTO. The fact that although a new dispute-settlement system has replaced the previous one, it does not work with the US. The fact that all decisions, including on minor issues, are still taken by consensus, and that the secretariat is not allowed to exercise its potential authority based on its first-class expertise. And that third one, in my view, is the main reason.

The WTO has not been able to develop new trade-opening agreements in areas where international trade has moved a lot – digital trade for instance, which matters a lot for services – and we should always remember that international trade is goods plus services, plus the invisible part of international exchange trade today, which is about trillions of pieces of data.

Then we have a big problem, which is China, which is a problem for every country. It’s a huge problem for us Europeans because we have a mega trade deficit, growing in an unsustainable way. And for the European Union, addressing this problem is a very tough task.

The main reason behind it is the macroeconomic imbalance of China, which is structural, which Chinese authorities have not addressed, do not want to address, although they’ve been saying for many years that Chinese growth should be rebalanced – with more domestic consumption.

China already has plans to make itself self-sufficient in food – why not in services too later?

It is not happening, and we are in a situation where industry in China produces twice as much as it consumes in industrial goods, hence the debate about overcapacity.

China now has comparative advantages in most of the supply chains in manufacturing. Not yet in agriculture, and not yet in services. But I believe China wants to get there, following a policy developed by the Chinese government, mostly since 2010.

China already has plans to make itself self-sufficient in food – why not in services too later? Because of the strategic concept that China has to become more self-reliant. In energy, in manufacturing, in technology, China has, so far, been formidably efficient in constructing self-sufficiency; other sectors will come.

This is a major systemic problem, because trade opening has always been based on the theory of comparative advantage. I do something better than you do. You do something better than I do. We have a rational interest to trade, which is, by the way, the philosophical basement of the WTO.

The WTO is built with the mission of promoting open trade because opening trade is a good way to create growth and welfare, because it is based on the efficiencies stemming from the exchange of comparative advantage, the international division of labour.

This game seems to be over with China today. China has gained comparative advantages all along the industrial production chain for various reasons. Some of which are legitimate. They have a huge market. They have a formidable education capacity, and this is something where they have built their own comparative advantage, and they have a political regime that allows a level of strategisation, coordination, multilayered intervention, which is incredibly efficient.

This has a lot to do with the political regime, and this is something, of course, that we Europeans would hesitate to emulate for a variety of reasons. China also uses its state-owned sector, its state-owned banks, its budget to heavily subsidise sectors – which is not in the spirit of a fair international division of labour – benefiting from the fact that WTO disciplines on subsidies, state support and state ownership, have remained very weak.

This is the situation we Europeans now have to face. It’s not just a bit different from what it was before, where maybe we could adjust the recipes here and there with a bit more or a bit less of anti-dumping or countervailing duties. The size of the deficit is now out of reach of the normal instruments which the WTO provides to regulate trade and absorb import shocks. With China trade dynamics, we are entering a new world, a new paradigm, which opens a lot of questions about WTO disciplines.

The French government’s high commission for strategy and planning has called for 30 per cent tariffs on all Chinese imports, and Paris and Berlin have expressed a desire for fast measures rather than long WTO-style investigations. Is China right that the EU is turning protectionist, and would Brussels be better off saying so openly, telling Beijing it has no choice if it wants to keep its industry?

You are absolutely right, we Europeans are reaching a moment of truth with trade and China. Either we can convince China to rebalance the system and decrease its exports or we will have to go protectionist. Let’s test the willingness of China to seriously address the problem. This is the first option and in my view, the good option, provided China shows signals that it is ready to address the problem. This is Plan A. We need a Plan A, but we also need a Plan B.

Some in the US argue it was a mistake to let China into the WTO. You were the one who closed the EU’s bilateral accession deal in Beijing in May 2000. With hindsight, was the mistake letting China in, or was it what the West failed to write into the terms? Would you sign the same text today?

Yes and no. I think letting China into the WTO was the right thing to do precisely because it brought about an exchange of comparative advantage, and China wanted to join the WTO to benefit from an insurance policy against export restrictions. China paid a high price for subscribing to this insurance in opening its economy.

China opened its economy as a developing country, roughly three times more than its developing country equivalents at the time and more than Russia 10 years later. The maximum tariff China accepted on goods was 10 per cent.

China made a big effort, which led to a big divide within the Chinese leadership: between those who said [former paramount leader] Deng Xiaoping was right, we have to open to better combine Chinese characteristics and Western characteristics, and this is the way to go to grow China more rapidly, represented by [former premier] Zhu Rongji.

And then there was another camp, more conservative within the leadership, that thought that opening trade with Western countries might make China more vulnerable. The first camp won and China opened its economy, which became very profitable for the rest of the world during the next 10 years.

There was an end to that, which roughly coincided with the aftermath of the 2008 crisis, where the Chinese government switched back to a more ideological approach. Self-sufficiency became the new strategic priority to reach total strategic autonomy in the future.

The Chinese economy was, from then on, run on a geopolitical basis, not on a geoeconomic basis. China then pushed, very successfully, to go from low-wage value addition, which was a comparative advantage 25 years ago, to where China is now, competing with the US on the frontiers of technology.

To answer your question, we were right to let China in, and we were wrong not to reinforce the WTO’s rules on subsidisation and state support before China entered. The reason we did not do that – “we” being the big shots at the time: the US, EU and Japan – was we thought that we might end up restricting our ability to support our champions such as Airbus or Boeing, or Japan’s programmes to foster innovation.

We were subsidising a small part of our economy, and we mistakenly remained defensive. We did not forecast how large a part of the Chinese economy would remain de facto under state control and support. Or the importance of the state-owned sector, which had actually shrunk in the first 10 years after China joined the WTO and then grew again from 2010 on.

We did one thing right, which was letting China in, which benefited everybody for quite a bit of time, but we did not properly identify the risk that China’s state-owned system would drive the economy in such an efficient way, including in subsidising a strategic industry heavily at the beginning, then creating a lot of competition. The best example is what we see in electric vehicles, which were heavily subsidised at the start, and now there’s cutthroat competition within China until the system stabilises with maybe a handful of surviving producers.

How do you see the current EU-China negotiations, with Brussels demanding “tangible progress” by October? Can both sides still avoid a trade war? Some argue China and the EU are already in one. Do you agree?

First of all, I don’t think we should use the word “war” about trade. I’m talking to you from Ukraine, I was a naval officer in my youth. I know the meaning of the word “war”, and we shouldn’t use it lightly.

We have trade frictions, we have trade disputes, we have trade tensions. There are trade tensions between China and the US. There are trade tensions between the US and Canada that were triggered by Trump because he thinks Canada should become a new US state. We have trade tensions between the EU and China, which stem from the fact that we have such a huge and growing deficit with China.

The European Union today still has a trade surplus as a whole. What does this mean? This means that, overall, the EU, in what is traded today, can compete with the rest of the world. We have a trade surplus vis-a-vis the US. We have a trade surplus with many of our trade partners, except with China. If you remove €350 billion (US$407 billion) of trade deficit between the EU and China, we have a big trade surplus, which means that we are competitive with anybody on this planet except China.

Now there are reasons for that, which I can totally understand. It stems from what I describe as Chinese organisation: they’ve been extremely good at gaining a comparative advantage all along the supply chain, including, for instance, in critical materials, which is extremely important for electrification and the economy.

Of course, China did not do it for the pleasure of doing it. China built a comparative advantage in critical materials because China wanted to electrify, and the reason China wanted to electrify was that it wanted to be less dependent on oil or coal or gas imports.

We Europeans have to try to convince China that it is in their interest, as it is in our interest, to reduce our trade deficit massively

It’s not because China suddenly became a believer in the necessity to reduce emissions – although I’m happy that China is doing this. China built the comparative advantage in rare earths to become less dependent on fossil fuel imports. They built this control, which now gives them a monopoly that they can weaponise.

We Europeans have to try to convince China that it is in their interest, as it is in our interest, to reduce our trade deficit massively, not just by €10 billion or €20 billion. We have a €350 billion trade deficit, and this cannot be addressed by a little bit of this or a little bit of that. The problem is the magnitude of the problem.

Either we can convince China to address this problem, which will need a lot of unilateral market power exercised by the Chinese side to export less, or we will have to look for other options. I hope we do not have to do this. I interpret the Sefcovic mission [aimed at rebalancing trade] and the time between now and the October deadline as a test of whether China is serious about addressing this or not.

As usual, the EU gave priority to negotiation, consultation, discussion. We are not the US, and nobody wants to play Trump on the EU side, we are not brutal. We try to understand problems. We try to address this peacefully, respectfully and through negotiation. But if that does not work, we have to look at other options.

Europe says it wants to be neither dependent on the US nor overwhelmed by China. Is a third position actually available, or does reducing exposure to one side mean aligning with the other?

Solving this issue will not, by itself, solve Europe’s No 1 problem, which is growth. The EU’s growth potential is half of that of the US, one-third that of China and one-quarter that of India. This is a worrying situation, and one we will have to work hard on to improve our competitiveness. But becoming more competitive will not solve our China trade problem, given its magnitude and the threat it represents to the survival of some of our production systems.

How did we get here, to this level of trade imbalance? Is that a story about Chinese competitiveness or industrial policy?

It is overall competitiveness, all along the supply chain, which leads to this. If you have a competitive advantage all along the supply chain, there is no more fair trade. You are absolutely right, this is the result of Chinese competitiveness.

Chinese competitiveness has various sources, which I mentioned: the size of the market, the organisation of the state and its capacity to subsidise efficiently. It’s not just subsidising, because you can subsidise inefficiently too. The Chinese system has learned to use subsidising efficiently, giving the industrial policy a coherent logic: what strategic priorities, what the state does, in which sector, what the regions do and what the municipalities do. There is a lot of competition within. It’s a formidable mix of non-competition, which is the state, and competition, which is a part of the economy.

What would China have to do to prove that it is a defender of multilateralism and free trade?

Beef up domestic consumption. Stop pushing, pushing and pushing for increasing manufacturing, which is way beyond the consumption capacity of Chinese consumers. Chinese households have a saving rate that is way too high, coming from the fact that they want to hedge against old age, children’s education spending, pensions and so on, so China also needs to create somewhat of a welfare state.

Secondly, import more, export and subsidise less. Or in the case of subsidies, renegotiating the WTO rules on subsidies – what we in the EU call “state aids” – to level the playing field, which is now heavily unbalanced in the subsidisation capacity between China and Europe. And convince China to invest more in Europe in areas where tech transfers and ownership arrangements are doable, which was China’s position 30 years ago. Boosting Chinese investment in Europe is, in my view, part of the solution.

item.title: [SCMP] Could Chinese explorers have settled New Zealand before the Maori?
item.description:
For generations, the narrative of New Zealand’s human settlement has held that Polynesian voyagers – the ancestors of the Maori – arrived and settled the islands in the 13th century, followed by European explorers in the 17th century.

This timeline underpins New Zealand’s history and its political model. The Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between the British Crown and about 540 Maori chiefs, served as New Zealand’s founding document, paving the way for Britain to claim sovereignty and incorporate the country into the British Empire.

Outside the halls of universities and government institutions, two independent researchers are on a quest to discover pre-Maori Chinese presence in New Zealand.
item.content:encoded:
For generations, the narrative of New Zealand’s human settlement has held that Polynesian voyagers – the ancestors of the Maori – arrived and settled the islands in the 13th century, followed by European explorers in the 17th century.

This timeline underpins New Zealand’s history and its political model. The Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between the British Crown and about 540 Maori chiefs, served as New Zealand’s founding document, paving the way for Britain to claim sovereignty and incorporate the country into the British Empire.

Outside the halls of universities and government institutions, two independent researchers are on a quest to discover pre-Maori Chinese presence in New Zealand.

Citing underwater shipwrecks, carbon-dated structures and anomalous artefacts as evidence, scholar and author Sheng-Wei Wang has proposed a theory that a Chinese “treasure ship” fleet met its end there around 1435-1436 owing to the impact of a meteorite.

Wang also contends that Chinese mining and trading activities date back to 190BC, challenging the accepted 13th-century Maori settlement timeline and suggesting that these pre-European contacts have been overlooked or suppressed.

While mainstream academics and Maori groups voice scepticism, Wang and others argue that acknowledging this lesser-known history could reshape New Zealand’s national identity and improve its relations with China.

Speaking this month at the Commonwealth of World Chinatowns conference in Penang, Malaysia, Wang raised the question of whether fleet leader Zheng He died in New Zealand during his final voyage.

Zheng was a Chinese admiral who led seven massive naval expeditions across the Indian Ocean during the early Ming dynasty.

While Zheng is widely believed to have died in 1433 in Calicut, or today’s Kozhikode, a coastal city in southern India, after setting sail in 1431, his exact fate was still unverified, Wang said.

“We know that Zheng disappeared during the seventh voyage. There were different kinds of proposals about what happened to him.

“Could he [have died] while he visited the Americas? Or in India near Calicut – he was ill, and because the weather was so hot that his body couldn’t be brought back to China? Or just like in this case that he died because of the unexpected tragic event?”

Wang said a meteorite was believed to have crashed in the Tasman Sea, southwest of New Zealand.

“My estimate of the date is around 1435 or 1436, when a squadron of the Ming Treasure Fleet reached New Zealand after they explored the Americas during their seventh voyage to the Indian Ocean and beyond,” she said, adding that the impact carbonised all the ships in the harbour.

“One of the possibilities is that the whole fleet disappeared there, which may have included Zheng because there is no satisfactory evidence to show where or when he died,” she said. “There was no convincing record, so I am proposing that.”

Wang’s research draws on field surveys by the late independent British surveyor T.C. Bell, who used magnetic anomaly surveys to detect underwater and buried structures throughout New Zealand. The method measures local variations in the Earth’s magnetic field to locate metal objects.

“When Bell went to New Zealand for surveys in 2003, 2006 and 2017 … he was able to detect 78 shipwrecks of various dimensions,” she said.

“Twenty-four of them are of the super-junk or treasure-ship size. They are around over 100 metres (328 feet) in length, about 40-something [metres] in width, and all these large ships are characterised by their unique double-fluke anchors.”

The specialised Chinese anchor consisted of a central wooden bar connected to two huge rocks, Wang said, and was designed to cut into the sea floor to secure the ship in place.

She proposed a route for Zheng’s last voyage that “went to America for several months and came back by rounding the southern part of South America, Cape Horn. They followed the Humboldt Current, then the [South] Equatorial Current and they could have gone to Asia”.

“Naturally they would have been brought westward to New Zealand.”

Wang described the seventh fleet as on its way back to China. Carbon dating results indicated a Chinese presence in New Zealand predated the seventh Ming voyage, extending from as early as 190BC through 1600, Wang said.

She pointed to a “scrub-covered, small-moated Chinese fort platform” at Governors Bay, South Island, which was carbon-dated to 190BC, and the years 800 and 1600.

“In my opinion, in Bell’s opinion, [New Zealand] became the headquarters of Chinese business trading ships.”
